requirements.text:
**BroadcastResult:**

```
BroadcastResult
├── outputs: map<string, ChannelOutput>         # on_event() results per channel
├── delivery_outputs: map<string, ChannelOutput> # deliver() results per channel
├── reentry_events: list<RoomEvent>             # Response events for reentry loop
├── tasks: list<Task>                           # Accumulated tasks
├── observations: list<Observation>             # Accumulated observations
├── metadata_updates: map<string, any>          # The targets' room metadata updates,
│                                               # merged (§10.1 step 15)
├── blocked_events: list<RoomEvent>             # Chain-depth-blocked events
└── errors: map<string, string>                 # Per-channel error messages
```

requirements.applies: §10.2 Broadcast Pipeline; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Solicitation.** Step 3c asks a channel to act. For transport channels that
is unconditional; for intelligence channels the set is narrowed by the
event's address and by the room's agent-response policy (§19.3). Narrowing
solicitation MUST NOT narrow *visibility*: the two filters are independent,
and an event hidden from a channel by §7.3 is hidden whether or not it was
addressed to it. An unsolicited intelligence channel is not called at step 3c
at all — not asked, and not told — and rebuilds what it missed from the
timeline when it is next solicited (§19.3.2). In a room a discussion holds
(Section 19.7.5), no agent is solicited at step 3c: the discussion reads the
event's names from the text it commits with, once its `BEFORE_BROADCAST`
hooks have run, queues the agents the event asks for, and gives each its
turn later, a rerun planned for that agent alone.

requirements.applies: §10.3 Edit and Delete Processing; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
When an event has type EDIT or DELETE, the framework MUST perform additional
validation and state updates before broadcasting. The validation is §10.1
step 8a, and it runs on every pass that commits an event: an inbound
message's, a response's (§10.1 step 14), that of an event a hook injects
(§9.4) and a direct injection's (§10.5).

requirements.applies: §10.3 Edit and Delete Processing; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Validation:**

1. An event is an edit when its type is EDIT and its content an
   `EditContent`, a delete when its type is DELETE and its content a
   `DeleteContent`. A type and a content that disagree name no target that
   can be checked, and are refused with `target_event_not_found`; so is a
   change held anywhere else, at any depth (an edit's new content, a
   composite's part), which the commit would write on its target, or a
   channel apply natively, without this check.
2. The framework MUST verify that `target_event_id` references, read under
   the room lock, an event of the same room that is not `BLOCKED`, not
   deleted (`metadata.deleted`) and not itself an edit or a delete;
   otherwise `target_event_not_found`. An edited event may be edited again.
   A delete of an event already deleted is refused: a client that retries a
   delete gives it an idempotency key, and the retry is answered as the
   first (§13.4).
3. An event's author is, for an event that travelled OUTBOUND (a channel's
   own output, an agent's response), the channel itself, whatever
   participant it names: a channel never speaks as a participant. Otherwise
   it is the participant its sender id names on its channel (Section 5.5);
   else the sender id on its channel; else nobody. Authorship does not
   depend on the participant's status: a participant who left, or was
   banned, is still the author of their messages.
4. For `DeleteContent` with `delete_type = SENDER`, or `EditContent` with
   `edit_source = "sender"` or null, which is the sender's, the framework
   MUST verify that the sender is the original author of the target event:
   a change whose event or target has no author is refused with
   `identity_required_for_edit`, and two authors that differ with
   `not_original_author`. An agent edits its own responses, and no one
   else's.
5. For `DeleteContent` with `delete_type = ADMIN`, the framework MUST verify
   that the sender has administrative authority as the participant it is on
   its channel (Section 5.5): an OWNER or an AGENT, neither LEFT nor BANNED.
   Otherwise `not_authorized`: an id that names an owner on another channel
   grants none, and a channel's own output holds no participant's
   authority, whatever participant it names. A sender who names no one is
   refused with `identity_required_for_edit`.
6. For `DeleteContent` with `delete_type = SYSTEM`, or `EditContent` with
   `edit_source = "system"`, which claim the system's authority, the framework
   MUST verify that the event comes from a hook, since no channel is of the
   type SYSTEM (§6.2); otherwise `not_authorized`. `edit_source` is
   `"sender"`, `"system"` or null: an implementation that accepts another
   value checks it as the sender's (rule 4), never as the system's. An EDIT or a DELETE a hook injects (§9.4) is the
   hook's, whatever source it names, and makes a SYSTEM change only (a SYSTEM
   delete, an edit whose `edit_source` is `system`): any other, one that claims
   the sender's or an administrator's authority included, is refused
   `not_authorized`, so a hook never edits or deletes in a participant's name.
7. If validation fails, the framework MUST reject the event: nothing of it
   is stored, and no hook runs on it. A refused inbound message returns a
   blocked result with the reason (§10.1 step 8a), a direct injection
   raises (§10.5), and a refused response or injected event is logged at
   warning level.

A hook's modify keeps what the validation checked (§9.4): the target, the
`edit_source` and the `delete_type`, and the kind of content. The hook's new
content of an edit and its reason of a delete stand, unless that new content
holds a change, which leaves the original's. A replacement of an edit by
content of another kind is taken as the edit's new content, so a hook that
redacts an event as text redacts an edit too; one that is or holds a change,
in a composite included, leaves the original's. A replacement of a delete by
content of another kind leaves the original's.

requirements.applies: §10.3 Edit and Delete Processing; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**State updates** (applied only after BEFORE_BROADCAST hooks allow the event —
a hook that blocks the EDIT/DELETE MUST leave the target event unmutated):

1. On successful EDIT: the commit writes the target with
   `EditContent.new_content` as the hooks left it and `metadata.edited =
   true`, the target's other metadata kept. The EDIT event itself MUST be
   stored in the timeline.
2. On successful DELETE: the commit writes `metadata.deleted = true` on the
   target, its other metadata kept. The DELETE event itself MUST be stored
   in the timeline.
3. The change, its target's update and the room's counters MUST be one
   transaction (§14.3): a commit that fails leaves neither the change nor
   the target's update, and one whose target is gone by then fails whole.
   The target's update keeps the `delivery_results` the store holds, which
   only the record of its deliveries writes (§14.3).
4. An accepted change is committed with its own visibility, narrowed by its
   source binding's (§7.3), narrowed again to its target's: a correction of
   a message an advisor alone saw never reaches the customer. An injected
   change reaches those of its targets that could see the target.
5. The change's delivery set reads the target as the commit left it.

A change the kit's persistence policy keeps out (§14.3) is the exception to
the change's own row and to the one transaction of items 1 to 3: no row of
it is stored, and its target is written alone, as items 1 and 2 say
(`write_change_target`, §14.1), the room's counters unmoved.

requirements.applies: §10.3 Edit and Delete Processing; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**What a channel is handed of a deleted event.** A soft-deleted event's
content is withheld from every history a channel is handed (§7.5 rule 8):
the context a channel parses a message with, and the one each target of a
broadcast is told and delivered with. The event is there with an empty text
in place of what was said, and without the provider's original payload
(`source.raw_payload`), which holds the text. An edit of a deleted event has
its new content and its raw payload withheld alike, since it holds a version
of the deleted text. The event keeps its id, index, type, its source with
the provider's message id, its thread, its metadata with `metadata.deleted`,
and its `channel_data`: the delete that follows names an event the reader
holds, a transcript keeps the event's place, the reader tells a deleted
event from one that said nothing, and a channel that deletes natively still
finds the provider's references. An empty text rather than a placeholder: a
placeholder's words would be the framework's, in one language, read by a
model as the sender's line (§6.4), while the mark already says what
happened. The stored record keeps its content, and so do the contexts hooks
receive: the store and the hooks are the host's, which owns the record, and
a hard delete (below) is how a host removes it.

requirements.applies: §10.3 Edit and Delete Processing; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Mutation triggers:** After a successful EDIT the framework MUST fire
`ON_EVENT_UPDATED` with the mutated target event; after a successful DELETE it
MUST fire `ON_EVENT_DELETED`, each with the target as the commit left it.
Firings follow the async-hook locking rule of §10.1: they come once the room
lock is released, before the change's `AFTER_BROADCAST` hooks. A blocked or
refused EDIT/DELETE MUST NOT fire either trigger. Whatever the change's
origin (an inbound message, a response, an event a hook injects, a direct
injection) and whether or not any channel receives it:

- The trigger's context MUST hold the room's history and counters
  (`event_count`, `latest_index`) as the change's commit left them: the
  target as rewritten, every event committed ahead of the change during its
  hooks, and the change itself in the history, the newest event, at its
  committed index and as its hooks left it.
- The trigger's payload is the target, not the change, and its hooks'
  filters (§9.1) MUST apply to that payload: `channel_types`, `channel_ids`
  and `directions` read the target's source, and a filter on event types,
  where an implementation offers one, reads the target's type. A hook
  registered for an SMS channel's events observes the correction of an SMS
  message whichever channel or agent made it, and one filtered on EDIT
  events observes none, since a target is never a change (Validation,
  rule 2).

These triggers let observers (e.g. maintainers of denormalized projections
over the timeline) see every stored-state change regardless of origin.

requirements.applies: §10.3 Edit and Delete Processing; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Direct mutation (host-owned):** The framework SHOULD also expose direct APIs
— `update_event(room_id, event_id, content|source|metadata)` and
`delete_event(room_id, event_id, cascade_replies)`, each naming the caller's
`organization_id` or none — for host applications that own authorization on
their own surfaces. Direct `update_event()` replaces the provided fields
wholesale and adds no `edited` marker; the record of the event's author stays
the one fixed at its commit (§10.1 step 12). Direct `delete_event()` is a HARD
delete, which MUST remove:

```
delete_event(room_id, event_id, cascade_replies = true) → list<string>
├── The target
├── Its replies, unless cascade_replies is false: the events whose
│   parent_event_id names the target (no self-referential FK protects
│   them), one level deep: every path that commits an event roots its
│   parent at that commit, each streamed row at its own (§10.1 step 8), so
│   an answer to any reply of the target names the target itself, and one
│   level is the whole thread. An event whose
│   parent names one of the replies, which no path writes any longer, is
│   not removed with them
└── Whatever cascade_replies says, the changes of the target and of its
    replies, the replies it removes: the EDIT and DELETE events whose
    target_event_id names one of them. An edit holds its target's
    corrected content, which a host deleting the message means to remove,
    and a change of an event that no longer exists changes nothing. A
    change of a change is not removed with them
```

An event that is both a reply of the target and one of those changes is
removed once, among the replies, or among the changes when `cascade_replies`
is false.

It MUST return the ids it removed, in this order: the target's, then its
replies' in index order, then the changes' in index order. Both calls MUST
serialise against inbound processing via the room lock, whatever the room's
status, its due timers applied first (§5.1): a change to what the room
stored is no new event. Both MUST fire the corresponding mutation trigger
once the room lock is released, with the room's context read then:
`ON_EVENT_UPDATED` once, with the event as it now stands, and
`ON_EVENT_DELETED` once per event removed, in the order of the ids returned,
each with the event as it was stored, so that a projection over the timeline
sees every row that went. A failure of that read does not fail the call: the
change is stored and stands (§13.6), the implementation logs the failure,
and the triggers fire with the context the call held under the lock. A room
or a target the store does not hold, another room's event included, MUST be
a no-op that fires nothing: `update_event()` returns null and
`delete_event()` no id. So is a room of another organization than the one
the call names, or of none when it names one, with nothing written in it,
its due timers included (§17.2); a call that names no organization reads the
room unscoped. An update that changes nothing writes nothing and fires
nothing, and returns the event as stored.

requirements.applies: §10.3 Edit and Delete Processing; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**A direct change from the room's work.** A direct `update_event()` that
changes something, a direct `delete_event()` of an event the room holds, and
a regeneration of the last answer (Section 13.6) are no pass, and have no
budget of their own to bound a hook that repeats them. Made from the body of
an ASYNC hook a cascade fires once an event's delivery set has run (§10.1
step 16, the mutation triggers above), each MUST draw one of that cascade's
hook calls (§8.3) before it writes, the regeneration as it starts; past them,
it MUST raise a reentry-loop-cap error and write nothing. Made from other
work of the room, a delivery, a turn, a locked section or an admission, it
draws nothing. Its own triggers run on the budget of the room's work it is
made in, the cascade's whose frame it runs in, or on a budget of its own
when it comes from outside the room's work: the mutation triggers' hook
bodies draw their calls on it, and, in a room no discussion holds, a
regeneration's cascade its passes and its hooks' calls; a regenerated turn a
discussion gives has a budget of its own (Section 19.7.5 rule 11). A
regeneration made within a turn or a hook's body is at least as deep as a
call made there (§8.3): its re-broadcast, and in a discussion the turn it
queues, stand at that depth, so its answer is one deeper. A hook that updates
its event on every update, or deletes on every deletion, therefore stops at
the cap, and one that deletes and regenerates after every answer at the depth
limit. A change the implementation itself makes for the room's work, such as
restoring held messages (§11.7.6), runs its triggers on that work's budget
alike.

requirements.applies: §10.3 Edit and Delete Processing; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Broadcast behavior:**

During broadcast, for each target channel:

1. If the target channel's `capabilities.supports_edit` is true (for EDIT events)
   or `capabilities.supports_delete` is true (for DELETE events), the framework
   MUST deliver the event natively.
2. If the target channel does NOT support the operation, the framework MUST
   apply transcoding fallback (see Section 6.6).
3. An intelligence channel is handed the change as any target, and MUST
   open no turn on it: a change is no message a turn may answer, its fallback
   text (`[Message deleted]`, or `Correction: …`) no request. No speak policy
   is asked about it (Section 6.4), and a turn of the channel that runs
   meanwhile is not handed it as a message (Section 6.4, "A message for the
   running turn"): a channel that takes the room's turns one at a time keeps
   its place in line, for no turn. A strategy that takes an
   agent's turns (Section 19.7) asks none on it either: it is no task for a
   producer, reviewer or worker. The agent answers the next message, in the
   room the change left: the target as edited, or the message deleted
   withheld (§7.5 rule 8). A host that reacts to a change does so with
   `ON_EVENT_UPDATED` or `ON_EVENT_DELETED` (above).
4. A transport that hosts a model (a realtime voice channel, a conference
   with a realtime model plugged in, Section 12.4) is an agent too (Section
   8.3): it MUST inject the change into the model's session silently, as an
   event a hook injected (Section 9.4), and so it does for any event it
   takes into the session that opens no turn (a notice, a reaction: Section
   6.4). The session learns the correction, the deletion or the notice, and
   the model answers nothing until the next message.

requirements.applies: §10.4 Inbound Room Routing; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
When an inbound message arrives without a pre-determined room_id, the framework
MUST route it to an appropriate room.

```
InboundRoomRouter (interface)
└── route(channel_id, channel_type, sender_id, metadata,
          organization_id, identity) → string | null
        # organization_id: the organization the caller acts for, null when
        # it names none; identity: the sender's, or null. Returns a room id
```

The router is given the organization the caller acts for and the sender's
identity, which the framework reads once per message before the first route,
scoped to that organization (`resolve_identity`, §14.1, §17.2), so that the
router and the check made when the sender is recorded (§10.1 step 2) name
the sender alike; a message with no address reads none, and its router is told
null for its sender. The default strategy
searches that organization's rooms only, every room when the call names
none. A router answers a room id, or null; the id is held to step 2's rules
whoever gave it: another organization's room fails the message, and a room
missing from the store is created with the id. A custom router's answer is the
host's decision, as a provided `room_id` is: a room that binds the channel is
held to the conditions below under the lock, and one that does not has the
channel attached, whoever writes (§10.1 step 2), which is how a new channel joins
a conversation. A router SHOULD NOT route on a field the sender chooses without
authenticating it.

requirements.applies: §10.4 Inbound Room Routing; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Default routing strategy:**

1. Find the newest ACTIVE or PAUSED room whose binding of this channel names
   the sender (§5.7); otherwise, the newest ACTIVE or PAUSED room where a
   participant who is the sender was reached through this channel (its
   `connected_via` names the channel, whatever the participant's status: a LEFT
   or BANNED record still says whose conversation the room is). Within each
   lookup the sender is named by their address or by their identity: a binding
   names them when its correspondent is either, or, naming none and not
   `group`, when its recipient is their address (§5.7); a participant record,
   when its id or its `identity_id` is either, or when it is the record of
   their own the identity pipeline left them pending under on this channel
   (§11.2). The newest room either name
   finds wins, so an older room found by the address does not hide a newer one
   found by the identity; a member the integrator added under their identity is
   found by an address linked to it. The newest is the most recently created,
   and of rooms created at the same instant the one with the greatest id, so
   the answer never depends on the order rooms are read in. An id names its
   participant only on a channel they are reached through (Section 5.5), and an
   identity reaches every channel its person uses: a room found through a
   participant record, by the address or the identity, is the sender's only
   when that participant was reached through this channel, so a message is not
   carried into a room of another channel, whose messages would then go out on
   this one. A PAUSED room is the sender's conversation as an ACTIVE one is:
   its timer paused it for inactivity, and the message's delivered commit
   resumes it (§5.1); the newest room wins whatever its status. On a chat
   channel the address routed by is the chat the message was posted in, not its
   sender (§5.7), here and in step 3.
2. If found → return that room.
3. Otherwise, if the channel is bound to exactly **one** room step 3 reads, and
   that room admits the sender (below) → return that room. Step 3 reads the
   ACTIVE rooms, and the PAUSED rooms whose binding of the channel is declared
   `group` (§5.7): a group's conversation is the channel's, and its next
   delivered message resumes it (§5.1). Any other PAUSED room is no one's to be
   admitted into, and does not count among the rooms the channel is bound to.
4. If not found → return null (framework creates a new room).

requirements.applies: §10.4 Inbound Room Routing; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Step 3 admits one conversation.** Step 3 is what routes a channel dedicated
to a single conversation. It is deliberately narrower than "the channel is
bound to some room": on a number shared by many correspondents, the one ACTIVE
room bound to it is someone's conversation, and a second correspondent routed
into it would be stored there, answered with that conversation as context, and
answered at that conversation's address. The room admits the sender only when
its binding of the channel is declared `group` (§5.7), or when all of the
following hold:

- the binding names no participant, or names the sender;
- on a channel with a recipient (§5.7), the binding holds none as §5.7 reads
  it, or its recipient names the sender (their address, or the identity it
  resolves to): a room that delivers to someone else is their conversation, and
  a value that is not a recipient (§5.7) is someone else's address, so a room
  the integrator opened with its recipient written `true` admits no sender;
- no participant of the room other than the sender was reached through this
  channel (its `connected_via`, whatever its status): a member the
  integrator added on the channel says whose conversation the room is before
  they have written;
- the room has received nothing on this channel from another sender: no
  stored event of the channel, a `BLOCKED` one excepted, whose source names a
  participant other than the sender.

The sender is known to the room by their address, by the identity the store
resolves that address to (`resolve_identity`, §14.1), and on the channel by
the record of their own the identity pipeline left them pending under
(§11.2): a participant or an event named by any of them is the sender's own.
When the sender is recorded under the lock (§10.1 step 2), a binding naming
the identity of a participant reached through the channel who is the sender,
as an advisor's resolution names it (§5.5), names the sender too. A message the framework writes
itself, under the sender `system` (a `deliver()` to the room, an
orchestration cue), names the room it writes to and no correspondent: it is
never recorded on a binding, and it counts as no one heard. A message that
would be routed by that name is therefore a sender borrowing it, on a channel
whose senders choose their id, and it is refused before it is routed (§10.1
step 2): nothing is written and no room opened. Under that sender a message
naming its room is the caller's, and enters: the room is the host's choice, so
a host naming the room MUST set the sender itself, never from what a client
sent. No sender is known by that name:
a router asked about it directly finds nothing at step 1, and step 3 admits it
through a `group` binding only; an identity with that id names no sender, a
channel's form does not rewrite the name on a binding, and a delivery status
for it finds no room. A member added under an id that
is neither the address nor a resolvable identity cannot be told from a
stranger, so the room is closed to step 3: its correspondent's messages are
routed by `room_id`, or the address is linked to the identity
(`link_address`, §14.1), unless the binding's recipient names them (§5.7),
in which case step 1 finds them through it.

A message with no sender address, its id empty or blank, is admitted by step 3
through a `group` binding only, whichever strategy chose the room: what it wrote
counts as no one heard, so a later sender admitted to that room would read it.
The binding step 2 makes for it when it is routed, in a room created for it or on
a channel attached for it, names `system` as its correspondent and no
recipient: that name is no sender's, so no one else is admitted through it. A
binding naming no one and holding no recipient that an ON_ROOM_CREATED hook made
in that room takes the name too. Such a room counts among the channel's rooms, so
a room the host prepared for the channel's first sender is no longer the one room
step 3 reads once such a message has come: no one reads the other's words, and
the next sender gets a room of their own. Two such messages hold a room each. A
recipient the integrator gives replaces the name, as on a binding naming no one
(§5.7), and a room the caller named for such a message names no one.

When step 3 admits a sender through a binding that names no participant and is
not `group`, the framework records the sender on it (§10.1 step 2): step 1
then finds them on their next message, and step 3 admits no one else. A room
the framework creates for an inbound message is bound to its sender from the
start. The sender is recorded when the message is routed, under the room lock,
before anything of the message is processed: two first messages arriving
together cannot both be admitted, since the second finds the binding naming
the first and is routed again. A room created for a routed message is held to
the same check once its creation hooks are over, so the first message leaves it
when another sender was recorded there while the hooks ran. Under that lock the
framework checks again the admission that chose the room, not only the binding
(§10.1 step 2): someone
else may have been heard on the channel, or reached through it, since the
router read the room, and recording the sender there would send that person's
answers to them. What the room heard is read from its whole timeline on the
channel, refused events set aside, however long ago it was written, as step
3 reads it. A room CLOSED or ARCHIVED by then, one PAUSED by then that is
neither the sender's conversation by step 1 nor bound to the channel as
`group`, or one no longer admitting the sender, is no longer the message's:
nothing is written, and the message is routed once more, a second failure
giving it a new room. The wait for that lock is bounded by `process_timeout`
(§13.6); past it the message is refused as a process timeout, never let in
unrecorded. A message a hook later refuses has been routed all the same:
routing decides which conversation a message belongs to, a hook what becomes
of it.

requirements.applies: §10.4 Inbound Room Routing; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**A delivery status follows its message.** A provider's delivery status that
names no room is routed by the same rule: the newest ACTIVE or PAUSED room
whose binding of the status's channel names its recipient, as step 1 finds a
sender's, unless it names no participant and its channel reads it as delivering
to someone else; else the one ACTIVE room bound to the channel unless its
binding names another correspondent (its participant, else its recipient, a
value that is not a recipient included, §5.7); else none. A status is no
activity, and resumes no room (§5.1). It is never dispatched with the context of one room among
several.

Every `ON_DELIVERY_STATUS` hook runs in that room, its filter unread, a status
being no event; the call that dispatched the status returns while they run. A
status naming a room is dispatched in it if it exists and, for a caller acting
for an organization, is that organization's; one naming a room that is missing
or another organization's is dispatched nowhere. A provider's webhook, once
read, is a message received unless its direction says `outbound` or its event
type `message.sent` or `message.finalized` (a direction `inbound` wins),
processed as an inbound message keyed by the provider's message id; else a
delivery status on its channel when its direction is `outbound` and its event
type `message.sent`, `message.delivered`, `message.failed` or
`message.finalized`; and it is acknowledged and ignored otherwise.

requirements.applies: §10.4 Inbound Room Routing; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**A binding speaks for its own channel.** The sender a binding names is found
through it on that channel only. A correspondent recorded on one number's
binding, writing to another number of the same type, is not taken to the first
number's room: on a kit serving a bank and a clinic, each on its own SMS
number, a customer the bank's number recorded writing to the clinic lands in
the clinic's conversation. A participant record is another matter: a member
the integrator added to the bank's room is found by step 1 on whatever number
of the room's they were reached through and write to, unless that number's
binding names another correspondent: a binding not declared `group` is one
correspondent's conversation, whose answers go to their address, and the
member then gets a room of their own (§10.1 step 2). Merging or separating a
person's conversations across channels is decided for participants, not by
bindings.

Example, on one SMS number with no room yet: alice writes first, and the room
created for her has a binding naming her. Bob's first message finds no room of
his at step 1; at step 3 the binding names alice, so null, and bob gets a room
of his own. Alice's next message is found at step 1 through her binding, and
lands in hers. Had the integrator opened alice's room itself, addressed to her
number or with her added as a member on the SMS channel, bob would be refused
the same way before alice ever wrote, and alice found at her first message;
had it opened the room naming no one, with no value under its recipient key,
the first sender would be admitted and recorded, and the second refused.

A conversation of several senders on one channel, such as a group chat bound
to its room, is declared `group` on its binding. Without the declaration, the
default router routes its second speaker to a room of their own, which is the
safe answer: nothing in the store tells a group channel from a shared number.

requirements.applies: §10.4 Inbound Room Routing; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**A router MUST NOT guess.** When the inputs it was given match more than one
room and nothing in them tells which conversation the message belongs to — for
the default strategy, a channel bound to several rooms step 3 reads — it MUST
return null rather than choose among them. Step 1 is not a guess: it returns
the most recently created of the ACTIVE or PAUSED rooms where the sender is
connected, a conversation the sender is in. Returning any one of several
candidates delivers a message into a conversation it does not belong to, and —
because the room it lands in is where the message is stored, broadcast to that
room's channels, and read back as context by that room's agent — the
disclosure is durable, not transient. Null is the safe answer: the framework
creates a new room, which is recoverable, whereas a wrong room is not.

This is not a hypothetical configuration. An implementation that lets a
channel be shared across rooms (§19, delegation) creates it as a matter of
course, and a channel re-attached after its room closed accumulates the same
shape over time. An integrator whose deployment genuinely needs a shared
channel routed by something else MUST name the room explicitly (§10.1 step 2)
or supply a custom strategy.

requirements.applies: §10.4 Inbound Room Routing; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Routing MUST be deterministic.** The same inputs against the same stored
state MUST select the same room, whatever the storage backend. An
implementation whose answer depends on insertion order in one store and on the
query planner in another does not satisfy this, and its behaviour cannot be
reasoned about from the specification.

Implementations MUST allow integrators to provide a custom routing strategy.
The framework records the sender on the binding of the room any strategy
returns (§10.1 step 2): a custom strategy that sends several senders to one
room declares that room's binding `group`.

requirements.applies: §10.5 Direct Event Injection; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
Integrators MAY inject events into a room directly, without an inbound channel
message (e.g., from a REST API or MCP tool call):

```
send_event(room_id, channel_id, content, event_type, ...,
           response_visibility | null, organization_id | null) → RoomEvent
```

The injected event traverses the SAME pipeline as an inbound message (Section
10.1): index assignment, BEFORE_BROADCAST hooks, the source write-permission
gate, EDIT/DELETE handling, persistence and broadcast planning under the room
lock, then its delivery lane, reentry passes, and AFTER_BROADCAST hooks. A
blocking hook therefore yields a `BLOCKED` event and suppresses delivery,
exactly as for an inbound message. That includes the off-lock check (§9.5.1,
step 5a): an injected event matched by a `needs_lock = false` hook takes an
admission ticket like an inbound one — unless its caller stands in the room's
admission order (under the room lock, or in an off-lock hook's body, a
handler its check's report awaits, or a message's parse), in which case it
takes none and commits ahead of the event being processed (§9.5.1,
Reentrance). Made under the room lock, it draws on the reentry budget of the
cascade that holds it (§8.3), or on a budget of its own under a lock the host
holds outside any pass (§9.5.1); made in the admission order, on that of the
event the work is for. Made from the room's work outside the lock (a turn, a
delivery, an ASYNC hook's body, §10.1 step 16), it is a new arrival: while
that work runs, one into its own room draws on the budget of the cascade that
delivers, or that fired the hook, as does any call of that
work that creates a room (§9.5.1), and one into another room that exists
already on a budget of its own, and one into any room is at least as deep as
the response of the deepest turn it runs within, or as the answer that issued
a tool call outside a turn (§8.3); once the work is over, it is a new arrival
with a budget and a depth of its own (§9.5.1). Past its budget it is stored
`BLOCKED` with `reentry_loop_cap`, unless its key makes it a replay, which
draws nothing and returns the event its key committed (§13.4).

An injection takes §10.1's steps 1 to 4 its own way. The channel it names
MUST be registered, a channel the room still binds included (a binding
outlives an unregistration), and the event is admitted as a message is before
anything is read: an instruction's refusals (§10.1.1), `standalone` on
another type,
the visibility `internal`, as its visibility or its response visibility
(§7.3); and a key in the publication namespace, which a message would merely
lose, is refused (§5.2). None of step 2 runs. The room is read scoped to
`organization_id` (§17.2), unscoped when the call names none: a room that
does not exist, or another organization's, raises. A channel the room does
not bind is not attached, and the call raises with nothing written: the host
named the channel itself, so it is a caller's error with nothing to audit,
unlike a stranger's message (§7.5 rule 2). There is no parse. Its
`response_visibility`, when it carries one, scopes its cascade as a message's
does (§8.5). The event's source is the channel it names, `INBOUND` for a
transport, whose event stands for a message coming in, and `OUTBOUND` for an
intelligence channel, whose event is its own words going out, as its
responses are.

Its result is the committed event, so every refusal before the commit point
that leaves no committed record is raised, never returned as an event that
was not written: a room whose status refuses new events (§5.1) raises a
room-closed error, a refused edit or delete (§10.1 step 8a) and a refused
instruction (§10.1.1) raise with their reason, and `process_timeout`
(§13.6), which bounds its wait for the off-lock check and the room lock as it
bounds its pre-commit phase, raises a process-timeout error once it has
emitted the `process_timeout` framework event. Nothing of the event is
written. A record stored `BLOCKED`, by a hook, by a source that cannot write
or past the reentry budget (§8.3), is the committed event and is returned; a
replay returns the event its key committed (§13.4); an instruction, never
committed, returns uncommitted, as its pass decided it (§10.1.1 step 5), and
so does an event the persistence policy keeps out (§14.3).

requirements.applies: §10.5 Direct Event Injection; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**The host's own voice.** The host, the application that embeds RoomKit,
writes to the people of a room in its own name: a notice, a workflow's
question, a reminder. It speaks through a host channel, a transport of type
`HOST` (§6.2) whose direction is `INBOUND` (§4.2): it brings the host's words
into rooms, receives no external payload, and is never delivered to. Its
event is `INBOUND`, as every transport's is: the room reads it as a party's
message, broadcasts it to its other transports under the usual visibility
(§7.3), and it solicits intelligence channels as a message does (§19.3). The
host's words MUST NOT come from an intelligence channel, which would make them
an agent's output: an unaddressed one would solicit no agent under
`ADDRESSED_ONLY` (§19.3.1), and a room holding a discussion refuses to bind an
intelligence channel that is not one of its agents. Nor do they come from a
`SYSTEM` source, which marks what the framework writes itself: it carries no
author record (§10.1 step 12) and may make the changes reserved to the system
(§10.3).

A host channel MUST be bound as a transport: an attach that binds one as an
intelligence channel, by the category it names or the one the channel
declares, MUST be refused before anything is written. A message handed to the
inbound pipeline on a host channel MUST be refused before anything is read
(§10.1 step 1): the host speaks through this section's calls only. Never
delivered to, a host channel is no transport an answer reaches: what a turn
may answer with (`target_capabilities`, `target_media_types`, §6.7) is what
the room's transports that send carry, and the host channel narrows none of
it. Its declaration lists every media type, since `content` may be any; each
transport the event reaches gets it transcoded for what it carries (§6.6).

An implementation SHOULD offer the host's voice as one call:

```
post(room_id, content, participant_id | null, addressed_to = [],
     metadata | null, channel_id | null, organization_id | null,
     idempotency_key | null, chain_depth = 0) → RoomEvent
```

`post()` injects `content` as `send_event` does (this section), from
`channel_id` when the call names one, which MUST be a registered channel of
type `HOST`, else from the kit's own host channel, registered on first use
under the id `host`. A `channel_id` that names a channel of another type, or
none registered, and, when the call names none, the id `host` held by a
channel of another type, MUST be refused before anything is written, as must
an argument `send_event` refuses before anything is read and a negative
`chain_depth`.

A room that never bound the host channel gets it attached first, an ordinary
attachment with its `CHANNEL_ATTACHED` record (§5.2), decided in one section
under the room lock, where binding and status changes run: the room is read
scoped to `organization_id`, its due timers applied (§5.1), then its binding
of the channel. A binding made by then, set up by the integrator before the
post or concurrently with it, is kept as it is, never replaced, so concurrent
first posts attach the channel once. A room whose status refuses new events
MUST raise a room-closed error. A room the host channel was detached from
MUST raise as a channel the room does not bind does: the post does not undo
the revocation (§7.5 rule 7), which only an explicit attach grants again.
Nothing is written either way. As step 2's attach (§10.1, §13.6), the first
post's wait for the room lock runs within the call's `process_timeout`, one
deadline from the call's start to its commit, and the section it opens runs
to its end whatever becomes of the caller. Made from the room's own work
(§9.5.1), the post draws its pass before the attach, after the room's scoped
read and the check of a revocation: past the budget, its event is stored
`BLOCKED` with `reentry_loop_cap` and the channel is not attached, no
`CHANNEL_ATTACHED` record written nor hook run.

`addressed_to` defaults to `[]`: the host's message solicits no intelligence
channel unless it names one (§19.3). `participant_id` names who speaks: it
MUST name a participant reached through the host channel the post comes from
(its `connected_via` names it), by their id or by their identity's, as a
turn's sender is read (§5.5), since an id names its participant on no other
channel; else the post is refused before anything is written, the first
post's attach included, the room read scoped to `organization_id` first so
that another organization's room is not found whoever the id names (§17.2).
A reader is shown the speaker's name (§10.1 step 12). An integrator makes a
member one by adding them on the host channel. `send_event` takes any id
(§5.5). `metadata` carries where the message comes from: a workflow, its
step, a job. `chain_depth` is `send_event`'s, the chain the post continues
(§8.3), 0 opening one: work that follows an agent's answer once the answer's
work is over, which begins fresh (§9.5.1), names the answer's depth plus one,
so that its round trips with the agent end at `max_chain_depth`.
`idempotency_key` is `send_event`'s (§13.4): a key the host channel holds in
the room makes the post a replay, which sends nothing again and returns the
event the key committed, read before the reentry budget when the room's own
work posts; a blank key is no key.

requirements.applies: §10.5 Direct Event Injection; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**A record outside the pipeline.** An integrator MAY commit an event that no
member is meant to receive (a trace, a display snapshot, a copy a branched
conversation starts from) without the pipeline:

```
commit_event(room_id, event, organization_id) → RoomEvent
```

The record names the room it is committed to: one whose `room_id` is another
room's MUST be refused before anything is read or written, so the room checked
is the room written, and so MUST one whose key is in the publication namespace
(§5.2), which would stand in for a publication. The room is read scoped to
`organization_id` (§17.2): a missing room, or another organization's, is not
found. A room whose status refuses new events (§5.1) MUST refuse the record
before anything is written, and emits no framework event: a record reaches no
one, and no subscriber waits for it. A record committed outside the pipeline
is never a replay (§14.3). The record is committed under the room
lock with the next index, which the room's delivery lane MUST pass at its turn
with nothing to run, as a record stored `BLOCKED` (§13.5): no delivery set, no
hook, and no broadcast follow it, and the next event of the room waits on its
index no longer than on the events before it. It counts in `event_count` and
`latest_index`, and is no activity: `last_activity_at` does not move, and a
PAUSED room stays paused (§5.1), since a trace nobody receives does not keep a
room alive. It is stored as the caller gives it (its status, its visibility,
its `delivery_results` and the rest), whatever the persistence policy, but
for its thread parent, rooted as every committed event's is (§10.1 step 8),
and its author record, which the room fixes, any `metadata.author` given
dropped (§10.1 step 12); rule 2 of §7.5 does not apply to it. An event the
members must receive is injected with `send_event` instead.

requirements.applies: §10.6 Turn Execution; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
An **intelligence turn** (a *turn* in this section) is one call of
`on_event()` on a binding of category `INTELLIGENCE`, from that call to the
end of the response stream it returns, when it returns one. Every turn MUST
run through a **turn backend**, which carries it between two roles:

- The **room owner** is the process that runs the delivery set the turn is a
  target of: the room's delivery lane (§10.2), or a delegation's worker run
  (§23.3). It plans, commits and broadcasts, and it reads the turn's output as
  the channel's `ChannelOutput`. The lane is the only runner of a room's
  delivery sets, in index order (§10.1, §13.5); a delegation's worker run is
  its child room's. A turn is one target of a delivery set.
- A **turn executor** builds the channel the turn needs, runs its `on_event()`,
  advances its response stream as the owner reads it, and sends what it reads
  as frames. An executor MUST NOT commit to the store, deliver to a transport
  or broadcast: what a turn produces reaches the room through the owner, as
  its output or as an owner call (§10.6.5).

An implementation's default kit MUST own an in-memory executor, so a
deployment that configures nothing runs every turn in the owner's process,
through the in-memory backend. Any process MAY run executors, the owner's
included.

```
TurnBackend (interface)
├── submit(request: TurnRequest) → TurnLink
│       # Owner side: start a turn. The link yields its frames in order,
│       # and sends its control messages and its call answers
├── control(message: ChannelControl) → ChannelResult | null
│       # Owner side: a message about a channel's per-room state, naming its
│       # channel and room (§10.6.3), or its build; null for room_attached,
│       # room_detached, channel_released
├── serve(executor: TurnExecutor) → void
│       # Executor side: receive the requests and the channel control of the
│       # channels the executor declares, until close
└── close() → void
        # Fail the turns in flight (backend_closed: the owner's backend
        # closed, its executor is not lost) and release the transport; on
        # the executor side, cut the turns it runs and write their end
        # within cancel_timeout first
```

requirements.applies: §10.6.1 Scope and the one path; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Scope.** Every turn runs through the backend, whichever call starts it, the
solicited target of §10.2 step 3c among them. An event a hook injects starts
no turn: it asks no agent (§9.4). Every intelligence channel is in scope: an
AI channel, an ACP agent channel and a channel of the integrator's own.

A strategy that takes an agent's turns in a room (a turn runner, Section 19.7:
a loop's produce and review, a supervisor's delegation passes) runs on the
owner, as the target the delivery set would otherwise have given the agent.
Each generation it asks of an agent (the producer's answer, a supervisor's
first pass, its presentation of the results) is a turn of its own, submitted
through the backend as a strategy turn (`strategy_turn`, §10.6.3) with the
event and the binding the runner gives it (an instruction for one call rides
that binding, §19.7.3). What Section 19.7 sets
up for a room on a shared agent (its turn runner, its tools, their
configuration) is kept by the owner per channel and room and travels in each
request: nothing is installed on a live channel object. A delegation's worker
answers in its child room (§23.3) and a discussion's turn is a rerun planned
for one agent (§19.7.5): both are delivery sets whose intelligence targets are
turns.

Out of scope: a speech-to-speech channel (§12.4), whose model holds the
conversation in the owner's process, and the fan-out of an event to live
connections held by another process.

requirements.applies: §10.6.1 Scope and the one path; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**One path (normative).** Every backend MUST carry the same serialized
messages (§10.6.3), written in the serialized form of Section 1.4. The
in-memory backend
MUST serialize each message and parse it on the other side, for two reasons.
Every test run against it then checks the exact messages a distributed
backend carries. And no object of the turn is shared between the owner and
the executor: neither the channel's stream, its response-metadata record, its
tool-call markers nor an exception crosses as a live object. One part of a
message is exempt: the events a `turn_request` carries (its `event` and its
context's history) are records nothing changes once made, committed events
the store shares with every reader (§14.4) or ones the owner made for the
turn (an instruction, a strategy's stand-in event). The owner, once it
submitted the request, and the executor, its channel and its hooks MUST NOT
change them. The in-memory backend MAY hand them to the executor as they
are, the rest of the request serialized and parsed. A history is most of a
request, so its parse is most of the cost of carrying one. A value of an
event's metadata that JSON has no form for then reaches an executor in the
owner's process as itself, and one reached across a distributed backend's
transport as its text; a suite that checks the wire runs against such a
backend. An
implementation MUST NOT keep a local shortcut that hands the owner the
channel's objects; a distributed backend carries the in-memory backend's
messages on another transport, never a second path. The behaviour
this document gives intelligence channels MUST hold through the in-memory
backend: an implementation's conformance suite for intelligence channels MUST
be runnable against it, and SHOULD run against it by default.

requirements.applies: §10.6.2 Channels on each side; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**On the owner, a declaration.** The owner knows each intelligence channel by
its declaration, registered as a channel is. It needs no live object of the
channel to plan, broadcast, run a strategy or read a turn, except a strategy
that drives a realtime session, which runs each agent's own prompt (Section
19.5, Section 19.6).

```
ChannelDeclaration
├── channel_id: string
├── channel_type: ChannelType
├── category: ChannelCategory               # INTELLIGENCE
├── capabilities: ChannelCapabilities
├── identity: AgentIdentity | null          # what Section 19 reads of an agent
├── thinks_while_listening: bool            # it carries a thinker (§6.4), which
│                                           # a discussion refuses (§19.7.5)
├── takes_owner_tools: bool                 # its turns declare the tools the
│                                           # owner serves (§10.6.5); an external
│                                           # agent's (§6.4) do not
├── recent_events_window: int               # the history the owner's context
│                                           # build reads for its turns
├── serializes_room_turns: bool             # its turns in a room run one after
│                                           # the other, in the order the owner
│                                           # keeps (§6.4)
└── steers_room_turns: bool                 # a message for the room's running
                                            # turn is read by it, its turns
                                            # serialized (§6.4, §21.3)

AgentIdentity                               # an Agent's identity fields (§19.1)
├── name: string | null
├── role: string | null
├── description: string | null
├── scope: string | null
├── greeting: string | null
├── language: string | null
├── purpose: string | null                  # what a supervisor's roster says
│                                           # of a worker (§19.7.3)
├── voice: string | null                    # its TTS voice (§19.1)
└── auto_greet: bool                        # greets on a session start (§19.1),
                                            # default true
```

A channel the host registers on the kit as a live object is declared by it.
A declaration registers as a channel does, through the same door, and the
owner finds it wherever it looks a channel up: routing, delivery, a binding's
creation, a delegation. Its binding is an intelligence binding: a declared
channel has no object in the owner's process to deliver to or take a message
from, and the owner MUST refuse binding it otherwise. The owner's own
executor MUST NOT build a channel the owner holds by declaration alone: its
turns run on an executor whose host builds it, and fail with `no_executor`
when none takes them (§10.6.7). A channel declared and the same channel
registered live MUST read alike on the owner, its greeting included.
What Section 19.7 and Section 23.4 set up for a channel (its turn runner,
its tools, a delegation's result tool) is kept by the owner, per channel and
room, beside the declaration.

requirements.applies: §10.6.2 Channels on each side; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**On the executor, a factory.** The executor builds the channel through a
factory the host gives it: an agent holds live objects (its provider, its MCP
clients, its memory). A factory that builds nothing for a channel the executor
declares fails that channel's turns and channel calls with `no_executor`
(§10.6.7). An executor MAY keep a bounded number of channels built: past its
bound, it lets go of the build it used least recently that nothing runs on
(a turn, a channel call, a committed event, a room's attach or detach), as
`channel_released` lets a build go (§10.6.3), and its next turn builds the
channel anew, its request carrying what the turn reads (§10.6.5). A turn or
a channel call uses a build; a committed event does not, and a build begun
for a committed event alone is the least recent. What the build held for its
rooms that the room does not keep (an ACP session, a speak policy's listening
state) starts anew, as after the executor's restart; a bound below the number
of agents an executor serves at once makes that routine. The kit's own
executor reads the live channels the host registered on the kit, and declares
them; it alone runs them, closed or not: once it closed, their turns fail
with `no_executor` rather than run on another executor's copy (§10.6.7). The
executor gives the channel what the kit gives a channel it registers, each
on the executor's side:

- the hooks the channel fires, against the executor's own registry
  (§10.6.6), the after-response hook every intelligence channel gets included;
- its realtime publications, turned into `ephemeral` frames;
- the framework events it emits (§8.2), turned into `framework_event` frames;
- its readers of state that lives in the owner's process (the room's
  background tasks, §23.4; what a vision provider last saw, §12.8.7), turned
  into owner calls;
- the host's media resolver and attached-media reader (§6.4), which the host
  gives the executor as it gives the kit;
- what its turn reads of the room, which comes with the turn (§10.6.5), and
  the room's context for its hooks, which the owner gives (§10.6.6).

requirements.applies: §10.6.2 Channels on each side; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Per-room state.** A channel MAY keep state per room between two turns on its
executor. An AI channel keeps a room's thought and its speak policy's
listening state (§6.4), its plan, the results it evicted and reads back, the
skills it activated, and the tools Tool Search revealed or it used;
an ACP agent channel keeps the room's session. That state is the executor's,
not the room's, and is one of two kinds, which an implementation documents per
state:

- a **cache**, rebuilt from the timeline and the store when absent (the tools
  it used, reseeded from its rows, §6.4);
- **session state**, which starts empty when absent, as after a restart (a
  plan, a thought). Some of it the room needs: an ACP session, whose agent
  holds the conversation, and a speak policy's listening state, a request to
  stay quiet that is a state of the room (§6.4).

Each request names the room's previous turn of the channel (`previous_turn`,
§10.6.3): the one the owner sent last, ended or not. The owner records it as
it sends it, so a turn sent while the previous one runs names it. A backend
marks a request handed as it gives it to an executor, before any wait on
the executor's answer: a turn that failed before (no executor declares it,
the backend closed, it cannot be serialized, its placement failed) is never
named, while one handed stays named whatever followed (a cancel, a timeout),
since its executor may have begun it; a refusal that applied nothing (a
closing process's) takes the mark back. A channel call (§10.6.3) leaves the
room's state as a turn does: it names the previous turn or call too, and the next
turn names it. An executor that holds state for the channel and room not left
by that turn or call MUST discard it before running the turn or the call's
verb: the turns of a room may have run elsewhere since, and a state they made
obsolete (a speak policy told to talk again, a plan revised) MUST NOT come
back. It discards it as the channel lets go of a room it is detached from
(§6.4), every state it keeps for the room included, a cache rebuilt
afterwards. An executor that can no longer vouch for the state it holds
treats it as not left by the previous turn: when it stops keeping its record
of which turn left a room's state (a bounded record), it discards that state,
and a discard that failed is attempted again at the room's next turn.
Placement (§10.6.7) keeps a room's turns where its state is.

requirements.applies: §10.6.2 Channels on each side; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**State the host sets for the room.** Some per-room state is set by the host
through a channel call and is needed again on another executor (an ACP
session's configuration values, §6.4). That state is the room's, not the
executor's. A channel's result reports it when the verb changed it. The owner
MUST store it in the room's metadata (§5.1), under a key of the
implementation's own namespace (`roomkit:`), and MUST drop that key, with a
warning, from any other write (a room's creation or metadata update, a
`TurnHost` verb, §5.1). It
hands it to the executor with each request, in the room its `RoomContext`
carries, and with each channel call, before the turn or the verb runs. The
channel takes it back when it holds none for the room. A detach forgets it.

requirements.applies: §10.6.3 Messages; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text: Five families, each message a record in the serialized form of Section 1.4.

requirements.applies: §10.6.3 Messages; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**The request**, owner → executor:

```
TurnRequest
├── turn_id: string
├── room_id: string
├── channel_id: string
├── event: RoomEvent                    # transcoded, max length applied (§10.2
│                                       # step 3a-b)
├── binding: ChannelBinding             # as the runner gives it (§10.6.1)
├── context: RoomContext
├── strategy_turn: bool                 # a generation a turn runner asks
│                                       # (§10.6.1): the channel answers, past
│                                       # its speak policy and its thinker (§6.4)
├── notes: list<string>                 # the runtime's own blocks for the turn
│                                       # (a discussion's turn notes, §19.7.5
│                                       # rule 14); never read from event metadata
├── in_place: bool                      # a discussion's turn: the event keeps
│                                       # its place in the history (rule 9)
├── owner_tools: list<OwnerTool>        # the tools the owner serves (§10.6.5)
├── room_hooks: list<string>            # the names of the room's hooks on
│                                       # executor triggers (§10.6.6)
├── previous_turn: {turn_id, executor_id} | null
│                                       # the room's previous turn or channel
│                                       # call of the channel (§10.6.2)
├── channel_rows: list<RoomEvent>       # the channel's own rows its turn reads,
│                                       # oldest first (§10.6.5)
└── trace: map<string, string> | null   # trace context of the broadcast span

OwnerTool
├── tool: AITool                        # its declaration (§6.7)
└── waits_by_design: bool               # bounded by its own bound, not the
                                        # channel's default (§21.6)
```

requirements.applies: §10.6.3 Messages; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Frames**, executor → owner, each carrying the turn id:

| Frame | Carries |
|---|---|
| `accepted` | The executor's id: it took the turn |
| `heartbeat` | Nothing: the turn is still running |
| `output` | `on_event()` returned: the `ChannelOutput` without its stream (`responded`, `response_events`, `response_metadata`, `tasks`, `observations`, `metadata_updates`, its error as an error record), and whether a stream follows |
| `item` | One item of the stream, within what the `pull` messages granted: a text delta (or the text deltas the channel yielded together, joined, with their number), a reasoning delta, a call's start (its id, name, arguments, and its intent when it has one), a call's end (its id, the sequence number of its start's frame, name, arguments, result, status, outcome, duration, error, structured content, `refused_but_ran`, and its intent when it has one), a segment break, what a generation used (usage, model, provider), the loop's end (reason, rounds, usage, the limits it ran under, the last generation's usage, whether every generation reported its counters, model, provider), or the stream's end |
| `tool_args` | The arguments a call runs with once its gate fixed them (a `BEFORE_TOOL_USE` rewrite, §9.3), naming the call's start frame |
| `tool_ended` | A call's end known before the `item` carrying it was read (§10.6.4): the start's frame and the end |
| `record` | The turn's response-metadata record as it stands (§6.7), sent before the `item` it was read with whenever it changed (§10.6.4) |
| `ephemeral` | An ephemeral event of the turn (thinking, tool-call composition, custom), which the owner publishes on its realtime backend |
| `framework_event` | A framework event the turn emitted (§8.2), with its payload, which the owner emits on its own bus |
| `input_request` | A tool asked a human for input: the request's id, tool and prompt, with its room, channel, tool call and the actor of its turn (§10.6.5) |
| `input_closed` | A request settled on the executor other than by an `input_answer`: its id and its outcome (answered, rejected, timed out), from the host's handler, a hook's block, its bound or a release (§9.3) |
| `input_taken` | Whether an `input_answer` settled its request: false when the request was settled first (§10.6.5) |
| `steer_result` | The number of loops a `steer` reached, or none when the channel cannot steer the turn (§10.6.8) |
| `error` | `on_event()` or the stream raised: an error record (§10.6.8) |
| `end` | The turn ended; nothing follows |

requirements.text:
**Control**, owner → executor, on a turn's link:

| Message | Carries |
|---|---|
| `pull` | Grant the reading of the stream's next items: their number, and how many items the owner's reader read, a joined `item` counting its deltas (§10.6.4) |
| `close` | The reader closed the stream (§10.6.4) |
| `cancel` | The reason the owner cancels the turn (§10.6.8) |
| `steer` | A steering directive (§21.3), answered by `steer_result` with the number of loops it reached |
| `input_answer` | The outcome recorded for an `input_request`: answered with its value, or rejected with its reason |
| `heartbeat` | Nothing: the owner still reads the turn (§10.6.8) |

requirements.text:
**Delivery.** Every message of a turn's link, in both directions (frames,
control, calls and their results), carries a sequence number and MUST reach
the other side exactly once and in order. A side MUST drop a duplicate and
fail the turn with `frame_lost` on a gap in the sequence; the owner MUST drop
a message of a turn that ended or failed.

requirements.text:
**Calls**, executor → owner, each answered once by its result:

| Call | Result | Serves |
|---|---|---|
| `tool_call` | `tool_result` | A call to a tool the owner serves (§10.6.5) |
| `call_cancel` | none | The executor withdraws a `tool_call` or a `host_call` whose turn it cut or whose bound expired (§21.6): the owner cancels its handler |
| `host_call` | `host_result` | A verb of `TurnHost`, or a reader of owner-process state (§10.6.5) |

requirements.text:
**Channel control**, owner → executor, outside any turn, about a channel's
per-room state, or its build:

| Message | Carries |
|---|---|
| `room_attached` | The channel was attached to the room: the room's binding of it (§5.7) |
| `room_detached` | The channel was detached from the room: its state for the room is dropped (§6.4) |
| `committed_event` | An event committed in the room that the channel's memory is handed (a discussion's, §19.7.5 rule 3), answered by nothing |
| `channel_released` | The channel's build is stale (its host changed what it is built from): an executor holding a build lets it go, answered by nothing |
| `channel_call` | A per-room verb of the channel, answered by `channel_result` (an ACP session's `set_config_option` or `close_session`, §6.4); an implementation documents each channel's set. It carries its `call_id`, its channel and room, the verb and its arguments, what the room keeps for the channel as the owner stores it (§10.6.2), and `previous_turn`; a later request's `previous_turn` names the call by its `call_id`. Cutting a running turn is never a channel call: it is the turn's `cancel` or `steer` |

`room_attached` and `room_detached` reach every executor that may run the
channel's turns: the owner's own executor alone for a channel the owner holds
live (§10.6.7); every executor that declares the channel otherwise. They
need no result: an executor holding a build of the channel applies them as
the channel's own attach and detach would for a channel the kit holds, and
logs what the channel raises; one holding no build has nothing to apply and
builds none for them, so a channel is built at its first turn, channel call
or committed event on an executor (§10.6.2). A binding of category
`INTELLIGENCE` (§5.7) is therefore kept when its channel raises on
`room_attached`, and a detach does not report what
the channel raised; only a backend that cannot carry `room_attached` fails
the attachment, which is then undone. After `room_detached`, the owner names
no previous turn for the channel in the room (`previous_turn` is null), so an
executor that missed the message still discards the room's state at its next
turn (§10.6.2), and the owner forgets what the room kept for the channel,
even when the message could not be sent.

`channel_released` reaches the same executors. One that built the channel
lets the build go: the next turn, channel call or committed event of the
channel builds it anew, and the build let go is closed once the turns running
on it, or still getting it, end, which it never cuts for this. One that holds
no build builds none for the message. For a channel the owner holds live it
changes nothing: that channel is the owner's registry's, and its host
replaces it there. A host sends it through the kit's
`release_channel(channel_id)`, which fails when the kit holds no channel of
that id.

A `committed_event` reaches one executor: the owner's own for a channel the
owner holds live (§10.6.7), else the one that holds the room's state for the
channel, else one that would take the room's turns (the room's hooks it
carries included, §10.6.6). It never makes that executor
the holder: it leaves the room's state as it is and names no
previous turn. The executor hands the event to the channel (an AI channel's
memory, §20), logs what the channel raises, and applies it before any later
request of the owner for that channel and room. One no executor takes is
dropped and logged by the owner.

A `channel_call` is made for a channel attached to the room, in the room's
organization (§17.2). It reaches one executor: the owner's own for a channel
the owner holds live (§10.6.7), else the one that holds the room's state for
the channel, else one that declares the channel. Its
`channel_result` is that executor's: the verb's result as data or its error
record, what the room keeps for the channel when the verb changed it, and
the executor's id. A backend answers a call on the call's own exchange, so
the result names no call. A `channel_call` no executor takes fails with
`no_executor`, at once from a backend that knows every executor (§10.6.7),
else within `accept_timeout`; the owner then names the previous turn it
named before the call. A host makes one through the kit's `channel_call`,
naming the channel, the room, the verb and the verb's arguments; a verb the
channel does not have fails with the channel's own error. An executor closes the channels it built when it
closes; the kit's close closes its own executor's.

A `committed_event` or a `channel_call` that reaches an executor that closed,
or a process that is closing, is refused unapplied, as a request is
(§10.6.7): the owner places it again, never on the executor that refused it,
and one no other executor takes is dropped and logged, or fails, as above.

requirements.applies: §10.6.3 Messages; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Outside a turn**, executor → owner, through the port to the owner the
backend gives each executor it serves:

| Message | Answer | Carries |
|---|---|---|
| `room_call` | `host_result` | A `TurnHost` verb made after its turn ended (§10.6.5): its `call_id`, the channel and room, the executor's id, the id of the turn the work began in, the verb and its arguments; the turn being over, the verb is a new arrival at its own event's depth (§10.6.5) |
| `room_publication` | — | A realtime publication or a framework event made after its turn ended, as `ephemeral` and `framework_event` carry them, with the channel, room, executor and turn |

The owner accepts one only from the executor of the last turn it sent for
the channel and room (`previous_turn`, §10.6.2), and anything else is
refused, an owner that restarted included, until its next turn. A
`room_call` MUST also name that very turn: work an earlier turn began writes
nothing once a later turn was sent. A `room_publication` may name an earlier
turn of that executor, which still holds the room's state: an external
agent's update (§6.4) is handled under the turn prompting its session, or
outside any turn when none is. It publishes what it accepts as it
publishes a turn's `ephemeral` and `framework_event` frames, for the room
and kinds a turn may publish, and publishes its ephemerals only as §8.4
allows for the turn it names: that turn's trigger, as it was sent, and the
binding as the room holds it then. A turn the owner no longer knows, or a
channel call, which has no answer, publishes none; a publication never
takes a later turn's scope.

requirements.applies: §10.6.4 The stream: pulled, never pushed; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
The owner hands its reader a `ChannelOutput` built from the `output` frame.
When a stream follows, its response stream yields the items the `item` frames
carry, so the consumer that stores segments and the streaming targets that
render them (§10.2, Appendix A.9) read it as they read a local stream.

The reader sets the pace, as it does locally: a model round and a tool call run
only as the stream is read, a reader that stops leaves no call started after
that point (§12.2), and a stream closed unread makes no provider call (a muted
binding, §7.5). The owner's reads of its stream send
`pull` messages, each granting a number of items: the executor advances the
channel's stream by at most the items granted, and MUST NOT advance past an
item other than a text or reasoning delta or what a generation used (a call's
start, a segment break, a loop's end) until a later `pull` grants it, so a call
or a round starts only once the reader asked for what follows it. A later `pull` is one the owner
sent once its reader read that item: each `pull` says how many items the
reader read, and the executor takes one that says fewer than it had read
through that item as granting nothing. Within a grant the executor reads
deltas, and what a generation used, ahead of the reader, so a round is decided
as its generation ends, whatever its reader is still showing. Text deltas the channel yields without waiting
between them MAY cross as one `item` holding their joined text and their
number, which counts as that many items against the grant: the text is kept,
not where it was cut, so a reader that decides between deltas decides on the
text (a sentence budget reads it a sentence at a time, §12.2 step 12s.e).
Closing the owner's stream sends `close`, and the executor closes the
channel's stream as a local reader's close would: it is the reader's close,
not a cancellation (§10.6.8). A close that finds the executor reading ahead,
past a delta, cuts that read at once, since a local reader's close would have
found the stream waiting at the item it yielded; a read only a later `pull`
let start (a call running past its start) finishes first. Items read ahead
that the owner had not read when its stream was closed or the turn cut are
dropped: what the consumer stores is what its readers read (§10.2).

The consumer reads in frames what the channel changes after yielding it:

- each segment is stored with the record of the last `record` frame received
  before the `item` that ended it: a tool handler's write mid-loop reaches the
  segments that follow (§6.7);
- a call's arguments are its `tool_args` frame's when it has one, its start's
  otherwise;
- a call's end names its start's frame, so two calls under one id stay two
  calls (§6.4);
- a call that ended before the stream was closed or the turn cut is closed
  with its own outcome: the executor sends its end once, before the next
  item it sends and so before the turn's `end`, and the owner closes as
  cancelled only a call no end was sent for, a reader that stops between a
