  round's end items included.

The executor compares the record with the last one it sent before each `item`
that is no delta (the stream's end included), before the `error` a failed
stream ends with, and once the stream is closed, so each of those reaches
the owner after every change written before it.
Before a text or reasoning delta it MAY look only for a write to one of the
record's keys, so that a delta costs nothing for the record's size: a change
made inside a value the record already holds then reaches the owner before
the next `item` that is no delta, the one ending the segment stored with it.

requirements.applies: §10.6.5 What a turn asks of the owner; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Owner-served tools.** A tool runs where the live objects it needs live. The
tools that read or change the owner's state are served by the owner: the tools
orchestration sets up for a room (handoff, Section 19.6; the strategies' tools,
Section 19.7; a delegation's result tool, Section 23.3) and the tools the
implementation binds to the kit (a delegation's status and cancel tools,
Section 23.4), which a host attaches on the owner, to the channel's
declaration (§10.6.2), never through the executor's factory. The owner lists
them in the request's
`owner_tools`, and the executor's channel declares them to its model with its
other tools, in the order the request lists them, whether or not a tool waits
by design; the owner lists those it set up for every room the channel serves
in the order it set them up. Their gate (`BEFORE_TOOL_USE`) and their report
(`ON_TOOL_CALL`) run on the executor, as for every call of the turn; only the
handler runs on the owner:

- `tool_call` carries the per-call context the implementation keeps for the
  call (§21.4), at least: its id, its name, the arguments its gate left, the
  turn's room, chain depth, actor and allowed names, who asked for the turn
  (the author label a strategy heads a task with, §19.7), and the id of the
  voice session it serves when it has one. The owner installs that context
  around the handler, so the handler reads what it reads locally.
- `tool_result` carries the handler's answer as §21.4 reads it, its outcome
  (served, refused, failed, served by nothing, §9.3), the failure's class and
  the structured copy.
- A `tool_call` or a `host_call` the executor withdraws (its turn cut, or the
  tool or hook that made it cut by its bound, §21.6) sends `call_cancel`, and
  the owner cancels the handler or the verb. The owner also cancels every
  call of a turn it cuts or loses itself. Unless the turn is cut, the
  executor sends `end` only once each call it sent was answered.

An executor whose channel already declares a tool under the name of one of
the request's `owner_tools` MUST refuse the turn, with an error naming the
tool: which of the two handlers a call reaches would otherwise depend on the
executor. The owner refuses the same clash when it sets up the tool on a
channel it holds live, and cannot for one it holds by declaration alone. The
owner MUST refuse to set up a tool for a channel whose declaration says its
turns do not take the owner's tools; a delegation's result tool is not set up
for it, and its result is its text.

The tools the implementation installs that hold the channel's state (a plan,
§6.4; the human-input tools, §9.3) run on the executor. The host's tools need
the host's live objects (its MCP clients, its sandbox, its database): they run
on the executor.

requirements.applies: §10.6.5 What a turn asks of the owner; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**TurnHost.** A host tool or hook on the executor reaches a room only through
`TurnHost`, which it reads with `current_turn_host()` (§21.4). It is bound to
the turn's room inside a tool call of a turn and inside a hook the executor
fires while the turn runs, and, after the turn, in work the turn began (a task
or an `ASYNC` hook that outlives it) for the verbs below; it is empty anywhere
else, and any other verb called on it after its turn ended is refused. Between
turns (a background thinker's thought, §6.4) it is bound to the room of the
turn the work began in: `send_event`, `post_status`, `update_room_metadata`
and `add_observation` cross as `room_call` (§10.6.3), each a new arrival with
a budget of its own and the depth of its own event, the turn being over
(§9.5.1); a `send_event` made from the body of a hook run asynchronously names at least
the depth that body runs at (§8.3), which the owner keeps. `delegate`,
`wait_task` and the readers of owner-process state are
refused there, with an error naming the verb. What work a turn began publishes
after the turn (realtime publications, framework events) crosses as
`room_publication`: an executor never publishes it on the owner's realtime
backend or bus itself, and never writes the owner's store. Its surface is
minimal and enumerated: each verb is one `host_call`, every argument is data
(no callable crosses), and an implementation documents the set. It MUST carry:

```
TurnHost
├── send_event(room_id, channel_id, content, ...) → RoomEvent    # §10.5
├── delegate(room_id, agent_id, task, ...) → string              # the task id (§23.3)
├── wait_task(task_id, timeout) → DelegatedTaskResult | null     # §23.2
└── room_context() → RoomContext                                 # as the owner builds it now (§10.6.6)
```

An implementation adds the verbs its own tools and hooks need to write (a
status post, §19.8; a room-metadata update; an observation, §5.11), each
documented as one `host_call`.

A host's own code may need what only the owner's process holds (a person's live
connection, a service the owner runs). An implementation SHOULD let the host
declare verbs of its own on the owner, each served by name as one `host_call`,
its arguments and its result data. The owner runs a declared verb under what
the turn gave the call (its room, the actor of its turn, the requester, its
chain depth, the tool call it is made from), which the accessors a tool handler
reads answer for it (§21.4), and MUST refuse a name its own verbs or another
declared verb hold, and a verb no host declared. A declared verb needs its
turn unless the host declared it to be served between turns: work the turn
began then still sends it after the turn, as a `room_call`, and the owner runs
it for the turn's room and channel, with no actor nor tool call, as work that
starts fresh (§8.3). The owner MUST refuse, between turns, a declared verb not
declared so.

A `TurnHost` acts for its turn's room, in that room's organization: the owner
MUST refuse a verb that names another room or another organization than the
room's, and an argument the verb does not take. A status post it makes names
the turn's room (§19.8). An event it sends while the turn runs is at least as
deep as the turn's response (§8.3), and a task it delegates inherits the
turn's depth (§23.3), so a chain of turns writing through it stops at the
chain-depth limit as a local one does; an event that work the turn began sends
once the turn is over has the depth of its own event (§9.5.1). `wait_task`
answers for a task a `TurnHost` of the turn's room delegated, and answers null
for any other, as it does past its timeout. A room-metadata update through it
MUST NOT write a key of the implementation's own namespace (§5.1: a detach's
revocation, §7.5; what the room keeps for a channel, §10.6.2).

An executor holds no store. What a turn reads of its room comes with the
request: its context, and, for a channel run on an executor other than the
owner's own, `channel_rows`, which the owner reads for the turn: the channel's
own tool-call rows and the instructions it read, each once, those its history
replays and its latest calls, which rebuild
its tool memory and the skills it activated (§6.4, §24.4). A deleted row is
withheld (§7.5 rule 8), and a store that fails costs the turn those rows, not
the turn. Every write goes through `TurnHost`. Each call carries the room and the turn it is made from, and the
owner applies to it the reentrancy of its own task waiting on that turn when
the call arrives (the delivery-set target awaiting `output`, or the reader
awaiting an `item`): a call that would wait on the room's own delivery from a
task that delivery needs returns with its completion detached (§10.1 step 18),
as it does locally, rather than wait on the delivery set that runs the turn.
An implementation cannot keep a host's code from committing through another
kit it holds: a host that runs a kit beside an executor of another process
MUST NOT let that executor's turns reach a room through it.

requirements.applies: §10.6.5 What a turn asks of the owner; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**The in-memory backend's execution context.** The in-memory backend runs in
the owner's process, where a host's tool holds the kit itself and may call it
from a turn. It therefore runs a turn's work in a copy of the execution
context of the owner task that submitted the turn, and advances the turn's
stream in a copy of the context of the task that first reads it, kept for the
stream's life: the reentrancy guards that task holds (its room's delivery
lane, a room lock, a kit-held run) hold for the turn as they hold in the
owner's own code, and a tool that waits on the delivery of the event it sent
gets its completion detached rather than wait on itself. That context is the
only thing the in-memory backend carries beside the messages, and it is no
object of the turn. A turn's code also knows the turns it runs under, so a
close called from one of them cuts them without cutting the call that awaits
it, nor waiting for it (§12.10.4), and what it sends into a room while they
run is at least as deep as the deepest of their responses (§8.3).
An executor of another process has no such context: its turns reach a room
through `TurnHost`, whose verbs carry the depth.

requirements.applies: §10.6.5 What a turn asks of the owner; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Human input.** A tool waiting for a human's answer runs on the executor, and
the answer may arrive on the owner, which keeps the open requests of its
rooms' turns and offers their answer (`answer_input(request_id, value)`) and
their rejection (`reject_input(request_id, reason)`). It also offers each open
request as `ON_USER_INPUT_REQUIRED` reads it, by its id (`input_request`): its
room, channel, tool call and the actor of its turn, which `input_request`
carries, so the host's door can tell who was asked before it answers, and
nothing for a request that is no longer open or, given an organization, whose
room is another organization's (§17.2). The request settles
where its tool waits, once, first come first served: an answer the
human-input handler the host gave the channel takes, a hook's block, its
bound, a release, or the owner's outcome, whichever comes first; a later one
never retracts it (§9.3). The executor MUST send `input_request` before it
fires `ON_USER_INPUT_REQUIRED`, and the owner MUST hold an answer for an id
it does not know yet until the request arrives or `input_hold_timeout`
(default 60 seconds) passes, so a request is answerable from its creation
(§9.3); an implementation bounds how many answers it holds. The owner's
outcome reaches the executor as `input_answer`, which settles the request only
while it is still open: an answer the tool reads, or a rejection it reads as a
refusal (§9.3); the executor answers `input_taken`, and the owner's door
answers whether the waiting tool read its outcome. A request settled on the
executor otherwise sends `input_closed`, and the owner closes its record. A
request belongs to the turn that opened it; one still open when its turn ends
is withdrawn on both sides, its waiter reading it released, but a detached
one (a request no tool waits on, which its creator alone releases): the
owner's record goes with the turn while the request stays open on the
executor, answerable there. One a task opens after its
turn ended is the host's handler's alone.

requirements.applies: §10.6.6 Hooks; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
A trigger fires where the work it observes runs. These triggers fire on the
executor that hosts the channel, during a turn or between turns (a thinker's
thought, a human-input request's notification):

| Trigger | Fires on |
|---|---|
| `BEFORE_AI_CONTEXT_BUILD` (Planned) | Executor |
| `BEFORE_AI_GENERATION` | Executor |
| `ON_AI_THINKING` | Executor |
| `ON_AI_RESPONSE` | Executor |
| `BEFORE_TOOL_USE` | Executor |
| `AFTER_TOOL_ROUND` | Executor |
| `ON_TOOL_CALL` | Executor |
| `ON_USER_INPUT_REQUIRED` | Executor |
| `ON_SPEAK_DECISION` | Executor |
| `ON_THOUGHT` | Executor |
| `ON_PLAN_UPDATED` | Executor |
| Every other trigger of §9.2 | Owner |

On the owner fire, among others, `ON_ERROR` (from the turn's `error` frame,
§9.2), `ON_TASK_CREATED` (from the output's tasks), `BEFORE_BROADCAST` on each
stored segment (§9.5), `AFTER_BROADCAST`, and the triggers that owner-served
tools and discussions fire (`ON_HANDOFF`, `ON_TASK_DELEGATED`,
`ON_STATUS_POSTED`, `ON_SPEAK_QUEUE`, `ON_DISPATCH_DECISION`).

requirements.applies: §10.6.6 Hooks; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Registration.** A hook on an executor trigger registers on the executor
that runs the turns it observes. Registered on the kit, it is a registration
on the kit's own executor: it fires for the turns of the channels the kit
holds live, and for the calls outside any turn below. A channel the kit holds
by its declaration alone (§10.6.2) runs its turns on another executor, where
such a hook would never fire. An implementation MUST therefore refuse a hook
on an executor trigger registered on the kit that such a channel could fire
(its channel filter does not leave the channel out), and the declaration of
such a channel while such a hook is registered, naming the executor where the
hook registers instead. A room hook on an executor trigger registered on the
kit is refused while the kit holds any channel by its declaration alone: the
room's channels are not known when it registers. A host registers its turn
hooks with one function it runs on every executor, the kit's own included, so
its setup takes one path too. The implementation's own hooks on these triggers (a scorer of turns, a
console's view of tool calls) register on executors the same way, and one that
writes (a scorer recording an observation) writes through `TurnHost`.

A trigger of the table that fires in the owner's process outside any turn (a
speech-to-speech session's tool calls and its reasoning delegations, §12.4 and
§12.4.1; a conference's tool calls, §12.10) fires the hooks registered on the
kit's own executor: one registration covers both.

requirements.applies: §10.6.6 Hooks; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Room hooks.** A room hook on an executor trigger the kit registers for a
room (above) is its own executor's hook for that room, and no request names
it. One for a channel other executors run (§9.1) is registered on the
executors under a name. The owner keeps which names a room has, as it keeps
the room's other hooks, and the request carries them in `room_hooks`: the
executor runs the hooks registered under those names for that turn. An
executor that has not registered every name a request carries does not take
it (§10.6.7), so a turn never runs without one of its room's hooks. On an
executor a name carries at most one hook per trigger, and a hook registered
again under a name and a trigger it already carries replaces the first. A
name the room enables joins the room's scope (§9.1): enabling a name a hook
of the room already holds, the room's own or another enabled one, MUST be
refused, so that a room never holds two hooks of one name.

requirements.applies: §10.6.6 Hooks; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Context.** A hook on the executor receives the `RoomContext` its room's
owner builds when the hook fires, asked as the `host_call` verb `room_context`,
as a hook on the owner does; once its turn is over, or when a cut leaves the
owner no longer answering it, the context the turn started with. Outside any
turn (an external agent's own activity between two prompts) it receives the
context of the last turn the executor ran in that room, and none when it ran
no turn there. A context the owner fails to build is one the hook does not
get, as on the owner. A hook
changes a room only through `TurnHost` (§10.6.5); between turns, where
`TurnHost` is empty, it changes none.

requirements.applies: §10.6.7 Placement; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
An executor declares the channels it can host and the names of the room hooks
it registered. The backend MUST deliver a request only to an executor that
declares the request's channel and registered every name of its `room_hooks`;
a request no executor accepts within `accept_timeout` fails (§10.6.8). An
executor declares its channels as ids and prefixes: an entry ending in `*`
declares every channel whose id starts with what precedes it (`acme-*`), and
`*` alone every channel; an entry with a `*` anywhere else is refused when the
executor is built. A distributed backend tells these entries to the other
processes as they are. An executor given a predicate, or given no
declaration at all (every channel), takes the turns of its own process only.
A pool of executors that build an organization's agents from its
configuration declares the organization's prefix, so an agent created after
the pool started needs no executor told of it. A declaration names no room
and no organization (§17.2): an executor declaring `*` takes the declared
channels of every organization its backend's owners serve, and a host keeps
apart what it must by the channel ids it assigns. A turn or channel call
placed on an executor whose factory builds nothing for its channel fails with
`no_executor`, and is not placed again (§10.6.2). That executor still holds
the room for the channel, so the room's next turns go to it while it lives
and takes them: a host gives every executor a factory that builds every
channel its entries cover.
A turn placed on an executor of the owner's own process is carried in that
process, as the in-memory backend carries it; one placed elsewhere crosses
the backend's transport. A backend that knows every executor alive (the
in-memory one; a distributed one keeping a registry of the executors alive and
what they declare) fails at once, with `no_executor`, a request none of them
declares. The owner's own executor, the one that runs the channels the owner
holds live, takes their turns, channel calls and committed events: a backend
MUST place them on it and on no other executor, whatever else declares the
channel, and one it does not take (a room hook it does not define) fails with
`no_executor`. Once the owner's own executor closed (a host closing it while
the owner runs), they fail with `no_executor` too: they are never placed on
another executor, whose copy of the channel would run without the live
channel's state. The channel's `room_attached` and `room_detached`
(§10.6.3) reach that executor alone, for the same reason. An agent a host
runs on an executor of its own is one the owner holds by its declaration
(§10.6.2). A request MUST reach one executor at
most: a process that refuses it
(its executor closed) has it placed again; one that does not answer it within
`accept_timeout` loses the turn (`executor_lost`), which is never handed to
another. A
backend MUST place a room's turns of a channel on the executor that ran its
previous one while that executor lives and takes the turn, so its caches stay
warm and its session state stays, the session state the room needs among it
(an ACP session, a speak policy's listening state, §10.6.2): "the same
executor for the session's life" is the case where one executor holds the
room. The executor that holds a room's state for a channel is the one that
took its last turn or channel call, while it serves and declares the
channel. A channel control message is placed as §10.6.3 says.

requirements.applies: §10.6.7 Placement; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Which agents can answer.** A backend lists the executors it carries turns
to, the owner's own aside: each one's id, process, declared entries, room hook
names, last beat, and whether it is online, that is not closed and beating
within `heartbeat_timeout` (§10.6.8); a closed executor is not listed, and a
silent one stays listed, offline, until its process's entry is forgotten. An
agent is online in a room while an executor online covers it there, declaring
its channel and defining the room's enabled hooks; an agent the owner holds
live, while the owner's own executor takes its turns there. The owner answers
a room's agent presence, each agent with the executors covering it, sorted by
channel id. It publishes an agent's presence in a room as the presence
ephemerals of §8.4 (`presence_online` / `presence_offline`, `user_id` the
agent's channel id): as the agent is attached there, and, for an agent it
holds by its declaration, in each active or paused room the agent is attached
to when the executors covering it change. It looks at the executors at each
heartbeat interval, and at once when an executor of its process other than its
own is served or closes, so an executor's silence turns its agents offline at
`heartbeat_timeout`, never at one late beat. A backend keeps the presence last
published per agent and room, and each change is published by the owner that
records it there first: of the owners that see the same change, one alone
publishes it, and, where the backend keeps it beyond the owner's process (a
distributed backend), an owner restarting publishes nothing that did not
change. A publication, or a claim, that fails is tried again at a later look
of the owner that made it, while that owner runs; closing, it lets go of the
claims it could not publish, which the room's next change or attach, or an
owner that starts, then publishes. A detach, and a room's close, forget what
was published for the agent in the room. A backend that cannot list its
executors has the owner publish nothing for the agents it holds by
declaration, whose presence it cannot tell.

requirements.applies: §10.6.8 Liveness, cancellation and errors; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Liveness, both ways.** While a turn runs, each side MUST send a message on
its link at least every `heartbeat_interval` (default 2 seconds), a
`heartbeat` when it has nothing else to send, the in-memory backend included.

- The owner MUST fail the turn when `accepted` does not come within
  `accept_timeout` (default 10 seconds), with `no_executor` when no executor
  that could take the request (§10.6.7) ran meanwhile and `executor_lost`
  otherwise, and when the executor stays silent for `heartbeat_timeout`
  (default 10 seconds), with `executor_lost`.
- The executor MUST cut the turn as `owner_lost` when the owner stays silent
  for `heartbeat_timeout`, and stop sending its frames: its tools stop acting
  for an owner that no longer reads them, and an ACP session's next prompt is
  not held behind a turn nobody reads (§6.4).

Silence is counted only while the side that counts it runs: a stall of its own
event loop is not the other side's silence. In memory, where the executor's
CPU is the owner's stall, a busy turn is therefore never lost.

An executor in a process of its own MUST beat from a context the turn's work
cannot stall (a thread of its own), so a turn busy with its CPU, the case the
backend exists for, still beats. That beat MAY travel outside the turn's
numbered messages (a record of the executor alive that its thread refreshes,
on the transport's clock): once an executor took the turn, the owner counts
it as a message from that executor while that executor's process still runs
the turn, which it does until the turn's `end` is written (a turn whose work
ended without its `end` is then lost, not waited for); before, only `accepted` counts, so a turn no executor takes still fails
within `accept_timeout`. An executor beats as one process's: the same id
restarted in another process beats for none of the first one's turns. A slow
turn that keeps beating is never
failed by the owner: the framework sets no timeout of its own around
`on_event()` (§13.6), and the heartbeat tells a slow turn from a lost executor
without one. A turn that failed ends as an
`on_event()` that raised: its target is recorded failed in the delivery set,
`ON_ERROR` fires, and the caller reads the error (§10.1 step 18); a stream
already read ends as a stream that raised (§12.2 step 13s), its stored
segments kept. The owner cancels the turn's owner-served calls and sends
`cancel` to the executor it lost, best effort. The turn commits nothing by
itself, so its failure leaves no index unaccounted for, and the lane moves on.

requirements.applies: §10.6.8 Liveness, cancellation and errors; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Cancellation.** The owner's ways of ending a turn early keep their local
meaning, each its own message:

- the reader stops reading: `close` (§10.6.4), a reader's close;
- the turn's cascade is cancelled (§10.1, *Explicit delivery cancellation*;
  the kit's close, as it starts, with the reason `kit_closed`, §12.10.4):
  `cancel`, with the cascade's reason; the executor cancels
  the turn's work as its own process would cancel it locally, its running
  tool handlers included (§21.6). A turn its cascade would start once
  cancelled is never submitted, and a submission the cancellation interrupts
  after its hand-over gives the turn up: the backend releases it, and its
  executor cuts it as it would cut one whose owner was lost;
- a steering `Cancel` (§21.3): `steer`.

An executor cancels a turn's work once: a `close` and a `cancel` that reach it
in either order let the cleanup the first one started, the channel's
finalizers included, run to its end before `end`.

The turn then ends with what such an end produces locally (its loop's end with
reason `cancelled`, its open calls closed, §6.4 *A turn cut short*), then
`end`. An `end` that does not come within `cancel_timeout` (default 5 seconds)
after `cancel` is reported as incomplete drainage (§10.1): the turn ends
failed, the owner drops its later frames, and nothing reports its cleanup
done. After `close`, the owner waits for `end` while the executor keeps
beating: a call already running is let finish (§12.2 step 13s), within its
own bound (§21.6). A turn still open when its owner itself closes (the kit's
close, once the grace it gives its running work is over, §12.10.4) is given
up and owes no `end`:
the owner waits for nothing more from its executor and drops its later
frames, and its reader fails it with `backend_closed`, a reason of its own (the
owner's backend closed; its executor is not lost, so never `executor_lost`),
which a host reads on the error a turn link raises; the call the kit's close
cut reads its cut (`kit_closed`), never that failure as its error. The
backend releases the turn, and its executor cuts it as it would
cut one whose owner was lost, at once when the release reaches it, else after
`heartbeat_timeout` of silence, except the turns the close runs under, those
of every `close()` the kit's shutdown answers (§10.6.5, §12.10.4); a cascade
that read it counts its cleanup done. A turn already over
keeps what its end reported: one whose `end` is owed stays incomplete.

requirements.applies: §10.6.8 Liveness, cancellation and errors; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Steering.** The owner offers the host an asynchronous `steer(directive,
channel_id, room_id | turn_id | null)` that answers the number of loops it
reached; across the backend a turn's id names its loop. It resolves the target
turns from the turns it submitted, in the order it started them, under the
rules of §21.3 (a room's most recent loop is the loop of its most recently
started turn still running, the channel's most recent loop that of its most
recently started turn in any room), sends `steer` on each target's link, and
sums their `steer_result`. A channel without steering, or one whose steering
cannot reach the turn yet (it answers none), receives a `Cancel` as the
turn's `cancel`: the owner then waits for `end` as after `close`, without
`cancel_timeout`, and the turn counts as one loop reached. An ACP agent
channel steers a `Cancel` alone, for the turn it names, as its own
cancellation (§6.4 item 7): it answers one once the turn holds its Room
(§6.4 item 7), its session being opened or its prompt out; before that it
answers none, and the owner cuts the turn. A discussion that holds the room cuts its turns this way
(§19.7.5). The turns a host can steer are those the process it
steers from submitted: with several owner processes, it steers from the one
running the room's delivery (§10.2), and another reaches none of them.

requirements.applies: §10.6.8 Liveness, cancellation and errors; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Errors.** An error record carries the error's kind (the implementation's
name of its class), its message, its arguments and the attributes JSON
carries (what classifies it: a provider's status code and whether it is
retryable, a cut turn's reason, an application's own code), the kinds of the
classes its class derives from, nearest first, and its causes, each a record
of its own, in order. The side that reads a record (the owner for a turn's
error, the executor for what an owner-served call or a host verb raised)
rebuilds one error per record, its causes chained, so what reads it
(`ON_ERROR`'s `error_type`, a task's failure, §23.3, a reader that compares
the error it holds with the turn's, the host's own classification) reads it
as it reads a local one:

- an error of a class the side rebuilds comes back of that class, with its
  arguments and attributes. A side rebuilds the implementation's own classes,
  the language's built-in ones, and the classes its host declares, each with
  its subclasses, a class nested in another or defined in a function
  included. Each side reads what the other raised, so a host declares its
  classes to the owner and to each of its executors, an executor in another
  process included. One that cannot be rebuilt so that it gives back its
  message (a field its message reads did not cross) comes back as the generic
  turn error below, also of that class, its message kept;
- any other comes back as a generic turn error that keeps the kind, the
  classes it derives from and the attributes, and that is also of the nearest
  of those classes the side rebuilds: a host's subclass of a provider error
  still reads as a provider error (its log line, §15.3; `ON_ERROR`);
- a generic turn error that crosses again crosses as the error it stands
  for, its kind and classes unchanged.

A side MUST NOT import a module, nor run a module's code (an attribute hook,
a lazy loader), to resolve a kind or a class a record names: it looks the name up among the
classes already loaded, and one it does not find there is a class it does not
rebuild. The message is for logs and hooks, never for a model (§9.3).

requirements.applies: §10.6.9 Telemetry and prerequisites; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Telemetry.** The request carries the trace context of the broadcast span;
the spans the executor records for the turn (its generations, its tool calls,
its hooks) are its children, so a tracing backend shows one trace across the
processes.

requirements.applies: §10.6.9 Telemetry and prerequisites; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Prerequisites.** An executor in another process needs no store (§10.6.5):
the store is the room owner's, and several owner processes share theirs
(Section 14). The distributed lock manager of §13.5 is what several owner processes need among themselves; an
executor takes no room lock. Every process of a backend keeps the same
timeouts (§10.6.8).

requirements.applies: §10.6.9 Telemetry and prerequisites; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Addressing and trust.** Work a turn began that reaches the owner after the
turn (§10.6.3) goes to the owner process that submitted the turn, which the
backend records as it carries the request, and is waited for while that
process lives; with several owner processes, the others do not see it. A
channel control a distributed backend carries is applied on the executor
before the owner goes on, as in memory. A distributed backend's transport is its trust
boundary: the executor ids and owner addresses its messages carry are not
authenticated beyond it, so whoever can write to the transport can act as an
executor or an owner, as whoever can read it reads the rooms' turns. It is
restricted as the rooms are (credentials, encryption in transit).

requirements.applies: §10.6.9 Telemetry and prerequisites; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**On the owner.** Ordering (per room, in index order), the reentry of response
events as commit passes, chain depth (§8.3), the persistence of streamed
segments and their hooks, the delivery to streaming targets, the turn record
(§6.4) and the caller's `turns` are the owner's, read off the frames.

requirements.applies: §11.1 Identity Resolver Interface; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
```
IdentityResolver (interface)
└── resolve(message: InboundMessage, context: RoomContext) → IdentityResult
```

requirements.applies: §11.1 Identity Resolver Interface; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**IdentityResult:**

```
IdentityResult
├── status: IdentificationStatus            # IDENTIFIED, AMBIGUOUS, UNKNOWN, PENDING, CHALLENGE_SENT, REJECTED
├── identity: Identity | null               # Resolved identity (if IDENTIFIED)
├── candidates: list<Identity>              # Candidate identities (if AMBIGUOUS)
└── metadata: map<string, any>              # Resolution metadata
```

requirements.applies: §11.2 Resolution Pipeline; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
```
Inbound arrives (channel_type, sender_address)
      │
      ▼
IdentityResolver.resolve(message, context)
      │
      ▼
Returns IdentityResult
      │
      ├── IDENTIFIED (1 match)
      │   └── Create participant with identity_id set
      │
      ├── AMBIGUOUS (N matches)
      │   ├── Fire ON_IDENTITY_AMBIGUOUS hook
      │   └── Hook returns:
      │       ├── resolved(identity) → use that identity
      │       ├── pending() or null → create pending participant
      │       ├── challenge(inject) → commit the challenge (§9.4), block processing
      │       └── reject() → reject the message
      │
      └── UNKNOWN (0 matches), or the resolver's REJECTED
          ├── Fire ON_IDENTITY_UNKNOWN hook
          └── Hook returns:
              ├── resolved(identity) → use that identity
              ├── pending(candidates) → create pending participant
              ├── challenge(inject) → commit the challenge (§9.4), block processing
              ├── reject() → reject the message
              └── null → UNKNOWN: process the message, its sender unresolved;
                         REJECTED: block it with the resolver's message,
                         else identity_rejected
```

Identity hooks receive the event, the room context and the IdentityResult, and
run in registration order. The first one that returns a result decides; one
that raises is logged and the next one runs. A result whose status the trigger
does not act on is read as null. A hook registered on these two triggers
through HookRegistration (Section 9.1) runs after them as an observer and
cannot decide. The pending participant carries the resolver's candidates on
ON_IDENTITY_AMBIGUOUS, and on ON_IDENTITY_UNKNOWN the hook's, else the
resolver's.

A resolver's REJECTED is its refusal: the identity hooks of
ON_IDENTITY_UNKNOWN read it as REJECTED, with its message, and may still
name, pend, challenge or reject the sender, but when none of them decides,
the message is blocked with the resolver's message, else `identity_rejected`,
and nothing of it is stored.

A pending sender is never given a record under the id the channel gave: the
event is sent under the room's record of that id when one was reached through
the channel (a member the host added), else under the sender's own record,
created for them: `pending-` and the first 16 hexadecimal digits of the
SHA-256 of the channel id, U+001F and the sender id, one per sender and
channel. A sender who chooses their id (on a WebSocket, in an HTTP body) could
otherwise take an identity's id: the pending record under it
would be completed when that identity is resolved on another channel, and
its impostor's next message would pass for an identified sender (§11.6). The
sender's address names that record on its channel (§5.5): an advisor's
resolution of it spares the sender resolution (§11.6), and routing finds
their room by it (§10.4 step 1).

requirements.applies: §11.3 Identity Hook Result; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
```
IdentityHookResult
├── status: IdentificationStatus            # The outcome (below)
├── identity: Identity | null               # For IDENTIFIED: the sender
├── display_name: string | null             # Set by pending(); not read
├── candidates: list<Identity> | null       # For PENDING, on UNKNOWN only
├── inject: InjectedEvent | null            # For CHALLENGE_SENT: the challenge
├── reason: string | null                   # For REJECTED: the block's reason
├── challenge_type: string | null           # Not read by the framework
└── message: string | null                  # Set by challenge(); not read
```

`resolved(identity)`, `pending(display_name, candidates)`,
`challenge(inject, message)` and `reject(reason)` set `status` to IDENTIFIED,
PENDING, CHALLENGE_SENT and REJECTED; `reject` defaults its reason to
"Unknown sender". A challenge blocks the message with the reason
`identity_challenge_sent`, and its `inject` is committed as an injected event
(§9.4), in a cascade of its own; a REJECTED result with no reason blocks it
with `identity_rejected` on ON_IDENTITY_AMBIGUOUS and `unknown_sender` on
ON_IDENTITY_UNKNOWN.

requirements.applies: §11.4 Channel Type Filtering; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
Implementations SHOULD support configuring which channel types trigger identity
resolution. Not all channels carry meaningful identity information (e.g., an
internal WebSocket may not need identity resolution).

requirements.applies: §11.5 Timeout Handling; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
If identity resolution exceeds the configured timeout, the implementation MUST:

1. Treat the result as UNKNOWN.
2. Emit an `identity_timeout` framework event.
3. Continue processing the inbound message (do not block).

requirements.applies: §11.6 Senders With Nothing To Resolve; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
A resolver maps an **address** — a number, an email, a handle — to an Identity.
Two senders carry no such question, and an implementation MUST NOT run
resolution for them:

1. **The channel names its own senders.** A channel MAY declare that its
   inbound `sender_id` is a room `Participant.id` rather than an address. A
   conference is the case this exists for (Section 12.10.4): its utterances
   carry the identity a track was published under, and resolving that is the
   "resolve on the opaque identity" Section 12.10.2 rule 3 rules out.
2. **The room has already identified the sender.** Where the event's
   `participant_id` names, on the event's channel (Section 5.5), a Participant
   of the room whose `identification` is IDENTIFIED, the sender's own record
   (Section 11.2) included, the question has been answered and the answer is
   on the roster. The same id on a channel the
   participant was never reached through answers nothing, and is resolved.

Case 1 is not the conference alone. The test is where the `sender_id` comes
from. A channel that reads it off the wire carries whatever the remote network
put there, and is not this case. A channel the implementation itself names the
sender of — an interactive terminal, whose sender is a Participant the
implementation chose rather than a party that reached it from outside — is the
same case as the conference, and declares it for the same reason. A channel
whose `sender_id` is supplied by the integrator is neither: it may carry an
address or it may not, which is why Section 11.4 leaves that one to
configuration rather than to the channel.

`PENDING` and `AMBIGUOUS` participants are deliberately not in case 2: a
participant the room *has* is not a participant the room has *identified*, a
resolver may still be what settles it, and the identity hooks of Section 11.2
may still want to challenge or refuse it.

This is not an optimisation. Re-resolving a sender the room has already
identified produces UNKNOWN — no resolver matches a framework identifier — so
`ON_IDENTITY_UNKNOWN` fires per message, and the refusal pattern Section 11.2
provides for (`reject`) then blocks every message from a participant the
implementation itself identified. Skipping it is what keeps that pattern
composable with channels that name their own participants.

When resolution is skipped, the event's `participant_id` MUST be left as the
channel set it, but in case 2 for an event the sender's own record (Section
11.2) names, which is sent under that record's id as their events were while
it was pending; and no
participant record is created or modified: the sender is either already a
participant or deliberately unattributed.

requirements.applies: §11.7 Identity Verification; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
Identification says whose an address is; **verification** says the person
writing has proven it. A number that resolves to Alice says the phone is
Alice's, not that Alice is typing. A service that answers account questions
over a channel needs both. An implementation that supports verification
carries the state, its lifecycle, a label on every message and the hooks;
the integrator keeps the **method** (how a person proves who they are: a
page behind a link, a code, a login) and the **policy** (what a message from
an unverified sender may reach). Verification applies to an IDENTIFIED
sender only; an identification challenge (§11.2) is another matter.

requirements.applies: §11.7.1 State; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
```
Verification
├── identity_id: string
├── organization_id: string | null         # Its scope (§11.7.7)
├── status: VerificationStatus             # §5
├── method: string | null                  # The integrator's name for it ("link", "code", "sso")
├── verified_via: string | null            # Channel the completing request was opened on
├── verified_at: datetime | null
├── expires_at: datetime | null
├── ended_reason: string | null            # "expired", "revoked", "failed" once ended
├── request_id: string | null              # The request open for the identity
└── completed_request_id: string | null    # The request that completed it: its end is
                                           # announced in that request's room
```

A verification belongs to the **identity**: once verified, the person is
verified on every channel and in every room their addresses reach, and
`verified_via` tells where they proved it, for an integrator that requires a
channel of its own. An identity with no record is UNVERIFIED.

requirements.applies: §11.7.2 Requests; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
```
VerificationRequest
├── id: string                             # Public reference
├── identity_id, room_id, channel_id: string
├── organization_id: string | null         # The room's
├── method: string                         # "link", "code", or the integrator's
├── secret_hash: string                     # The secret is never stored in clear
├── window_start: datetime                 # Reception of the message that opened it
├── created_at: datetime
├── expires_at: datetime
├── attempts: int                          # Failed attempts so far
├── max_attempts: int                      # The policy's bound when it was opened
└── status: OPEN | COMPLETED | FAILED | EXPIRED | CANCELLED
```

`request_verification(identity_id, room_id, channel_id, method, window_start)`
opens a request and returns it with its secret, once: the integrator puts the
secret in its link or sends it as a code, and the implementation keeps only
its hash. Its lifetime and attempts come from the configured policy. A
request takes its room's organization, the scope whose messages it verifies;
a caller acting for another organization is refused as for the room itself
(§17.2). An identity that is not verified becomes PENDING; one already verified
stays VERIFIED meanwhile (asking again does not end a verification in force).
Opening a request cancels the identity's earlier open one. `complete_verification(request_id, secret,
method)` is called by the integrator once its own check passed (the page's
PIN, the login); it compares the secret in constant time and refuses a
request that is not OPEN or has expired. A mismatch counts as an attempt, and
so does a failure of the integrator's own check, which it reports with
`record_failed_attempt(request_id)` (a wrong PIN on its page): the bound is
the request's, so a PIN cannot be guessed through the integrator's page. At
the policy's bound the request FAILS, and a request that fails while the
identity is VERIFIED ends that verification too: whoever could not prove it
is not let on as the person (fail closed). A request that expires unanswered
changes nothing. A completion makes the identity
VERIFIED until `now + ttl`, emits `verification_completed` and fires
ON_VERIFICATION_COMPLETED (ASYNC).

requirements.applies: §11.7.3 Labels and holding; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
The inbound pipeline stamps `source.verification` on every event of an
identified sender (§10.1 step 5b), so a hook, a router, a user interface and
a context builder read one fact. An identified sender is the identity the
pipeline resolved for the event, or the IDENTIFIED participant the event's id
names on its channel (Section 5.5): an identity's id arriving through a
channel it was never resolved on carries no verification. While the
identity is not VERIFIED, every such event fires ON_VERIFICATION_REQUIRED
(SYNC), whose hooks decide per message:

- **hold** (the default when no hook passes it): the event is stored and
  delivered marked held, its scope narrowed to the transport channels it
  reached — those both its own visibility and its source binding's include
  (§7.3) — so the room's people and transports (an advisor's console) see
  it and no intelligence channel reads it, in delivery or in context.
  Holding never widens what a message reached. The mark is the event's
  metadata `roomkit:verification_held`: `{visibility, identity_id,
  organization_id}`, the scope it was committed with, which its release
  restores, and whose message it is;
- **pass**: the event goes on as the hooks left it, labelled — where an
  integrator lets a general question through. A hook passes a message
  explicitly, its result's metadata `roomkit:verification` set to `pass`
  (`HookResult.allow_unverified()`); a hook that merely allows it (as one
  that only watches does) does not, nor does a hook that fails, one past
  its timeout among them: the trigger fails open (§9.3), and the message
  is held;
- **block**: the message is refused with the hook's reason,
  `verification_required` when it gives none, before anything of it is
  stored: no record, no delivery.

Where the policy holds, an edit or a deletion (§10.3) from an unverified
sender is refused `verification_required` unless a hook passes it, nothing
of it stored: held, it would still change a message the agents read. The
trigger's ASYNC hooks observe the message the chain let through, never a
blocked one.

Labelling and holding apply where the integrator configured verification;
a configuration MAY label without holding. Opening a request and telling
the sender (sending the link, the code) is the hook's: the method is the
integrator's. The hook reads the sender's verification with
`sender_verification(event, context)`: whose it is, in the room's
organization, and whether a request is open. It answers on the sender's
first message too, when the sender is not a participant of the room yet. A
hook that opens a request only when none is open leaves a sender who writes
again meanwhile in silence; reminding them means opening a new request, since
a secret is never kept to be sent again.

The mark of a held event is the runtime's: the inbound pipeline removes one
that a sender's message carries, and only an event the pipeline held and
labelled not VERIFIED is ever released (§11.7.6). A mark copied by any other
way releases nothing.

Labelling and holding act on messages. In a speech-to-speech session
(§12.4) the model hears the person before any message exists, and their
transcript is recorded afterwards: nothing there is labelled or held, and
holding a transcript would not keep the words from the model. An integrator
that requires verification gates the session itself: it starts the session,
or gives it the instructions and tools that reach an account, only once
`verification_of` reads VERIFIED for the identity in the room's
organization, and on ON_VERIFICATION_ENDED it ends or reconfigures the
session. The implementation does not claim to hold anything there.

requirements.applies: §11.7.4 Codes in the conversation; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
With the method `code`, the secret is a short code the person replies with in
the conversation. A message from the request's identity, in its room, whose
whole text has the code's form (the policy's code length of characters
Unicode gives a digit value, the whitespace around them left out) is an
attempt and is consumed (§10.1 step 5b): the call is refused `verification_code`, its text is never stored nor
broadcast, no agent reads it, and the attempt is recorded by the framework
events alone. A wrong code counts as an attempt and is consumed all the
same. Any other message is an ordinary one: digits with no code request
open, or a code sent in another room. A code is short, so its request's time
and attempts MUST be bounded tightly.

requirements.applies: §11.7.5 The end of a verification; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
A verification ends when its time runs out (EXPIRED) or when the integrator
revokes it (`revoke_verification(identity_id, reason)`, REVOKED); a request
ends when it fails, expires or is cancelled. Each end emits
`verification_ended` and fires ON_VERIFICATION_ENDED (ASYNC) with the reason
and what ended (`ended`: `verification` when the verification in force ended —
expired, revoked, or a request that failed while it held — `request` when a
request alone did, the identity's verification as it was), **when it
happens**, not on the sender's next message: the implementation
arms a timer at `expires_at`, and when it starts it ends the verifications
whose time passed while nothing ran and re-arms the timers of the others,
from the store (`check_verifications()`). A policy MAY open a new request at
once; otherwise the sender's next message meets ON_VERIFICATION_REQUIRED.

requirements.applies: §11.7.6 Releasing held messages; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
When a request completes, the messages its sender wrote while it was open
are released to the room's intelligence channels, unless the policy says
otherwise: the held events of that room whose sender is the identity,
received from `window_start` to the completion, never released before and
not deleted since (a deleted message is no longer said, §10.3), within the
policy's bounds of number and age, the latest by index when more qualify.
Only a message the pipeline itself held is released: its hold mark is the
pipeline's own (§11.7.3), and a mark a sender's message carries releases
nothing. Releasing an event restores the visibility it had before it was held
(`update_event`), its ON_EVENT_UPDATED hooks running on the budget of the
work the release is made in (§9.5.1, §10.3), and the room's intelligence
channels act on it as on any inbound message of its author: nothing is
copied, and the last released event alone solicits an answer, the earlier
ones being its context. The event is handed to the intelligence channels
alone, never again to a transport, and nothing of its first delivery runs
again. A completion releases within its call: a code reply's (§11.7.4)
before the reply's call returns; one made under the room's lock, from a hook,
places the answer in the room's lane at the release, ahead of that work's own
delivery, and the answer leaves its place once that work is over, on the room
as that work left it: a hook that completes the request and lets its event
through has the released message answered first, and one that then closes the
room has no agent answer it. The answer is a regeneration of the released
event (§13.6): `process_timeout`
bounds its wait for the room's lock (`process_timeout` with
`operation = regenerate`), and a room closed or deleted while it waited in the
lane refuses it before any agent runs (`room_refused_event`,
`operation = regenerate`, its `status` null for a room deleted, §8.2); a read
of the room that fails there runs no agent either, the failure recorded as the
regeneration's error.

A held message whose delivery was cancelled (§10.1, *Explicit delivery
cancellation*), before its commit, while it was delivered or while it waited
for its release, is released all the same and solicits no answer: when it is
the last released, no agent answers the release, and the earlier ones are
not answered in its place, since their answer would read the cancelled
message as context. The cancellation is recorded with the held event, so a
release in any process honours it; a cancellation by key reaches the held
messages of the process that received them. The key names the held message
from its call's decision on, a message the room's own work adopted (a hook's
call into its room, §9.5.1) as any, so a release during the message's own
delivery set names its answer too; a message nothing will release, blocked after it
was held or held under a policy that releases nothing, is named no longer
than its call. A completion handle (§10.1, step 18) follows the delivery set
alone: it cancels a held message while that set runs, and past it the key is
what names the message.

A released message MUST reach an agent as its **author's own turn**, never as
an instruction or anything else carrying the application's authority: a
message an unverified sender wrote, quoted or not, gains none by its author
proving who they are. Nothing outside the window is released: what was
written before the request — before a verification was revoked, during a
request that failed — may not be the verified person's.

requirements.applies: §11.7.7 Security floor; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
- A secret carried in a link has at least 128 bits of entropy; a code is
  short, so its request is short-lived and allows few attempts.
- A secret is stored only as its hash, compared in constant time, used once,
  and never logged.
- A completion is refused after the request expired, failed, was cancelled
  or completed, and after the verification was revoked.
- Every transition emits its framework event (§8), the audit trail.
- A link is a bearer secret: forwarded, it verifies whoever opens it and
  passes the method's own check. That check (a PIN, a login) is the
  method's; a method with none SHOULD NOT guard anything that matters.

A request's bound on attempts holds within the reach of the lock manager the
implementation serializes an identity's transitions with (§13.5), under the
key `verification:<organization>:<identity>`: two attempts at a request's
last one count once. A deployment of several processes on one store shares
its lock manager, as it must for its rooms.

Verification state is scoped to the organization as identities are (§17.2).
A message is labelled by the verification of its **room's** organization:
one proven to an organization never verifies the person in another
organization's conversation, whatever the organization the resolver's
identity names.

requirements.applies: §12.1 Architecture Overview; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
RoomKit supports four real-time media architectures:

```
Architecture 1: STT/TTS Pipeline (VoiceChannel)
┌──────────┐     ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────┐     ┌─────┐     ┌──────────┐
│ Client   │────→│Audio Pipeline│────→│   STT    │────→│Room │────→│   TTS    │────→ Client
│ (audio)  │     │(denoise/VAD/ │     │Provider  │     │Kit  │     │Provider  │
└──────────┘     │ diarization) │     └──────────┘     └─────┘     └──────────┘
                 └──────────────┘

Architecture 2: Speech-to-Speech (RealtimeVoiceChannel)
┌──────────┐     ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────────────────┐     ┌──────────┐
│ Client   │────→│Audio Pipeline│────→│ Speech-to-Speech API     │────→│ Client   │
│ (audio)  │     │  (optional)  │     │ (OpenAI Realtime, etc.)  │     │ (audio)  │
└──────────┘     └──────────────┘     └────────────┬─────────────┘     └──────────┘
                  denoise, diarize                  │
                                              transcriptions
                                              tool calls
                                                    │
                                                    ▼
                                               ┌─────────┐
                                               │ RoomKit │
                                               │ (events)│
                                               └─────────┘
```

requirements.applies: §12.1 Architecture Overview; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Choosing between architectures:**

| Criterion | VoiceChannel (STT/TTS) | RealtimeVoiceChannel (Speech-to-Speech) | VoiceChannel (Bridge) | ConferenceChannel (SFU) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Latency** | Moderate (~500-800ms TTFA with streaming) | Lower — end-to-end streaming | Lowest — direct audio forwarding | Low — SFU forwards media directly between clients |
| **Control** | Full — choose STT, LLM, TTS | Limited — provider bundles all; with reasoning delegation (Section 12.4.1) the reasoning model is the integrator's | Full pipeline, no AI required | Control plane only — media plane is external |
| **Text access** | Always — utterances become RoomEvents | Optional — if transcription configured | Optional — if STT configured | Per-track STT, attributed per participant |
| **Multi-channel** | Native — text routes to any channel | Requires transcription | Requires STT for text routing | Native — transcripts are RoomEvents |
| **AI involvement** | Required (generates responses) | Required (speech-to-speech) | Optional (observer/monitor) | Optional (bot participant) |
| **Voice quality** | Depends on TTS provider | Native speech generation | Original voice preserved | Original voice preserved |
| **Pipeline control** | Full audio pipeline (all stages) | Pipeline optional | Full pipeline (all stages) | Per-track inbound lanes (no AEC/diarization) |
| **Use when** | AI voice agent with text in the loop | Lowest latency AI with native voice | Human-to-human calls, conferencing, call center | Multi-party video conferences, AI in meetings |

All four architectures MAY coexist in the same room. For example, a room could
have a VoiceChannel for a human participant (PSTN/SIP) and a RealtimeVoiceChannel
for the AI agent, with text events bridging them. Or two VoiceChannels in bridge
mode for a human-to-human call with optional AI observation.

```
Architecture 3: Audio Bridge (VoiceChannel with bridge=True)
┌──────────┐     ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────┐
│ Client A │────→│Audio Pipeline│────→│ Audio Bridge  │────→│Audio Pipeline│────→│ Client B │
│ (audio)  │     │  (inbound)   │     │ (forward/mix) │     │  (outbound)  │     │ (audio)  │
└──────────┘     └──────────────┘     └───────┬───────┘     └──────────────┘     └──────────┘
                                              │
                                         (optional)
                                       STT transcription
                                              │
                                              ▼
                                         ┌─────────┐
                                         │ RoomKit │
                                         │ (events)│
                                         └─────────┘
```

```
Architecture 4: SFU Conference (ConferenceChannel — Section 12.10)
┌──────────┐           ┌─────────────────┐           ┌──────────┐
│ Client A │◄─────────►│                 │◄─────────►│ Client B │
│ (browser)│   media   │  External SFU   │   media   │ (browser)│
└──────────┘           │  (media plane)  │           └──────────┘
                       └────────┬────────┘
                                │ bot participant
                                │ (subscribed tracks, published TTS)
                                ▼
                       ┌─────────────────┐
                       │     RoomKit     │
                       │ per-track STT,  │
                       │ vision, TTS bot │
                       │ (control plane) │
                       └─────────────────┘
```

requirements.applies: §12.2 Voice Channel (STT/TTS Pipeline); the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
The Voice Channel processes audio through a pipeline of STT and TTS providers,
converting speech to text events and text responses back to speech.

requirements.applies: §12.2 Voice Channel (STT/TTS Pipeline); the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Required components:**

| Component | Interface | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| VoiceBackend | See below | Real-time audio transport (WebRTC, WebSocket) |
| STTProvider | See below | Speech-to-text conversion |
| TTSProvider | See below | Text-to-speech synthesis |

requirements.applies: §12.2 Voice Channel (STT/TTS Pipeline); the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**VoiceBackend interface:**

```
VoiceBackend (interface)
├── connect(room_id, participant_id, channel_id) → VoiceSession
├── disconnect(session) → void
├── send_audio(session, audio_chunks) → void
│       # Decoded 16-bit PCM only; encoding for the wire is the backend's
│       # An exception raised by audio_chunks MUST reach the caller once the
│       # backend has stopped playing; the backend MAY log and absorb errors of
│       # its own transport
├── send_audio_sync(session, audio_chunk) → void
│       # Send one chunk without awaiting, from an audio callback thread; the
│       # audio bridge sends through it (Section 12.7). Backends that support
│       # bridging SHOULD override the default, which schedules send_audio()
│       # on the calling thread's running event loop (adding latency) and
│       # drops the chunk with a warning when that thread runs no loop
├── cancel_audio(session) → void            # Cancel current playback (if supported)
├── send_dtmf(session, digit, duration_ms) → void  # Send outbound DTMF (RFC 4733)
│
│   # Raw audio callback:
├── on_audio_received(callback) → void      # Raw inbound audio frames from client
│
│   # Barge-in (transport-level detection):
├── on_barge_in(callback) → void            # Client audio detected during playback
│
│   # Session lifecycle:
├── on_session_ready(callback) → void       # Audio path is live, ready for send/receive
├── on_client_disconnected(callback) → void  # Client or transport disconnected
├── get_session(session_id) → VoiceSession | null  # null if sessions are not tracked
├── list_sessions(room_id) → list<VoiceSession>    # Empty if sessions are not tracked
│
│   # Server-side session acceptance:
├── accept(request) → VoiceSession          # Accept an inbound session (SIP/PSTN/WebRTC offer)
│
│   # Protocol tracing:
├── set_trace_emitter(emitter | null) → void  # Set callback for emitting ProtocolTraces
│
│   # Properties:
├── name: string                            # Backend identifier for attribution and logging
├── auto_connect: bool                      # Auto-create session when channel is attached to a room
│
├── capabilities() → VoiceCapability        # What the backend supports
└── close() → void
```

requirements.applies: §12.2 Voice Channel (STT/TTS Pipeline); the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Note:** `on_speech_start`, `on_speech_end`, `on_vad_silence`, and
`on_vad_audio_level` are removed from VoiceBackend. These events are now emitted
by the audio pipeline's VAD provider (Section 12.3). `on_partial_transcription`
is emitted by the STT provider. `on_barge_in` remains on VoiceBackend as it is a
transport-level concern (detecting client audio during active playback).

requirements.applies: §12.2 Voice Channel (STT/TTS Pipeline); the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**VoiceCapability** flags:

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| INTERRUPTION | Can cancel TTS playback |
| BARGE_IN | Detect user audio during TTS playback |
| NATIVE_AEC | Backend provides built-in echo cancellation (skip pipeline AEC) |
| NATIVE_AGC | Backend provides built-in gain control (skip pipeline AGC) |
| DTMF_INBAND | Backend receives in-band DTMF tones in audio stream |
| DTMF_SIGNALING | Backend sends and receives DTMF via signaling (RFC 4733) |
| NATIVE_BRIDGE | Backend can bridge audio at the transport level (RTP relay) |

When a VoiceBackend declares `NATIVE_AEC` or `NATIVE_AGC`, the pipeline MUST
skip the corresponding stage automatically, even if a provider is configured in
`AudioPipelineConfig`. This prevents double processing.

When a VoiceBackend declares `DTMF_SIGNALING`, DTMF events arrive via the
signaling layer (not the audio stream). The pipeline's DTMFDetector handles
in-band detection only. Implementations MUST merge both sources into the same
ON_DTMF hook.

requirements.applies: §12.2 Voice Channel (STT/TTS Pipeline); the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**VoiceSession:**

```
VoiceSession
├── id: string                              # Session identifier
├── room_id: string                         # Associated room
├── participant_id: string                  # Associated participant
├── channel_id: string                      # Associated voice channel
├── state: VoiceSessionState                # Current session state
├── created_at: datetime                    # Session start time
├── metadata: map<string, any>              # Session-specific data
└── last_usage: map<string, any>            # Read-only: what the provider recorded last (Section 12.4.2)
```

requirements.applies: §12.2 Voice Channel (STT/TTS Pipeline); the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**VoiceSessionState** enumeration:

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| CONNECTING | Session is being established (transport handshake, provider init) |
| ACTIVE | Audio is flowing bidirectionally |
| PAUSED | Session temporarily suspended (e.g., hold, mute) |
| ENDED | Session terminated — no further audio |

requirements.applies: §12.2 Voice Channel (STT/TTS Pipeline); the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Transitions:**

- CONNECTING → ACTIVE: Transport connected and provider ready.
- ACTIVE → PAUSED: Integrator pauses session (e.g., call hold).
- PAUSED → ACTIVE: Integrator resumes session.
- ACTIVE → ENDED: Session terminated (user hangup, timeout, integrator call).
- CONNECTING → ENDED: Connection failed.
- PAUSED → ENDED: Session terminated while paused.

Implementations MUST NOT allow transitions from ENDED to any other state. A new
session MUST be created if the participant reconnects.

requirements.applies: §12.2 Voice Channel (STT/TTS Pipeline); the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**STTProvider interface:**

```
STTProvider (interface)
├── name: string
├── supports_language_override: bool (default false)
│       # Whether transcribe/transcribe_stream honour a per-call language
├── supports_diarization: bool (default false)
│       # Whether final results say who spoke (Section 12.2.3)
├── keeps_stream_across_turns: bool (default false)
│       # Whether one stream carries turn after turn, a final for each
├── transcribe(audio_chunk, language: string | null) → TranscriptionResult
└── transcribe_stream(audio_stream, language: string | null) → async_iterator<TranscriptionResult>

TranscriptionResult
├── text: string
├── is_final: bool
├── confidence: float | null
├── language: string | null                 # The language the provider reports for the text
└── segments: list<SpeakerSegment>          # Who spoke which part of text (Section 12.2.3);
                                            # empty when the provider attributes nothing

SpeakerSegment
├── speaker: string | null                  # Provider label, stable within one stream; null = unattributed
├── text: string
├── start_ms: int | null                    # Offsets from the start of the stream
└── end_ms: int | null
```

`language` on a call overrides the provider's configured language for that
call only. A provider that cannot honour it MUST report
`supports_language_override = false`, and a Voice Channel MUST NOT pass a
language to such a provider. `TranscriptionResult.language` is what the
provider reports — what it detected when it was asked to detect — and MUST NOT
be back-filled from the request: null means the provider said nothing.

A Voice Channel SHOULD let the STT language be chosen per session at runtime.
The choice applies from the next stream opened for that session: a stream is
opened per utterance (VAD mode) or per turn (continuous mode, but for a kept
stream, below), and every streaming STT API RoomKit targets fixes the language
for the life of a stream.

requirements.applies: §12.2 Voice Channel (STT/TTS Pipeline); the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Kept streams.** In continuous mode a Voice Channel opens a stream per turn,
except for a provider that diarizes (its labels hold within one stream,
Section 12.2.3) or that reports `keeps_stream_across_turns`: its model cuts
the turns within one stream, a final for each, and keeps listening. The
channel MUST keep such a stream open across turns, as Section 12.2.3 *Stream
lifetime* says for a diarizing one: a new stream only when the provider ends
it, on an error, or on a language change; silence filling a pause; a final
discarded as echo leaving the stream open. Its finals MUST reach the room in
the order they were produced, the reply to one never holding back the next.
A provider whose text trails its turn events needs it: Voxtral Realtime 3
writes a word a streaming delay after hearing it, while its turn events come
at once, so on a stream per turn a turn started soon after the last one is
sent half to the stream being closed and reaches the room in pieces ("What
is the capital of Italy?", "Answer", "in one word.", reproduced 2026-10-21).
Such a provider gives a turn's final once its last words can have arrived,
and before the next turn's own words can: RoomKit's Voxtral provider waits the
delay plus 100 ms after the end, and 0.95 of the delay once the next turn has
started (a turn's last words came up to 0.9 of the delay after its end, the
next turn's first word no sooner than a delay after it, measured 2026-10-21).
The typical flow starts a session in a detecting mode (Deepgram `multi`), reads
the reported language, and pins the following streams to it. An implementation
MAY ship that flow as a policy; it MUST leave the primitive reachable from
hooks.

requirements.applies: §12.2 Voice Channel (STT/TTS Pipeline); the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Audio between streams.** In continuous mode, audio that arrives while no
stream is open (between two turns, during a reconnect after an error) is
carried into the next stream, so a reconnect loses no speech. What is carried
MUST be bounded: a reconnect that takes long (a service that does not answer
its handshake) would otherwise hand the next stream a backlog the service
refuses, or a lag behind the conversation that only grows. A Voice Channel
keeps the most recent audio and drops the oldest, and MUST expose how much it
dropped (RoomKit keeps 5 s and logs a warning naming the seconds dropped).
A provider whose service limits how far ahead of real time audio may be sent
MUST pace what it sends rather than send a backlog at once. Meta's realtime
service refuses a stream sent 7 s or more ahead at once ("Audio processing
backlog too large", measured 2026-10-07); RoomKit's Meta provider sends at
most 3 s at once, then at most twice real time until it has caught up.

requirements.applies: §12.2 Voice Channel (STT/TTS Pipeline); the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**TTSProvider interface:**

```
TTSProvider (interface)
├── name: string
├── supports_streaming_input: bool (default false)
│       # Whether this TTS accepts streaming text input
├── context_level: TTSContextLevel (default NONE)
│       # What conversation context this TTS consumes (Section 12.2.2)
├── max_dialogue_speakers: int (default 0)
│       # Distinct speakers one synthesize_dialogue call can voice; 0 = no dialogue
├── available_voices() → VoiceInfo[]
│       # Curated offline catalog (MAY be empty); no API call
├── list_voices(language: string | null, gender: string | null,
│               query: string | null) → VoiceInfo[]
│       # Live catalog; default: available_voices(), filtered
├── synthesize(text, voice: string | null) → AudioContent
```
