requirements.applies: §13.5 Room-Level Locking; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Serialization scope.** The room lock MUST cover the locked pre-commit
section, the commit point, and broadcast planning (§10.1 steps 6–12):
everything that reads room state to decide, assigns the index, writes the
timeline, or resolves the delivery set. A streamed response's rows are the
exception (§4, §9.5.1): their hooks and their commit run without the lock.
External delivery execution (§10.2 step 3) is NOT required to run under the
room lock — it MUST preserve per-room order
(the delivery lane, §10.2), which holding the lock trivially satisfies.
Implementations SHOULD NOT extend the room's critical section with external
I/O (provider calls, AI generation): under a distributed lock manager, lock
tenure is what serializes the whole deployment, and every await spent under
the lock is paid by every other worker waiting on that room. A
`BEFORE_BROADCAST` check that reads only the event is the hook-side case of
that I/O: registered with `needs_lock = false`, it runs off the lock, ordered
by the room's admission ticket instead (§9.5.1).

```
RoomLockManager (interface)
├── acquire(room_id) → lock
└── release(lock) → void
```

requirements.applies: §13.5 Room-Level Locking; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**A release that fails.** `release` can fail: a distributed lock manager can
lose its connection, or find its lease already expired. A failed release
MUST NOT change anything the locked section decided or wrote: an event it committed
stays committed, a refusal it decided stays a refusal, and the delivery it
planned executes. The operation reports what it did. An inbound result
carries the failure as its `error` when no earlier error was met (§10.1); a
failure met before the release stays the one reported. A lifecycle change
logs it, as does a direct injection, whose result is the committed event
(§10.5). The cascade goes on. The lock manager owns what a failed release
leaves behind, and the next locked section asks it for the lock again.

The room lock MUST be reentrant within one execution context (a task and the
tasks it awaits as its own): code that holds it may call an operation that
takes it again, as a host serialising its own changes of a room does (Section
19.7), and as a tool handler does where an implementation runs delivery under
the room lock (§10.2). Under delivery lanes a turn holds no lock, and a tool
handler's call into its room is a new arrival (§9.5.1). A hook's body lends
the lock its section holds only while the body runs: a task the body spawned,
awaited or not, takes the lock again while the body runs, and once the body
has returned it takes it as any later caller does, though the section still
holds it (§9.5.1).

requirements.applies: §13.5 Room-Level Locking; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Key spaces.** The framework's locks of other kinds than a room's (a room's
delivery claim, an identity's verification lock, §11.7) never share a key with
a room's lock, whatever a room id reads. An in-memory lock manager keeps each
kind in a map of its own, shared by the kits sharing the manager. A manager
shared across processes holds them among its rooms' keys, each led by a NUL
character; a room id holds no NUL character: `create_room` refuses one, and so
does the framework's taking of a room's lock, with the implementation's value
error, before it asks the manager, wherever the id came from (a room written to
the store straight, a router's answer), so that nothing is written. A room's
lock keeps its id: `lock_manager.locked(room_id)` holds the lock the framework
holds.

For single-process deployments, an in-memory lock manager (per-room async mutex)
is sufficient. When a persistent store is shared across multiple processes an
in-memory lock manager is **NOT** sufficient — per-process locks do not
coordinate, so concurrent writers on the same room can interleave. Such
deployments MUST either use a distributed lock manager (e.g. Redis or a
PostgreSQL advisory lock) or rely on storage-layer atomicity for the operations
that require it (index assignment, §8.1). Implementations SHOULD ship at least
one distributed lock manager, and SHOULD detect the unsafe combination of a
shared persistent store with an in-memory lock manager and warn (or refuse) at
initialization.

requirements.applies: §13.5 Room-Level Locking; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Delivery lanes across processes.** A process holds a delivery lane per room
it delivers in, and a lane runs only the delivery sets its own process
planned, since a plan holds live channels. When several processes share a
store, the room's delivery cursor orders them: `delivered_index` (§5.1), the
highest index whose delivery set has run, `-1` before any. A lane runs the set
of the index after the cursor, then advances the cursor by one, a
compare-and-set in the store (`advance_delivered_index`, §14.1) that succeeds
only from the index before. A cursor write the store fails changes nothing
the set did: it is logged, the set's aftermath runs (§10.1 steps 15 and 16),
its call is not cancelled, and the lane takes the cursor as past that index,
so that its own next set runs at once and skips nothing; it writes the cursor
again, from the index the store holds, one index at a time, when it next
moves it. Until then another process's lane waits on that index as on any
hole, and skips it past `gap_timeout`; a store or claim failure after a set
ran leaves the set as it ran too. The sets of one room run under its delivery claim,
a lock of the room's lock manager held apart from the room lock, so that one
event's set completes before the next one's begins across the deployment; a
lane never holds the claim and the room lock together. Every committed index
reaches the lane of the process that committed it once: an index with no
delivery set (a record stored `BLOCKED`, a lifecycle record, §5.1, a record
committed outside the pipeline, §10.5) advances the cursor at its turn and
runs nothing. An instruction's set, which has no index, runs once the cursor
has reached the latest index committed before it (§10.1.1). A committed index
whose set no lane runs (its process stopped between the commit and the
delivery) holds the cursor: a lane that has waited on it for `gap_timeout`
(default 30 s) while no lane held the claim forces the cursor past it and
emits `delivery_skipped` with the indexes skipped (§8.2). The loss is bounded
to what was in flight and observable, and the room never wedges; a lane that
finds its own set skipped drops it, since running it then would break the
room's order. A durable outbox that turns that loss into recovery is a
separate capability (§13.6).

requirements.applies: §13.6 Processing Timeout; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
Implementations SHOULD support a configurable `process_timeout`. Its semantics
are defined **relative to the commit point** (§10.1 step 12) — the atomic
transaction that stores the event as DELIVERED and updates the room counters:

- **Pre-commit phase** (§10.1 steps 1–11: routing, with the identity it
  reads, the router and step 2's waits for the room lock; context build,
  identity resolution, BEFORE_BROADCAST hooks, write-permission check, index
  assignment). This phase decides only and performs no durable write of the
  inbound event: the BLOCKED record that steps 10–11 owe is committed once
  the phase has ended, outside `process_timeout`, as the step 12 commit is.
  `process_timeout` MUST bound this phase, as one deadline from the call's
  start to its decision: a router or a lock that hangs holds the caller no
  longer than the bound. On expiry the implementation MUST abort **before**
  the commit point, leaving no partial durable state: the injected events,
  tasks and observations of the hooks that ran are dropped with the event,
  and the room's next event takes the index it never consumed. It returns
  `InboundResult(blocked=true, reason=process_timeout)` (direct injection,
  whose result is the committed event, raises instead, §10.5). The event MUST
  NOT appear in the timeline. A room step 2 creates is completed whatever
  the deadline (its creation, its ON_ROOM_CREATED hooks, each within its own
  timeout, and its attach), and stays when the event times out next: it is
  the room's state, not the event's; so is step 2's attach or record of a
  routed sender in a room that exists, whose deadline bounds its wait for
  the room lock only. A hook's own timeout reached before the deadline is
  the hook's (`hook_timeout`, then the fail-open or fail-closed rule of
  §9.3); a deadline reached first is the call's: the hook is dropped, and
  nothing reports it as the hook's failure.

- **Commit point** (§10.1 step 12). Once the DELIVERED transaction has
  committed, the event is authoritative. `process_timeout` MUST NOT cancel,
  block, or re-mark it. An implementation MUST NOT wrap the commit and the
  subsequent broadcast in a single cancellable unit whose expiry could leave a
  committed event reported as blocked/failed.

- **Post-commit phase** (§10.1 steps 14–17: delivery-lane execution,
  reentry passes, side effects, async hooks). Slowness here MUST NOT
  invalidate the committed event.
  Each external delivery call is bounded by its transport channel's or
  provider's own timeout (the framework adds none around `deliver()` or
  `on_event()`; a turn's heartbeat tells a lost executor from a slow turn,
  §10.6.8), and failures are reported per channel via `delivery_failed`
  framework events — never by changing the source event's status or the
  returned result to blocked/failed.
  A degraded broadcast SHOULD surface as `broadcast_partial_failure`, with the
  source event remaining DELIVERED. A cascade that a failure stops runs no
  further pass, but still delivers every event it committed, an entry nested
  under its lock included: an event stored is delivered.
  A failure of this phase is reported on the caller's result `error`
  (§10.1, InboundResult), the first one met, and only when no earlier error
  was (a failed release of the room lock, §13.5): the first turn of the
  trigger's own delivery set that failed (each failure also fires ON_ERROR,
  §9.2), a stream the caller reads that raised, and a failure of the
  cascade's own work (a delivery set's execution, a response's commit
  pass); a side effect the store fails to write is logged and never the
  call's `error` (§10.1 step 15). The result's `event` stays the committed
  event, or the instruction its pass decided (§10.1.1). The caller of
  `process_inbound()` reads it on its result, waiting or through the
  completion handle of a detached call (§10.1 step 18), and so does the
  caller of a regeneration; a direct injection, whose result is the
  committed event (§10.5), reports none of it.

requirements.text:
**A caller that stops waiting.** A caller may stop waiting for its call (a
cancelled task, a client gone, an outer timeout of its own). Once the call is
decided (its event committed, a `BLOCKED` record included, or its instruction
decided, §10.1.1), its delivery runs whether or not its caller still waits:
every event it committed is delivered, unless the kit's close has started
(§12.10.4: a delivery queued behind another is dropped, one running, from
its placement in an idle lane on, is cut once the close's grace is over), and
a cancellation the implementation carries from the caller to the call stops
the cascade's turns, as an explicit cancellation does, never its delivery
(§10.1). A caller gone before the
decision makes the call expire as a passed `process_timeout` does, without
the `process_timeout` framework event, since no deadline passed: nothing more
of the trigger is written, the injected events, tasks and observations of the
hooks that ran are dropped with it, and what the call holds (its ticket, the
room lock) is released, the lock only once a call its locked hook's task
nested is over or cut at the call's deadline (§9.5.1). Every event already
committed is delivered all the
same, unless the kit's close has started (§12.10.4): the trigger's, when a
commit in flight wrote it, which decides the call, and the event of a call it
adopted (§9.5.1). A call it adopted that its work waits for and that has not
committed ends with that work, nothing of it stored, but for a call its locked
hook's task nested, which goes on as above (§9.5.1). A room step 2 creates is
completed whatever becomes of its caller, as it is whatever the deadline.

A regeneration re-broadcasts an event already committed, so it has no commit
point of its own: `process_timeout` bounds its wait for the room lock and its
choice of the event to replay, and MUST NOT bound the broadcast, which runs in
the room's delivery lane off the lock like any post-commit phase (§13.5). On
expiry it returns `InboundResult(blocked=true, reason=process_timeout)` and
emits `process_timeout` with `operation = regenerate`. The room's status is
read again when the lane takes the regeneration: a room closed while it waited
refuses it as at its start (§5.1), before the agent runs, with
`InboundResult(blocked=true, reason=room_closed)` and `room_refused_event`.

Implementations MAY additionally model outbound delivery with an explicit
`PENDING → COMMITTED | FAILED` state and an outbox, plus recovery of events
left PENDING, so that a crash between commit and delivery is recoverable. Such
a state applies to **delivery**, not to the committed timeline event.

requirements.text:
Implementations MUST provide a pluggable storage backend via the following
interface:

```
ConversationStore (interface)
│
├── Rooms
│   ├── create_room(room) → Room
│   │                                         # the room as the framework built
│   │                                         # it, its id §10.1 step 2's or a
│   │                                         # fresh one; refuses an id the
│   │                                         # store holds (§14.3)
│   ├── get_room(room_id) → Room | null
│   ├── room_exists(room_id) → bool        # get_room's answer, the room unread
│   ├── update_room(room) → Room              # the whole record, under the
│   │                                         # room lock; keeps the counters
│   │                                         # and the delivered index the
│   │                                         # store holds (§14.3)
│   ├── patch_room_metadata(room_id, patch, unset = []) → Room | null
│   │                                         # merges patch into the metadata,
│   │                                         # unset's keys removed first, and
│   │                                         # writes nothing else of the room;
│   │                                         # null for an unknown room
│   ├── delete_room(room_id) → void
│   ├── list_rooms(offset = 0, limit = 50) → list<Room>
│   ├── find_rooms(organization_id | null, status | null, metadata_filter | null,
│   │              limit = 100, offset = 0) → list<Room>
│   ├── find_latest_room(participant_id, channel_type | null, status | null)
│   │                         → Room | null
│   │                                         # the newest room holding the
│   │                                         # participant's record, on any
│   │                                         # channel, or a binding naming
│   │                                         # them, of channel_type when
│   │                                         # given: the last created, the
│   │                                         # greatest id by code point
│   │                                         # breaking a tie
│   ├── find_room_id_by_channel(channel_id, status | null) → string | null
│   │                                         # the oldest room binding the
│   │                                         # channel, as
│   │                                         # find_room_ids_by_channel
│   │                                         # orders rooms
│   ├── update_room_if(room, status, paused_at, last_activity_at) → Room | null
│   │                                         # update_room, only while the
│   │                                         # stored room holds the status,
│   │                                         # pause and last activity the
│   │                                         # write was computed from: the
│   │                                         # compare-and-set a timer
│   │                                         # transition writes (§5.1); null
│   │                                         # and nothing written otherwise
│   ├── load_room_context(room_id) → (Room | null, list<ChannelBinding>,
│   │                                 list<Participant>)
│   │                                         # the three reads a room's context
│   │                                         # takes (§10.1 step 3), together
│   ├── get_conversation(room_id, limit = 50, after_index | null) → list<RoomEvent>
│   │                                         # the conversation a context holds
│   │                                         # (§7.5 rule 8)
│   ├── get_timeline(room_id, event_filter | null, limit = 50, after_index | null,
│   │                newest_first = false) → list<RoomEvent>
│   │                                         # list_events of every type the
│   │                                         # room received
│   ├── get_delivered_index(room_id) → int    # -1 before any set ran (§13.5)
│   ├── advance_delivered_index(room_id, index, force = false) → bool
│   │                                         # compare-and-set from index - 1, or
│   │                                         # from any lower value when forced
│   ├── get_private_state(room_id, key) → map | null
│   │                                         # a key the implementation keeps for
│   │                                         # itself, apart from the room's
│   │                                         # metadata; the caller's copy (§14.4)
│   ├── set_private_state(room_id, key, value | null) → void
│   │                                         # under the room lock; nothing for an
│   │                                         # unknown room; null removes the key;
│   │                                         # removes the metadata's copy under the
│   │                                         # key; deleted with the room
│   │   # A key is the implementation's (the register of authors is
│   │   # author_register, §10.1 step 12; a discussion's task results to
│   │   # post are _speak_queue_results, §19.7.5 rule 16) and reserves the
│   │   # same key in the room's metadata: a store that keeps no private
│   │   # state keeps it there, and set removes the copy there. Only the
│   │   # runtime writes the key there (§5.1).
│   ├── find_room_id_by_binding(channel_id, participant_id, identity_id, filter,
│   │                           recipient_key) → string | null
│   │                                         # newest room whose binding of

│   │                                         # or identity_id, or, naming no
│   │                                         # correspondent and not group,
│   │                                         # holds participant_id under
│   │                                         # recipient_key, the channel's;
│   │                                         # recipient_key is null on a
│   │                                         # channel with no recipient key

│   └── find_room_id_by_participant(channel_id, participant_id, identity_id, filter)
│                                 → string | null
│                                             # newest room holding a participant
│                                             # whose id or identity_id is
│                                             # participant_id or identity_id,
│                                             # reached through channel_id
│       # Both serve §10.4 step 1: identity_id is the identity the caller
│       # resolved for the sender (resolve_identity, in the call's
│       # organization), null when none; filter names the statuses (ACTIVE
│       # and PAUSED for step 1) and the organization; the newest room is

│
├── Events

│   │                                         # the commit (§10.1 step 12): its
│   │                                         # index, the event and the room's
│   │                                         # counters in one transaction, the
│   │                                         # room's activity too unless
│   │                                         # activity is false (§5.1); target,
│   │                                         # a DELIVERED edit or delete's,
│   │                                         # written in it (§14.3); refuses an
│   │                                         # event whose source channel and
│   │                                         # idempotency key an event of the
│   │                                         # room carries, as a duplicate key
│   │                                         # (§14.3)
│   ├── add_event(event) → RoomEvent         # the event as it is, its index
│   │                                         # the caller's; the counters
│   │                                         # unmoved, the room's next
│   │                                         # index kept past it
│   ├── add_event_auto_index(room_id, event) → RoomEvent
│   │                                         # at the room's next index, never
│   │                                         # one given out before; the
│   │                                         # counters unmoved
│   ├── get_event(event_id) → RoomEvent | null
│   ├── list_events(room_id, filters) → list<RoomEvent>
│   ├── get_thread_summaries(room_id, root_event_ids) → map<string, ThreadSummary>
│   │                                         # per root with replies, a

│   │                                         # an event_id that is not an

│   │                                         # its delivery_results kept, the
```

requirements.text:
**Reading a timeline (`list_events`).** Two pagination modes exist:
offset-based (`offset` + `limit`) and cursor-based (`after_index` or
`before_index`, mutually exclusive; `offset` is then ignored). `limit` is 50
by default, for `list_events` and the timeline reads built on it, and a
`limit` of 0 returns no event, whatever the window. *Which* events a
page holds and the *order* they come back in are two different answers.
`before_index`, and in offset mode the `newest_first` flag (ignored under a
cursor), select the **window**: the `limit` events nearest the cursor, or the
room's tail instead of its head, with `offset` then counted back from the
newest end. The page itself MUST always be rendered in ascending `index`
order, whichever window was selected and whatever the order the rows were
written or stamped in (ties between events stored without an index are broken
deterministically by the store): its first element is the oldest event of the
window and its last element the newest. A caller that wants the most recent
event of a page reads its last element, never its first; an implementation
that fetches descending to find the window reverses the page before returning
it. The conversation and timeline reads built on `list_events` inherit both
halves of this rule.

requirements.applies: §14.1 Conversation Store; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**A timeline read serves what the room received.** By default `list_events`
MUST NOT return an event stored `BLOCKED` (§10.1 step 10, §7.5 rule 2, §8.3):
the room refused that turn, and a reader listing what was said in the room is
not asking for what was refused. The refused rows MUST stay readable on
explicit request (a filter flag, `include_blocked`) and by id (`get_event`),
because a host audits, copies or deletes them by those paths, and the filter
MUST apply before the page is cut, so a page of `limit` received events is
full whatever was refused around them. The conversation read that fills
`RoomContext.recent_events` asks for the whole timeline: hooks read it whole
(§7.5 rule 8), and the per-reader filter of that rule drops the refused rows
for channels. A refused row still consumes an index (§10.1 step 8), so the room's
counters keep counting it.

requirements.applies: §14.1 Conversation Store; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**A count follows the rule of the page it stands for.** `get_event_count`
without a filter counts every committed row, the refused ones included: a
refused row consumed an index (§8.3), and that count is the timeline's size,
the twin of the room's maintained `event_count` until a hard delete removes
rows, which leaves `event_count` as it was (§14.3). `get_event_count` with
an `EventFilter` MUST count exactly the rows `list_events` would serve under
that filter, with no page: the same criteria, and the same received-rows
default lifted by `include_blocked`, so a host that needs the exact number of
a subset (an agent's turns before an instant) never measures a page to get it
and never inherits the page's cap.

requirements.applies: §14.3 Consistency Requirements; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
- Event index assignment MUST be atomic within a room. For a persistent store
  that may be accessed by more than one process, this atomicity MUST be enforced
  at the storage layer — a single transaction plus a `UNIQUE(room_id, index)`
  constraint (§8.1) — not by an in-process lock alone.
- Room state updates MUST be consistent with event storage. Specifically,
  storing an event — DELIVERED at §10.1 step 12, BLOCKED at steps 10–11 — and
  bumping the room's `event_count` / `latest_index` form a **single atomic
  commit**: an observer MUST never see a stored event that is not reflected in
  the room counters, nor counters that count an event absent from the
  timeline, but one a hard delete removed (below). An EDIT or a DELETE and
  its target's update (§10.3) are part of that commit: the store writes the
  change, the counters and the target in one transaction, and fails the
  whole commit when the target is gone.
- A kit MAY be configured with a persistence policy: the event types its
  commits store (`persist_types`, every type when absent), less those it
  never stores (`exclude_types`, which wins). An event of a type it keeps
  out is delivered as any event, its hooks and its delivery set running,
  and nothing of it is stored: it takes no index, moves none of the room's
  counters, is no activity (§5.1) and is none of the call's
  `response_events`; it keeps the provisional index its hooks were shown,
  and its delivery set's context holds it as its newest event. It still
  takes its author record, which extends the room's register of authors
  (§10.1 step 12), so that a later source never holds the rank a reader
  saw it hold. A streamed row kept out is handed to no reader of the
  stream (§7.5 rule 2), and the turn's record lands as §6.4 says, among
  the rows stored; a discussion is not told of a message kept out, which asks no
  agent (§19.7.5 rule 8). An EDIT or a DELETE kept out still writes its
  target alone (`write_change_target`, §14.1), a delete marking the
  target's edits deleted, and its mutation trigger fires (§10.3). A
  lifecycle record kept out is not written: its change, a timer's
  transition included, is announced all the same. A hook's injected event
  (§9.4), a record stored `BLOCKED`, a record committed outside the
  pipeline (§10.5) and a delegation's trace in its child room (§23.3) are
  stored whatever the policy.
- A write naming what the store does not hold is refused, nothing written:
  `update_room` of a room it does not hold and `add_participant` into one
  (room not found), `update_event` of an event it does not hold (event not
  found). A store that wrote it would keep an event no timeline read finds,
  or a participant of no room. `add_participant` under an id the room has is
  refused too (participant exists, §5.5), the record it holds kept, and
  `update_participant` of a record the room does not hold (participant not
  found), and `update_task` of a task the store does not hold (task not
  found): an update is no creation, which `add_task` makes.
- A room is created once: a store MUST refuse to create a room under an id it
  already holds, and never replaces the room it holds. §10.1 step 2 creates
  a room under an id in hand, and a store that replaced the room would
  re-home another conversation, another organization's included.
- A hard delete (§10.3) leaves the room's counters as they are:
  `event_count` counts every index given out, and an index is never given
  again, so a store refuses a commit at an index below the room's
  `event_count`, a removed one included. A removed event's idempotency key
  goes with it (§13.4).
- A whole-record write of a room (`update_room`) is made under the room
  lock, from the room as read under that lock: a copy read before it would
  undo what was written since. It keeps the counters (`event_count`,
  `latest_index`) and the delivered index the store holds, which only a
  commit and the cursor's compare-and-set move. A change of the room's
  metadata alone goes through `patch_room_metadata`, which merges its keys
  and writes nothing else, so a concurrent writer's keys stand.
- Once committed (DELIVERED), an event MUST NOT be retroactively re-marked
  BLOCKED or FAILED. A processing timeout or a delivery failure after the
  commit point (§13.6) MUST NOT alter the event's committed status.
- Once stored, an event's `delivery_results` is written by the store's
  record of its deliveries alone (`record_delivery_results`, §14.1), which
  replaces that map and writes nothing else of the event. Every other write
  of a stored event MUST keep the `delivery_results` the store holds,
  whatever the copy it is given carries: an update of the event
  (`update_event`, §10.3), and the update of a change's target, which the
  change's commit writes (§10.3). So an edit or a delete committed while the
  event's deliveries ran never undoes their record, and the record never
  undoes the change. A record committed outside the pipeline is stored with
  the `delivery_results` it brings (§10.5).
- Idempotency key checks MUST be performed under the room lock. A key is
  looked up within its room and its source channel (§13.4): a store's index
  or uniqueness constraint on keys covers
  `(room_id, source.channel_id, idempotency_key)`, since a constraint over
  the room and the key alone would refuse one channel's message for
  another's. A proactive delivery's key is the exception: it names one
  publication in its room, whatever transport carries it (§22.1), and is
  looked up within the room, under the same lock, whatever channel
  committed it. It is stored in the namespace the pipeline reserves for it
  (`roomkit:publication:<key>`, §5.2), so the per-channel uniqueness never
  sets a publication against a message keyed alike.
- A store MUST refuse to commit an event when its room already holds an
  event of the same source channel with the same idempotency key, with
  nothing written: the commit fails as a duplicate key, with an error of its
  own that every store raises alike (`IdempotencyKeyTakenError`), never its
  storage driver's error, and never by replacing the event the key names.
  The pipeline looks the key up first, under the room lock, before it
  commits anything of the event, a record past the reentry budget included
  (§10.1 step 7, §13.4), so only a direct commit meets the refusal: a record
  committed outside the pipeline (§10.5), which is never a replay and fails
  with this error, or a caller of the store itself. A key a hard delete
  released (§13.4) is free again. An event under an id the
  store already holds is outside this rule.

requirements.applies: §14.4 Returned-Object Ownership; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
- A committed event changes only through the write interface (§4.3). An
  event, room, binding or participant object returned by a read
  (`get_event`, `list_events`, conversation reads, `get_room`,
  `list_rooms`, `find_rooms`, `find_latest_room`, `get_binding`,
  `list_bindings`, `get_participant`, `list_participants`) or by the write
  that stored it is a snapshot of the stored record: the caller MUST treat
  it as frozen and MUST NOT mutate it, and changes it through a copy and a
  write. So are the room, bindings and participants of the `RoomContext` a
  hook or a channel receives, which are read from the store. A store MAY
  return the same object to multiple readers (an in-memory store sharing
  its stored objects) or a fresh object per read (a SQL store deserialising
  rows) — both are conformant, and a portable caller can rely on neither
  aliasing nor isolation.
- A store MUST own its stored representation from the moment a write
  returns: a caller's later mutation of an object it passed to
  `commit_event` / `update_event` / `create_room` / `update_room` /
  `add_binding` / `update_binding` / `add_participant` / `update_participant` /
  `set_private_state` MUST NOT alter stored state (copy-in and
  serialisation both satisfy this).
- A room's private state returned by a read is caller-owned: mutating it
  MUST NOT affect stored state — changes are applied through
  `set_private_state`.

A message reads its room's records many times, so a store that shares its
reads saves a copy each time; one that copies per read stays conformant.

requirements.applies: §15.1 Logging; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
Implementations MUST use structured logging with named loggers. The following
logger hierarchy is RECOMMENDED:

```
roomkit
├── roomkit.core.framework
├── roomkit.core.router
├── roomkit.core.hooks
├── roomkit.core.locks
├── roomkit.channels.sms
├── roomkit.channels.email
├── roomkit.channels.websocket
├── roomkit.channels.ai
├── roomkit.channels.whatsapp
├── roomkit.channels.voice
├── roomkit.channels.voice.pipeline
├── roomkit.providers.sms.*
├── roomkit.providers.email.*
├── roomkit.providers.ai.*
├── roomkit.providers.voice.*
├── roomkit.identity
└── roomkit.store
```

requirements.applies: §15.2 Log Levels; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
| Level | What to Log |
|---|---|
| DEBUG | Full pipeline trace, raw payloads, hook decisions |
| INFO | Room created, event stored, channel attached, participant resolved |
| WARNING | Delivery failed (retryable), hook timeout, chain depth approaching limit, an AI turn that ended before its answer (a delegated worker's, a reasoning backend's: an expected outcome, logged without a traceback) |
| ERROR | Provider error (non-retryable), circuit breaker opened, store failure |

A failure is logged once, by the component that catches it, at the level
its cause calls for; a provider's error drops to DEBUG only where the
caller receives the error itself (on `InboundResult.error`, or raised) and
owns its line, and a stream a streaming target rendered keeps its line
even then, except a delegation's, whose task logs every failure of its
turn (§23.3). A failure no caller receives keeps its level: the failed
turn of an agent a `send_event` asks, the stream of a deferred call read in
the background, the turns of the agents a held message's release runs
(§11.7.6), whose result nobody reads.

requirements.applies: §15.3 Structured Log Context; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
Each log entry SHOULD include structured context:

```
{
    "room_id": "room_8f3a",
    "event_id": "evt_abc",
    "channel_id": "sms_customer",
    "provider": "twilio",
    "chain_depth": 0,
    "status": "sent",
    "latency_ms": 245
}
```

requirements.applies: §15.4 Voice Pipeline Observability; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
Voice pipeline stages SHOULD emit structured metrics for monitoring and
debugging. The following metrics are RECOMMENDED:

| Metric | Source | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `pipeline.stage_latency_ms` | All stages | Processing time per stage per frame |
| `pipeline.stt_latency_ms` | STTProvider | Time from speech end to final transcript |
| `pipeline.tts_latency_ms` | TTSProvider | Time from text to first audio frame |
| `pipeline.vad_speech_duration_ms` | VAD | Duration of detected speech segments |
| `pipeline.vad_false_positive_rate` | VAD | Speech detections that produced no transcript |
| `pipeline.aec_convergence` | AEC | Echo cancellation effectiveness (0.0 to 1.0) |
| `pipeline.agc_gain_db` | AGC | Current applied gain |
| `pipeline.dtmf_detected` | DTMF | Count of DTMF digits detected per session |
| `pipeline.recording_duration_s` | Recorder | Active recording duration |
| `pipeline.turn_detector_latency_ms` | TurnDetector | Time to reach turn decision |
| `pipeline.backchannel_rate` | BackchannelDetector | Ratio of backchannels to interruptions |
| `pipeline.barge_in_count` | InterruptionConfig | Count of barge-in events per session |
| `pipeline.debug_tap_bytes_written` | PipelineDebugTaps | Total bytes written to debug tap files |
| `pipeline.tts_context_turns` | Voice Channel | Turns in the TTS context passed to a call, per session (Section 12.2.2) |
| `pipeline.tts_context_audio_s` | Voice Channel | Seconds of audio held in the TTS context, per session |
| `transport.packets_lost` | VoiceBackend | Count of packets confirmed lost per session (Section 12.2.1) |
| `transport.concealed_frames` | VoiceBackend | Count of frames synthesized by packet loss concealment per session |

Voice pipeline logs SHOULD use the `roomkit.channels.voice.pipeline` logger
with the following structured context fields: `session_id`, `room_id`,
`stage_name`, `latency_ms`, and `frame_timestamp_ms`.

requirements.applies: §15.5 Framework Events for Monitoring; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
See Section 8.2 for the complete list of framework events; an implementation
owes the events of the features it provides. These MUST be emittable and
subscribable by integrators for monitoring dashboards, alerting, and
integration purposes.

requirements.applies: §15.6 Protocol Trace Infrastructure; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
Channels that interact with transport-level protocols (SIP, RTP, SMTP, etc.)
SHOULD emit `ProtocolTrace` records (Section 5.14) for significant protocol
events. The framework provides a layered trace infrastructure that routes these
traces to integrator-registered hooks at the room level.

requirements.applies: §15.6 Protocol Trace Infrastructure; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Channel-level trace API:**

```
Channel (trace extensions)
├── emit_trace(trace: ProtocolTrace) → void
│       # Emit a trace to all registered handlers
│       # Called by backend/transport implementations
│
├── on_trace(callback, protocols: list<string> | null) → void
│       # Register a user-level trace callback
│       # If protocols is set, only traces matching the filter are forwarded
│
├── trace_enabled: bool (read-only)
│       # True if any trace handler is registered (user or framework)
│
└── resolve_trace_room(session_id: string | null) → string | null
        # Resolve a room_id from a session_id via session bindings
        # Default: null (override in voice channels)
```

`emit_trace()` invokes all registered handlers: user-level callbacks (registered
via `on_trace()`), and the framework handler (set during `register_channel()`).
Handlers MAY be sync or async — async handlers MUST be scheduled as tasks and
MUST NOT block the caller.

requirements.applies: §15.6 Protocol Trace Infrastructure; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Trace bridging for voice channels:**

Voice channels (VoiceChannel, RealtimeVoiceChannel) bridge traces from their
underlying backend or transport to the channel's `emit_trace()`. This is done via
`set_trace_emitter()` on the backend/transport:

```
VoiceChannel:
    # Calls backend.set_trace_emitter(self.emit_trace) when trace is enabled

RealtimeVoiceChannel:
    # Calls transport.set_trace_emitter(self.emit_trace) when trace is enabled
    # Transport MAY forward to underlying backend (e.g., SIPRealtimeTransport → SIPVoiceBackend)
```

The bridge is activated lazily — only when `trace_enabled` becomes true (via
`on_trace()` registration or framework handler assignment).

requirements.applies: §15.6 Protocol Trace Infrastructure; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Framework-level trace routing:**

When a channel is registered via `register_channel()`, the framework sets a
framework trace handler on the channel. This handler:

1. Resolves the `room_id` for the trace:
   - Uses `trace.room_id` if set directly.
   - Falls back to `channel.resolve_trace_room(trace.session_id)` to look up
     the room via session bindings.
2. Fires the `ON_PROTOCOL_TRACE` hook for the resolved room.

requirements.applies: §15.6 Protocol Trace Infrastructure; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Pre-room trace buffering:**

Transport-level traces (e.g., SIP INVITE) often fire before `process_inbound()`
creates the room. Since hooks require a room context, these traces cannot be
delivered immediately. The framework MUST buffer such traces and replay them
when the room is created and the channel is attached:

```
1. Backend emits trace (e.g., SIP INVITE accepted)
2. Framework handler tries to fire ON_PROTOCOL_TRACE hook
3. Room does not exist yet → buffer trace in _pending_traces[room_id]
4. process_inbound() creates room, attaches channel
5. attach_channel() calls _flush_pending_traces(room_id)
6. Buffered traces are replayed as ON_PROTOCOL_TRACE hooks
```

This ensures that no protocol traces are lost, even for the initial signaling
messages that precede room creation.

requirements.applies: §15.6 Protocol Trace Infrastructure; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**SIP trace examples:**

A SIP voice backend SHOULD emit the following traces:

| Event | Direction | Protocol | Summary | Raw |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Call received | inbound | sip | `INVITE from +1555... to +1666...` | Serialized SIP INVITE request |
| Call accepted | outbound | sip | `200 OK (codec=16000Hz, ...)` | SDP answer body |
| Remote hangup | inbound | sip | `BYE from +1555...` | Serialized SIP BYE request |
| Local hangup | outbound | sip | `BYE (local hangup)` | null (library may not expose serialized form) |

requirements.applies: §15.7 Telemetry Provider; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
Implementations SHOULD provide a pluggable telemetry provider abstraction for
distributed tracing and metrics collection:

```
TelemetryProvider (interface)
├── start_span(name, attributes, parent) → Span
│       # Begin a new trace span for an operation
│
├── record_metric(name, value, attributes) → void
│       # Record a numeric metric value
│
├── record_event(name, attributes) → void
│       # Record a discrete event within the current trace
│
└── close() → void
        # Flush pending data and release resources
```

requirements.applies: §15.7 Telemetry Provider; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Required implementations:**

| Provider | Description |
|---|---|
| OpenTelemetryProvider | Industry-standard distributed tracing (OTLP export) |
| ConsoleTelemetryProvider | Human-readable console output for development |
| NoopTelemetryProvider | No-op implementation (telemetry disabled) |

Implementations SHOULD instrument the following operations with spans:
`process_inbound`, `broadcast`, `hook_execution`, `deliver`, `ai_generate`,
`stt_transcribe`, `tts_synthesize`, `identity_resolve`, and `store_event`.

Each span SHOULD include structured attributes: `room_id`, `channel_id`,
`event_id`, `provider`, and `latency_ms`. The spans a turn executor records
for a turn are children of the broadcast span, through the trace context the
turn's request carries (Section 10.6), whichever process runs it. The spans a
store records for the reads and writes of a room's delivery cursor (Section
13.5) made to deliver messages `process_inbound` brought in, a skip past a hole
included, are children of the span of one of those calls, wherever the delivery
runs, never trace roots.

requirements.applies: §15.7 Telemetry Provider; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**What a span holds.** An exporter often stands outside the application's
production data, so a span MUST NOT carry what can hold personal data unless
the application asks for it (`TelemetryConfig.record_sensitive_data`, off by
default, a provider handed alone included): a sender's or a recipient's address
is left out (`sender_id`, `delivery.recipient`), a provider's error too
(`delivery.error`), and a span's `error_message` reads the error's class or a
stable code (`ValueError`, `send_failed`), never its text, which can quote a
message or an address. A console provider MUST write out a value's line breaks
and control characters and quote it, so that no value forges a log line.

requirements.applies: §15.8 Audit System; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
RoomKit provides a two-tier auditing architecture for compliance, debugging,
and monitoring: **tool auditing** captures individual tool calls, and
**session auditing** captures the full conversation timeline.

requirements.applies: §15.8.1 Tool Auditing; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text: Tool auditing records every tool call with input, output, timing, and status.

requirements.applies: §15.8.1 Tool Auditing; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**ToolAuditEntry:**

```
ToolAuditEntry
├── ts: string                              # RFC 3339 time, in UTC (§1.4)
├── agent_id: string                        # Which agent made the call
├── tool_name: string                       # Tool function name
├── arguments: map<string, any>             # Input arguments
├── result: string                          # Tool output (truncated to 500 chars)
├── status: string                          # "ok", "failed", "error" or "cancelled"
├── duration_ms: float                      # Execution time in milliseconds
└── metadata: map<string, any>              # Optional extra data
```

requirements.applies: §15.8.1 Tool Auditing; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Status detection:**
- `"error"` — set when the tool handler raises an exception.
- `"cancelled"` — set when the call was cancelled before its handler answered
  (its turn or session ended, the provider abandoned it). A cancelled call
  MUST NOT be recorded as `"ok"`, and the cancellation still reaches the
  caller. A call the channel's per-call bound cut short (Section 21.6)
  reaches a wrapped handler as a cancellation and is recorded `"cancelled"`
  as well, its duration the bound; the channel reports it as failed.
- `"failed"`, structurally — set when the handler refused the call
  (`ToolRefusedError`), stated its failure in its own words
  (`ToolFailedError`, an MCP `isError` result: the structured form of the
  envelope below, which reads `"failed"` too) or declined it as not its own
  (Section 21.4).
- `"failed"`, from the body — read from the result body, which MUST be inspected for every
  failure envelope the implementation itself emits, not for one convention
  only: `{"status": "failed"}`, the `{"error": ...}` envelope a refused call
  and a wrapped MCP `isError` result return, and the `{"success": false}`
  convention hosts commonly use. Recognising one shape and not the others
  records a denied tool — the outcome an audit exists for — as `"ok"`.
- `"ok"` — the default, and a degradation rather than a contract: it is what a
  body outside every envelope reads as. A producer that can state its outcome
  structurally SHOULD do so (Section 9.3) instead of relying on this reading.

requirements.applies: §15.8.1 Tool Auditing; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**ToolAuditor** (interface):

```
ToolAuditor (interface)
├── record(entry: ToolAuditEntry) → void    # Record a tool execution
├── entries: list<ToolAuditEntry> (property) # All recorded entries
├── summary() → string                     # Human-readable summary
└── print_summary() → void                 # Log summary via logger
```

requirements.applies: §15.8.1 Tool Auditing; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Built-in implementations:**

| Implementation | Persistence | Description |
|---|---|---|
| JSONLToolAuditor | JSONL file | Appends one JSON line per call; maintains in-memory list |
| ConsoleToolAuditor | Logger | Real-time logging via Python logging module |

requirements.applies: §15.8.1 Tool Auditing; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Handler wrapper:**

The `audit_tool_handler(handler, auditor, agent_id)` function wraps any tool
handler to automatically record audit entries. It:

1. Measures execution time.
2. Records a raised exception as `"error"`, a refusal, a stated failure
   (`ToolFailedError`) or a declined call as `"failed"` and a cancelled call
   as `"cancelled"`, then re-raises each, so
   the channel reads the outcome it would have read without the wrapper.
3. Auto-detects `"failed"` from the response body otherwise.
4. Truncates the recorded result to 500 characters.
5. Returns the original handler result unchanged: the same object, never a
   printed copy of it, so content parts and structured values reach the
   channel as the handler gave them.

Integrators MAY implement custom `ToolAuditor` backends (e.g., Datadog,
Elasticsearch) by implementing the interface.

requirements.applies: §15.8.2 Session Auditing; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
Session auditing captures the full conversation timeline: speech turns, tool
calls, vision events, interruptions, and session lifecycle.

requirements.applies: §15.8.2 Session Auditing; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**SessionAuditEntry:**

```
SessionAuditEntry
├── ts: string                              # RFC 3339 time, in UTC (§1.4)
├── type: string                            # Event type (see below)
├── role: string | null                     # "user", "assistant", or "system"
├── content: string                         # Text, transcription, or description
├── duration_ms: float | null               # For timed events (tool calls)
└── metadata: map<string, any>              # Extra data (tool_name, args, status, etc.)
```

requirements.applies: §15.8.2 Session Auditing; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Session audit event types:**

| Type | Role | Trigger | Content |
|---|---|---|---|
| speech | user/assistant | ON_TRANSCRIPTION hook | Transcribed speech text |
| tool_call | assistant | Manual `record_tool()` | Tool result |
| vision | system | ON_VISION_RESULT hook | Frame description |
| barge_in | user | ON_BARGE_IN hook | "User interrupted" |
| session | system | ON_SESSION_STARTED hook | "Session started" |
| error | system | Application-specific | Error message |

requirements.applies: §15.8.2 Session Auditing; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**SessionAuditor** (interface):

```
SessionAuditor (interface)
├── record(entry: SessionAuditEntry) → void
├── entries: list<SessionAuditEntry> (property)
├── summary() → string
├── print_summary() → void
│
│   # ToolAuditor compatibility bridge:
├── record_tool(entry: ToolAuditEntry) → void  # Convert tool entry to session entry
├── tool_auditor: ToolAuditor (property)        # Bridge adapter
│
│   # Hook auto-registration:
└── attach(kit: RoomKit) → void                # Register hooks for automatic capture
```

requirements.applies: §15.8.2 Session Auditing; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Hook auto-registration:** When `attach(kit)` is called, the session auditor
registers hooks for `ON_TRANSCRIPTION`, `ON_BARGE_IN`, `ON_SESSION_STARTED`,
and `ON_VISION_RESULT` to capture conversation events automatically.

requirements.applies: §15.8.2 Session Auditing; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**ToolAuditor bridge:** The `tool_auditor` property returns a bridge adapter
that converts `ToolAuditEntry` records into `SessionAuditEntry` records. This
allows a single `SessionAuditor` to capture both tool calls and conversation
events in a unified timeline.

requirements.applies: §15.8.2 Session Auditing; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Built-in implementation:** `JSONLSessionAuditor` — writes entries to a JSONL
file and maintains an in-memory chronological list.

requirements.applies: §15.8.3 Audit Data Format; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
Both auditors use JSONL (JSON Lines) for persistence — one JSON object per
line, independently parseable:

```
{"ts":"...","agent_id":"exec","tool_name":"search","arguments":{"q":"roomkit"},"result":"...","status":"ok","duration_ms":1234.5,"metadata":{}}
{"ts":"...","type":"speech","role":"user","content":"Open Chrome","duration_ms":null,"metadata":{}}
```

JSONL files are append-only. Implementations MUST create parent directories
automatically. Write errors MUST be logged but MUST NOT propagate exceptions
to the caller.

requirements.applies: §15.9 Feedback; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
An implementation MAY let a host record how a room, or one of its
responses, was rated:

```
submit_feedback(room_id, rating, event_id | null, channel_id | null,
                comment = "", dimension = "overall", metadata) → void
```

The rating is a number from 0.0 to 1.0; a value outside is clamped. It is
recorded as an Observation of the room (§5.11): its `channel_id` the rated
channel (empty when none is named), its `category` `feedback:<dimension>`,
its `confidence` the rating, its `content` a line naming the dimension, the
rating and the comment, and its metadata `type = "feedback"`, `dimension`,
`rating`, `comment` and `event_id`, beside the caller's `metadata`. Once the
observation is stored, `ON_FEEDBACK` (ASYNC, §9.2) fires with it as its
payload, and `feedback` is emitted (§8.2) with the room, the channel, the
event, the dimension and the rating.

requirements.text:
