requirements.text: Agents request handoffs by calling the `handoff_conversation` tool:

requirements.applies: §19.6 HandoffHandler; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**HandoffRequest:**

```
HandoffRequest
├── target_agent_id: string                 # Agent to hand off to
├── reason: string                          # Why the handoff is happening
├── summary: string                         # Context summary for the target agent
├── context: map<string, any>               # Additional handoff context
├── channel_escalation: string | null       # "same", "voice", "email", "sms" (channel switch)
└── urgent: bool (default false)            # Priority flag
```

requirements.applies: §19.6 HandoffHandler; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**HandoffResult:**

```
HandoffResult
├── accepted: bool                          # Whether the handoff was accepted
├── new_agent_id: string | null             # Active agent after handoff
├── new_phase: string | null                # Phase after handoff
├── message: string                         # Human-readable result
└── reason: string                          # Rejection reason (if not accepted)
```

requirements.applies: §19.6 HandoffHandler; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Handoff protocol:**

1. Agent calls `handoff_conversation` tool with `HandoffRequest`.
2. `HandoffHandler` validates:
   - Target is an intelligence channel attached to the room, `human`, or a
     target the handler knows. A transport the room binds is not found: an
     active agent that is a transport leaves the room with no agent to answer.
   - Phase transition is allowed (per pipeline rules, if applicable).
   - With allowed transitions and a phase map, the target holds the phase: the
     one the map gives it, or one a rule of the router asks it in. A `human` or
     known target the map does not name passes; one it names does not, and a
     target it does not name otherwise holds no phase. A model's `next_phase`
     decides no more than that: a tool's `enum` is not enforced at run time,
     and a model reads what a sender wrote. The caller holds the room's phase
     by the same rule: an agent the room moved past hands nothing on. A caller
     the map does not name, neither `human` nor known, passes as the room's
     active agent, or its default agent while none is active. With no phase map,
     nothing ties an agent to a phase, and the target and the caller are free.
3. If valid:
   - Update `ConversationState.phase` and `active_agent_id`.
   - Fire `ON_HANDOFF` hook.
   - Fire `ON_PHASE_TRANSITION` hook.
   - Return `HandoffResult(accepted=true)`.
4. If invalid:
   - Fire `ON_HANDOFF_REJECTED` hook.
   - Return `HandoffResult(accepted=false, reason=...)`.

The handoff summary is injected into the target agent's context so it
has continuity, set apart as a summary of the conversation
(`<conversation_summary>`, Section 6.4) under the previous agent's id kept to
an identifier's characters. The reason the room's timeline records for the
handoff is quoted.

The timeline's record of a handoff is a system event from the calling agent,
visible to all, carrying `_orchestration_internal` in its metadata: an event
that carries it asks no agent, whatever its type, and still reaches the room's
transports. The key is the runtime's alone: a sender's is dropped at the door
(Section 10.1), or a sender would silence the room's agents.

`setup_handoff(agent, handler, tool, room_id)` wires the handoff tool into an
AI channel and serves its calls with the `HandoffHandler`. `tool` (default
null) replaces the default `handoff_conversation` definition; `room_id`
(default null) declares it in that one room's turns, as a strategy installed
in the room does (Section 19.7), and null declares it in every room the agent
serves. Setting it up again where it is already declared is refused.

requirements.applies: §19.6 HandoffHandler; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**A room held for a human (normative).** A handoff to `human` sets
`human_hold`. While it holds, the router selects no agent and stamps
`_routed_to: _none_`, whichever rule or default would pick one, and the message
still reaches the room's transports; an address naming an agent asks it and the
supervisor beside it (Section 19.4, step 4). A handoff to an agent MUST
be refused, by its tool and by the handler's own call alike, firing
`ON_HANDOFF_REJECTED`; a further handoff to `human` is taken. Only the host's
transition to an agent takes the hold off, with no model's tool on its way. A
model can start a hold by itself, so `ON_HANDOFF`, naming the human, is the
signal a host audits it by. A realtime session's call names no agent of its own:
its caller is the room's active agent, and this paragraph does not yet hold there.

requirements.applies: §19.6 HandoffHandler; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**A realtime handoff needs its agents (normative).** A realtime pipeline
reconfigures the room's sessions with the next agent's prompt on a handoff
(Section 19.5), and a handler's language change reconfigures them with the
active agent's: the agent's own prompt, which a declaration does not carry
(Section 10.6.2). A handler whose event channel is a realtime channel the kit
holds MUST refuse an agent held by its declaration alone, or an intelligence
channel that is not an agent, when it is given its agents; and a language
change on a realtime channel whose active agent is one MUST be refused before
the room's language is written, whoever put the agent among the handler's
agents. A handler with no realtime channel takes declared agents.

requirements.applies: §19.6 HandoffHandler; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**The room is the call's (normative).** A handoff acts on the room of the
call that requested it, read from the tool call context (Section 21.4). One
agent serves every room it is attached to, so a room captured when the tool
was wired, or left behind by a hook of another event, names whichever room
came first, not the one asking. A call made outside a tool call has no room
to act on, and the tool MUST refuse it rather than guess.

requirements.applies: §19.6 HandoffHandler; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**A handler's greeting (normative).** A handler's `send_greeting(room_id,
channel_id)` has the room's active agent say the line the handler's greeting
map gives it, through the kit's `send_greeting` (Section 19.1), whatever the
agent's own greeting and the room's language. It reads the room first: a room
missing is not found. With no active agent, no line or an empty one, or no
channel named by the call or by the handler's event channel, it says nothing
and does not fail. The channel is read only for a realtime channel, whose
sessions each take the greeting (Section 12.4); on any other, the greeting
reaches the whole room.

requirements.applies: §19.7 Orchestration Strategies; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
The following strategies are common patterns built on router and pipeline
primitives. Implementations SHOULD provide helpers for each.

requirements.applies: §19.7 Orchestration Strategies; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**A strategy in several rooms (normative).** A strategy is installed per room,
but its agents are shared: one agent object serves every room it is attached
to, and so does a realtime channel. What a strategy adds for a room is set up
for that room, kept by the room's owner for an agent (§10.6.1) and on the
realtime channel itself, and MUST reach that room only:

- a tool it adds for a room (a supervisor's delegation tools, a delegation's
  result tool, a loop's tool, a handoff tool) is declared in that room's turns
  and in that room's realtime sessions, not in every room the agent or the
  channel serves, and a call to it from another room is served as a call to
  an undeclared tool;
- the configuration that tool runs with (the workers, the reviewers, the
  strategy, the limits, the handoff's routing) is the one installed for the
  room of the call: a second room's install, with another configuration, runs
  its own, and changes nothing the first room runs;
- a turn the strategy runs in place of an agent's (a loop's produce and review,
  a supervisor's delegation passes) runs in the rooms it was installed in only,
  and an agent attached to a room with no such install answers there as
  itself;
- on a realtime channel, the active agent's configuration (Section 19.5) is the
  room's.

requirements.applies: §19.7 Orchestration Strategies; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**What a strategy hands a model (normative).** A strategy that composes a
model's input from other models' outputs (the workers' results a supervisor
reviews or presents, the team's work a next worker builds on, the content a
reviewer judges, a reviewer's feedback a producer revises with) sets each
output apart in a `<worker_output>` block of its own under its author's label:
one output cannot close its block, nor pass itself off as another worker's or
as a verdict. The user's goal or task it copies into such an input is a
`<task>` block. The input a model acts on as its own (the task framed for a
worker, a worker's own task) stays that model's input and is not set apart.
When several people speak in the room (the conversation's threshold, Section
6.4; a one-to-one conversation left as it is), the user's task such an input
holds as a `<task>` block is headed by who asked for it, by the label the
conversation gives the turn that led to it: `Alice asked:` before a
participant's own words, `Requested by Alice (2), in the delegating agent's
words:` before a task the delegating agent wrote. The heading names the
asker of the task the block holds and nothing else: the runtime's own
prompts and the input a worker acts on as its own carry no asker.

No install and no turn writes into the shared agent or channel on behalf of
one room: not its tools, its handler, its handling of events, its prompt, its
voice, nor a binding it shares. A write made for one room is read by every
other room the object serves, which would answer, or refuse, another room's
user with this room's configuration. Installing a strategy in a second room
MUST NOT declare a tool twice in a room. A flag it keeps while work runs for a
room is that room's, and its tools act on the room of the call (Sections 19.6
and 23.4). A tool set up on an agent outside any strategy (`setup_handoff`
without a `room_id`, `setup_delegation`, `setup_realtime_delegation`) belongs
to the agent whatever the room: it
is declared wherever the agent serves, and still acts on the room of the call.
What a strategy sets up for a room is kept by the room's owner, per channel and
room, and its turn runner runs there, each generation it asks of an agent a
turn of its own through the turn backend (§10.6.1).

requirements.applies: §19.7 Orchestration Strategies; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**One strategy per room, installed while the room lives (normative).** A room
holds at most one strategy. An implementation MUST provide
`install_strategy(room_id, strategy)` and `uninstall_strategy(room_id)` on
the framework, and `create_room(orchestration=...)` installs through the same
path:

- Installing on a room that already lives does what creating the room with
  the strategy does: the strategy's agents are registered and attached as
  intelligence channels, and its hooks, tools, turn runners and state are set
  up, the owner keeping an agent's for the room (§10.6.1). The room's
  timeline stays, and the agents' turns read it (Section 20.1).
  If the initial snapshot of the room cannot be read after the install
  claims it, the error is returned and the claim remains until an explicit
  `uninstall_strategy`. That failed attempt is over: an uninstall MUST NOT
  keep waiting for it, and releases the claim so another install can run.
- While a strategy is installed, installing another one is refused, whatever
  the strategy, the host's own included: one rule decides who speaks.
  `uninstall_strategy` comes first. One exception: a Discussion installed in
  a room that holds a discussion, installed in this process or followed from
  another (Section 19.7.5 rule 16), takes the place of the one the room holds
  and keeps its state (rule 1). That is how a process that restarted takes
  the discussion back, and how a host changes its agents.
- Uninstalling removes what the install added for that room, and only that:
  its room hooks, the tools and turn runners it set up for the room's agents,
  the agents it attached (an agent bound before the install stays bound), and
  the room state it wrote (`ConversationState`, a discussion's speak queue). A
  strategy MAY have an uninstall step of its own, run first (a discussion
  stops giving turns and posts the task results it took and has not
  committed, Section 19.7.5 rule 19). The timeline stays. The room then answers by its
  `agent_response_policy`, and another strategy may be installed. A
  discussion stores the agents its installs attached with it (Section 19.7.5
  rule 16), so any process serving the room uninstalls it, one where no host
  installed it included.
- A host MAY install and uninstall a strategy while it holds the room's lock
  (Section 13.5), as it does to serialise its own changes of the room: both
  take the lock again within the same task, and neither waits on work that
  needs it. Uninstalling a discussion cuts its running turn without waiting
  for that turn's end to be recorded (Section 19.7.5 rule 1).
- A strategy stored with the room (a discussion, Section 19.7.5 rule 16) can
  be replaced by another process's install. For such a kind, an
  implementation MUST provide `room_strategy_is_current(room_id, kind)`,
  which tells the host whether the strategy of that kind it installed in
  this process is the one the room stores now: false once another process
  installed another configuration, when this process installed none, or
  once the strategy was uninstalled. It reads the room's stored state when
  called; an uninstall another process made is taken at once, so
  `room_strategy(room_id)` answers none from then on, where a replaced
  install still names this process's own. Asked about a kind that is not
  stored with the room, it is refused rather than answered false, so the
  question keeps its meaning when another kind comes to be stored.

requirements.applies: §19.7.1 Pipeline; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
Agents are chained linearly. Each agent handles one phase and hands off to
the next:

```
Triage → Specialist → Resolution → Closing
```

The first agent is the entry point. Only forward transitions (and explicitly
allowed backward transitions) are permitted.

Each agent's phase is its channel id. The install MUST refuse a pipeline with
no agent; otherwise it sets the room's conversation state at the first agent
and its phase, and hooks its router on that room's `BEFORE_BROADCAST` at
priority -100.

On a voice channel the strategy names, the agents' voices are the channel's
voice map, and a handoff in a room the strategy runs MAY greet with the
agent it made active (a farewell spoken first), through hooks of that room
only. A realtime voice channel is refused: its sessions' configuration and
the handoff it serves are the channel's, for every room, as
`ConversationPipeline.install` wires them (Section 19.5), which a strategy
installed room by room cannot hold.

requirements.applies: §19.7.2 Swarm; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
Every agent can hand off to every other agent. No linear ordering. Useful
for collaborative agent pools where any agent may be most appropriate:

```
Agent A ⇄ Agent B ⇄ Agent C
```

Sticky affinity keeps the conversation with the current agent until an
explicit handoff occurs.

requirements.applies: §19.7.3 Supervisor; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
A supervisor agent talks to the user and delegates work to specialist agents.
Specialists run in isolated **child rooms** — their output is collected and
returned to the supervisor. When the workers run on the user's message
itself (one pass), a message its tasks cannot carry (a media, a composite,
an empty text) is answered by the supervisor alone: the workers' tasks carry
text, and the supervisor's own channel sees the media.

```
User ↔ Supervisor
              ├── delegates to → Worker A (child room)
              └── delegates to → Worker B (child room)
```

The supervisor MAY delegate sequentially or in parallel. In parallel, a
delegation that raises (its worker no longer held by the kit, for example;
a task that failed does not raise) ends the team's run with its error
without waiting for the other workers' work: each of them has started and
been posted `pending`, and their delegations are cut, each posting its
terminal entry `failed` with `cancelled`. None is left running unread.
Results are delivered back via the delivery strategy system (Section 22),
at the chain depth of the turn that delegated (Section 23.3); results presented within the turn leave
the supervisor's answer one deeper than the event it answers (§8.3). Results
of workers dispatched in the background are handed back to the supervisor
as a background delegation's are (§23.3 step 8): an instruction addressed to
it, each worker's output bounded at 4,000 characters, the default of
`max_result_chars`, never published as a participant's message. A background pipeline that fails before its results (a delegation
that raised) hands its failure back the same way: an instruction that the
work could not be completed, carrying the reasoning backend's fallback text
(Section 12.4.1) and never the error's message, which goes to the logs
(Section 9.3) and the status bus (Section 19.8). The supervisor told the user
results would follow;
it is told they will not, as the dispatching caller of a pipeline run within
the turn reads its error. A strategy's background tool serves one run per room
at a time, whichever voice channel's session called it, and the outcome goes
to the session that made the call (Section 23.3 step 8). The room is freed,
and any answer the tool serves a repeated call forgotten, before the outcome
is handed back: a dispatch answering the outcome starts a new run. The run posts one
terminal status entry once its outcome was handed back: `completed`, or
`failed` when the work failed, none of its workers' tasks completed, or its
outcome reached no one. A per-worker tool dispatched in the background is
followed by such a run, for that worker in that room: its delegation stays a
task of the framework's task runner (its id in the dispatch answer, which
cancels it), the run waits for it within the per-task timeout, past which it
is cancelled, the worker is free again before its outcome is handed back, and
the run alone hands it back. A background run ends with the framework:
closing the framework cancels it, which frees its room and posts its terminal
entry `failed`, with nothing handed back, once each worker delegation it
cut has posted its own.

Each worker's delegation, within the turn or in the background, is bounded
by the strategy's per-task timeout: a worker past it is cut, its task ended
cancelled, and it reads as failed. The worker is posted `pending` on the
status bus, then one terminal entry however the delegation ends: completed,
failed, timed out, raised, or cancelled by its caller. That entry names the
task (`task_id`) once the task exists, whatever ended it, so the task's line
on the bus (Section 23.4) ends with it, the progress its worker posted
meanwhile included, whatever action the run posts under (a Loop's
`iteration` and `review`, Section 19.7.4). The run marks its entries as its
own, a mark a turn's host refuses (Section 10.6.5), so no entry a turn posts
ends a task's line. A sequential team is
supervised (the supervisor frames and validates each step) whether it runs
within the turn or in the background; a supervisor without a model (a
configuration-only agent, as a voice supervisor often is) cannot frame nor
judge a step, and its team runs unsupervised, each worker given the task and
the work done before it. A run whose supervised chain stopped on a step the
supervisor left unvalidated did not complete its work, as the supervisor
reads it within the turn. A run asked for once the framework began closing
does not start.

An instruction a strategy needs for one turn (a supervisor's task-formulation
pass) is passed for that turn only, over the prompt the turn would have had.
The supervisor, like any channel, serves every room it is attached to, so its
configuration carries no turn's instruction: one written there and restored
afterwards leaks into the turns of other rooms running meanwhile.

The task-formulation pass is read as any streamed turn is (Section 6.4), and
fails as one does: its failure fires ON_ERROR once, as a streamed turn's
(`streaming`, with the correlation of the tool rows it wrote), is logged once,
and reaches the room turn's caller without a second report. It is a turn of
its own (Section 10.6.1): its rows carry a `correlation_id` of their own, and
the supervisor's presentation of the results, its rows, its answer and the
ON_ERROR of its failure carry another. A worker that raises once the pass
handed on its task (its channel no longer registered) fails the supervisor's
turn as a turn that raised: ON_ERROR once, `generation`, with no
`correlation_id`; the supervisor's delivery of the event failed, reported and
recorded with the event's other delivery results (Section 5.13); the caller
reads the error, and no presentation runs. The
task it hands the workers is its final answer, never the narration of its
tool rounds joined to it, and a pass its round cap, deadline or budget cut
short has none, so no worker runs. A pass that stopped short of its answer
(it ended for any reason but `completed`, save a stop someone chose,
`cancelled`) still answers the message it answered: the supervisor's
fallback message, the text a reasoning backend speaks when its delegated work
could not be completed (Section 12.4.1), stored and delivered as the
supervisor's response, carrying the turn's record (its `loop_end_reason`,
its `ai_usage`, what the turn wrote) as the turn's last message would. A
pass that failed with an error has no fallback: the error is the turn's, as
on any turn, logged once at its own level. Nothing of the pass's own stream
reaches the room's transports. Its tool calls are stored in the room as
any turn's TOOL_CALL rows, through the room's commit gate (Section 10.1) and
in the answered event's scope and thread. Its text is not stored: it is the
workers' task, an answer to no one in the room. Its record rides none of those
rows: the pass hands it on, and its fallback message carries it.

requirements.applies: §19.7.4 Loop; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
A single agent handles the conversation indefinitely, looping back for
refinement. Useful for iterative workflows (editing, code review, tutoring).
A message its tasks cannot carry (a media, a composite, an empty text) is
answered by the producer alone, as a one-pass supervisor answers it
(§19.7.3), through the same reading of the message: the loop's
tasks carry text, and the producer's own channel sees the media; it is never
left without an answer.
The loop's result is the agent's response to the event that started it, one
deeper than that event (§8.3). A producer's task that failed (§23.3 step 6)
stops the loop: the last output it produced, if any, is the result, not
approved, and says the loop stopped on that failure; with no output at all
the turn has no answer, never an empty response passed off as one. Either
way the loop's caller reads how the producer's last turn ended under `turns`,
keyed by the producer, with its usage, as a room turn's caller does (§6.4): a
turn its round cap, deadline, budget or a stop cut short is read there, is
no error and fires no ON_ERROR, as a room turn's does; a turn that failed
reaches the caller as the error it raised, its type unchanged (a provider's
failure as that provider's error), reported to ON_ERROR once, where the
producer's turn failed (its task's room), and logged once. An asynchronous loop
(a voice channel's `delegate_loop`) hands its outcome back to the voice
channel that started it as a background delegation's result is (§23.3 step
8): an instruction to that channel, its output bounded at 4,000 characters,
the default of `max_result_chars`, and set apart as a worker's, never published
as a participant's message. The text says how the
loop ended; for a producer's task that failed, that it failed and the cut
that ended its turn, never with the task's error. A loop that raised hands
back that the work could not be completed, carrying the reasoning backend's
fallback text (Section 12.4.1) and never the error's message, which goes to
the logs (Section 9.3) and the status bus (Section 19.8), as a supervisor's
background pipeline does (Section 19.7.3), one loop per room and in the session that
made the call. The room is free for a new loop before the outcome is handed
back: the model's turn on it may start one. A loop its producer's task
stopped posts its terminal status entry as `failed`. The producer and the
reviewers are delegated as a supervisor's workers are (Section 19.7.3),
without a per-task bound: each is posted `pending`, then one terminal entry
however its delegation ends. Parallel reviews end as a parallel team does:
a review that raises fails the loop without waiting for the others, which
are cut, each posting its terminal entry. An asynchronous loop ends with
the framework as a supervisor's background run does.

requirements.applies: §19.7.5 Discussion; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
Several agents and one or more people hold one conversation in a room. Any
agent may address any other, a person may address any agent, and no flow is
fixed in advance: who speaks next follows from who was addressed. One agent
speaks at a time.

```
Person ⇄ { Agent A ⇄ Agent B ⇄ Agent C }      one at a time, addressed by @name
```

Swarm (Section 19.7.2) passes the conversation from one agent to the next:
the active agent talks with the user and the others wait for a handoff. In a
discussion every agent stays in the conversation and speaks when it is
addressed, the way people in a group chat do. Neither replaces the other.

A room of several agents left to the default policy dogpiles: every agent
answers the same event at once, each reading the room as it was before the
others answered, and every answer solicits the others again (Section 19.3.1).
`ADDRESSED_ONLY` stops the dogpile by stopping the agents from answering each
other at all. A discussion keeps them talking and takes the turns itself.

This version covers text: AI channels (Section 6.4), Agents among them, and
external agents (ACP agent channels, Section 6.4), in rooms whose people
write. Its terms are those of Section 6.4, which speaks
for text and voice alike, so that voice can join it without renaming
anything (see "Left out").

```
Discussion
├── agents: list<AIChannel | ACPChannel>      # The agents of the discussion: AI channels (Agents among them) and external agents
├── handles: map<channel_id, string> | null   # The name each agent is addressed by (rule 4; null or absent: derived)
├── people: set<string> | null                # Names agents address people by (null: the room's people, §6.4)
├── addressed_only: bool (default false)      # A person's message asks only the agents it names (rule 8)
├── everyone: list<channel_id> | null         # Asked, in this order, by a person's message that answers no one (null: all agents)
├── max_turns: int | null                     # Turns given in the room's lifetime (null: no bound but max_depth)
├── max_depth: int | null                     # The depth limit of its turns (null: the kit's max_chain_depth)
├── done: function(room_id) → bool | null     # The discussion is over once it holds
├── silent_token: string (default "(silent)") # The answer of an agent that stays silent
├── rules: string | null                      # How the room works, as each turn's notes give it (rule 14; null: the default)
├── dispatch: DispatchPolicy | null           # Picks who takes a person's message that names no agent (rule 18)
└── dispatch_timeout: float (default 5 s)     # How long a decision may take (rule 18)

SpeakQueue (one per room, readable by the host)
├── speaking: channel_id | null               # The agent whose turn runs now
├── queue: list<channel_id>                   # Agents owed a turn, in the order they get it
├── listening: set<channel_id>                # Agents that only listen (rule 12)
├── asked: list<(channel_id, person)>         # Agents that asked a person, and whom, waiting for the answer
├── waiting: bool                             # Whether the discussion waits for a person
└── over: bool                                # Whether the discussion is over (rule 15)
```

requirements.applies: §19.7.5 Discussion; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Normative rules:**

1. **The room is the discussion's.** The intelligence channels the room binds
   are the discussion's `agents`, and no other: the install refuses a room
   that binds another intelligence channel, a voice or realtime channel
   (Section 12), an agent that thinks while it listens (Section 6.4), or that
   has a router or another strategy installed; while the discussion is
   installed, binding such a channel to the room and installing a router or
   another strategy in it are refused. One rule decides who speaks, never two:
   the supervisor a router always solicits (Section 19.4 step 4) has no place
   in a discussion. The room's `agent_response_policy` plays no part while the
   discussion is installed; uninstalling it (Section 19.7, one strategy per
   room) gives the room back to its policy at once and forgets the
   discussion (its queue, who only listens, what agents asked people, the
   turns given, whether it was over), so a discussion installed later starts
   fresh. The turn running when it is uninstalled is cut, as listening only
   cuts it (rule 12), in whichever process gives it (rule 16), and nothing of
   its end is recorded in the forgotten queue; a process that stops (rule 16)
   records it, its queue being kept.

   Installing a discussion in a room that holds one, in any process (Section
   19.7), replaces its configuration and keeps the rest: the queue, who only
   listens, what agents asked people, the turns given, whether it is over,
   and the running turn of an agent it keeps. An agent it no longer holds
   leaves the queue (an instruction it was owed is reported dropped, rule 16),
   its running turn is cut as listening only cuts it (rule 12), and it is
   unbound when an install of the discussion bound it; an agent bound
   otherwise is an intelligence channel the room cannot keep, and the install
   is refused, as above.
2. **People.** A person is a participant of the room that is neither a bot
   nor an observer, the roles Section 6.4 leaves out of who takes part; a
   person's message is an event such a participant sent through a transport
   channel, or one a transport channel brought in with no participant record
   behind it (a room whose people the host never recorded still has people). A
   delivery (Section 22), which a transport brings in from the framework's
   own sender, is no person's message: it is an event from another sender
   (rule 8).
3. **The strategy takes the turns.** No event solicits an agent at broadcast
   (Section 10.2, solicitation): the strategy queues the agents an event asks
   for and gives each its turn later (rule 7). The address keeps its meaning
   (Section 19.3): only the channels it names are asked to act, it is stored
   with the event, and what changes is *when* they act. Transports receive
   every event as before (Section 19.3 rule 1). An agent is not delivered an
   event at broadcast, as no channel left unsolicited is (Section 19.3.2); a
   turn reads the room when it starts (rule 9), filtered by what visibility
   lets the agent see (Section 7.5 rule 8). Its memory provider (Section 20)
   is still handed every message the agent may see (visibility and access,
   rule 4), the agent's own excepted, as the message is committed, as a room
   with no discussion hands it, through the turn backend to the executor that
   holds the agent's state for the room (`committed_event`, §10.6.3): a provider that learns as messages arrive (an
   index, a summary) learns the whole conversation, not only the messages
   that asked for the agent. The turn that answers a message does not hand it
   again. Every agent's memory is handed it at once, so the commit waits for
   the slowest memory, not for the sum of them; an agent offline (rule 7) is
   handed nothing, as no executor would take it.
4. **Names.** An agent's answer and a person's message address agents by
   naming them: `@` followed by an agent's handle; `@all` names every
   agent. A name starts the text or follows a character that is neither a
   letter, a digit, `_` nor `@`; it is the longest run of the characters an
   identifier holds (letters of any script, digits, `_`, `-`, `.`) that
   follows, a final `.` excepted, and it matches a handle ignoring case.
   Each agent has one **handle**, the name the room addresses it by: the
   one `handles` gives it; else its channel id, when the channel id is a
   handle; else its `name` (an Agent's identity, Section 19.1, or an
   external agent's, Section 6.4) kept to a name's characters (`Research
   Desk` gives `ResearchDesk`), when that is a handle. A handle is a run of
   those characters, at most 32 of them, with no final `.`, that an
   identifier keeps as it is (the transcript labels the agent's turns with
   it, Section 6.4: `dev-` and `a--b` are none), and is not `all`. A channel id such as `agent:3f2a…` cannot be one (`@agent:3f2a`
   reads as `@agent`), and a 36-character identifier is no name for a model
   to copy or a person to read: an agent named `Jev` is addressed as `@Jev`.
   The discussion is refused at construction when an agent has no handle,
   when `handles` gives one that is not a handle or names a channel that is
   not one of its agents, and when two agents' handles read alike ignoring
   case. A channel id that is not its agent's handle is no name: the
   address a name sets, the queue and every hook keep channel ids. A host
   names no handle after another channel of the room: a sender with no name
   on that channel would carry the same label (Section 6.4). Names are read in
   the text the event commits with, once its `BEFORE_BROADCAST` hooks have
   run (Section 10.1): never in a tool's arguments or result, an agent's
   reasoning, a fenced code block or a quoted line. They set the event's
   `addressed_to`, the speaker left out, in the order named, alongside an
   address a transport set; a name that is no agent of the room addresses
   nobody. A name queues an agent only when the event's visibility includes
   it and its access lets it read the event (Section 7.5): a name is no way
   around visibility; the visibility is the one the event carries, its own
   intersected with its source binding's at commit (Section 7.3). A person's
   name addresses no intelligence channel: it records that the agent asked
   that person (rule 10). The names people are addressed by are those of the
   room's people as the transcript labels them (Section 6.4: a participant's
   name, a transport's stamp, else the channel of a sender with no name), only
   those `people` lists when it is set, kept to an identifier's characters and
   at most 32 of them: a longer name addresses nobody, never cut short, since
   a cut name could be another person's whole one. What is recorded is the
   person as the transcript labels them, and only when one person answers to
   the name: a name two people answer to (`Alice Martin`, `AliceMartin`)
   records no one, and a look-alike's ranked label (`Alice (2)`, Section 6.4)
   is addressed by no name. Where a person's name and an agent's handle read
   alike, the name is the agent's. This is the mechanism Section 19.3.1 leaves
   open: an agent MAY address another agent.
5. **A turn queues each agent once.** Each event a turn commits carries its
   own names when it is committed (Section 19.3 rule 4). The queue takes them
   when the turn has ended, from the turn's delivered events only: an event a
   hook blocked, the depth limit stopped or the source's access withheld
   queues nobody, and an agent named in three segments of one turn is queued
   once.
6. **A turn's end.** A turn has ended once every event it produced is
   committed. A turn that fails, or that a round cap, a deadline, a budget or
   a `Cancel` cuts short, has ended too: the events it committed before the
   cut stay in the room and queue whom they name, the agent is not queued
   again for that turn, and a failure is reported as any turn's is (Section
   9.3).
7. **One turn at a time.** The strategy gives the next turn once the current
   one has ended. It goes to the first agent of the queue that can take it:
   one that does not only listen, or whose turn rule 12 lets it take while it
   listens, and whose turn stays within the depth limit (rule 11). The agent
   whose turn just ended does not take the next one while another agent of the
   queue can, a person's message that put it first included: an agent that
   asks a person at every turn would otherwise keep the turns from the agents
   it waits on. Every turn an agent of the room takes goes through the queue.
   An instruction addressed to agents (Section 10.1.1) queues each of them at
   the front for a turn of its own, which takes the instruction as its input
   (rule 16). A regenerated answer queues at the front, for a turn of its own,
   each agent that answered the event (each agent the event asked for, when
   no answer to it is left), once per agent and event. Such a turn is given
   even while the discussion waits for a person (rule 10), to an agent that
   only listens, and to the agent whose turn just ended. Requests that put
   agents at the front are served in the order they came.
   An agent offline when its turn comes, one held by its declaration that no
   executor online covers in the room (§10.6.7), is not given it, rather than
   given a turn that fails with `no_executor` at each message: its entry
   leaves the queue and the skip is announced (rule 17), then an instruction
   it was to take is dropped. Whether it is offline is read as the turn
   comes, not from a list read earlier, which may miss an executor started
   since. Once an executor covers it, it takes its turns again. A
   turn backend that does not list its executors tells nothing, and the turn
   is given; a task's result to post (rule 19) is posted whatever the agent's
   presence.
8. **The queue.** An agent an agent names is queued at the back, or keeps its
   place when already queued: the request merges into its pending turn, one
   turn for every event that asked for it. A person's message puts the agents
   it addresses at the front of the queue, in the order addressed. A person's
   message with no address (`addressed_to` null, and no name read in it)
   answers the agents that asked that person (`asked`), and puts them at the
   front in the order they asked; when none asked, it puts `everyone` there,
   in their order; each only when the message's visibility includes it and its
   access lets it read the message (rule 4). The message is routed so before
   rule 10 clears what was asked. With a dispatch policy, such a message is
   left to the policy instead, whether agents asked that person or not
   (rule 18). A message whose address is empty, or that
   names only people, asks no agent (Section 19.3 rule 3). An event from any
   other sender (a bot, a webhook, a delivery, Section 22) queues the agents
   its address names, at the back; with no address it asks no agent. An
   event a hook injects asks no agent, whatever its address (Section 9.4). A
   merged turn answers the latest person's message among the events that asked
   for it, else the latest of them. The order of `everyone` is the host's, so
   the agent that should open (the one that looks at the facts before the
   others act) comes first; the discussion does not rotate it. With
   `addressed_only`, a person's message asks only the agents it addresses, as
   `ADDRESSED_ONLY` asks only the channels an event names (Section 19.3.1):
   one that names nobody asks no agent, the agents that asked a person
   included, which wait for a message that names them. People who talk among
   themselves in the room are then never cut into by an agent; a host that
   wants agents to judge for themselves whether an unaddressed message is for
   them leaves `addressed_only` off and gives them a speak policy (Section
   6.4), or gives the discussion a dispatch policy, which judges once for the
   room (rule 18).
9. **A turn reads the room as it is.** A turn a message asked for is a rerun
   of the event it answers, planned for that one agent under the room lock and
   run in the room's delivery lane, as a regeneration re-broadcasts an event
   already committed (Section 13.6): its context is built when the turn
   starts, so what was said while the agent waited is in it. The event it
   answers is passed as the turn's `current_event` and keeps its place in the
   history, before what came after it (Section 20.1), and a speak policy reads
   the conversation up to the turn's start in `SpeakTurn.recent` (Section
   6.4). The turn's notes say which event the turn answers (its author's label
   and a quote of it, Section 6.4) and every speaker that asked for it. An
   external agent, whose session keeps its own history, is sent what it has
   not read yet and the event it answers as its request (Section 6.4). A turn is never given by publishing a message or an
   instruction in the room for the agent to answer, which a model reads as a
   third party's words and may rightly refuse to obey.
10. **Asking a person, waiting for one.** When an agent names a person, the
    discussion owes that person an answer (`asked` records the agent and the
    person as the transcript labels them, rule 4), and a person's message,
    once routed (rule 8), clears what was asked of them: of that label alone,
    so a sender who takes another's name (ranked apart, Section 6.4) answers
    for nobody else. With a dispatch policy, the policy judges whether the
    message answers them (rule 18); what was asked is cleared all the same. With `addressed_only`, only a message that names the
    agent clears what it asked. When no agent of the queue can take a turn,
    the discussion waits for a person's message, its `waiting` reading true,
    if the room has a person to wait for (one of its participants is, or a
    person's message reached it) and it owes a person an answer, an agent of
    the queue only listens, or the depth limit stopped the next turn. Until a
    person writes, whatever the message asks, or the cause of the wait is gone
    (the agent it waited on talks again), it gives no turn but those of rule 7
    (an instruction, a regenerated answer). With no person in the room, or
    nothing to wait for, a discussion that can give no turn is idle, not over:
    the next event that asks for a turn opens it again.
11. **Depth.** A turn the strategy gives answers an event (rules 8 and 9) and
    carries its `chain_depth + 1` (Section 8.3). A person's message is at
    depth 0, so each one opens a chain. `max_depth` takes the place of
    `max_chain_depth` for the turns the discussion gives and the events they
    produce, and cannot be disabled (Section 17.5). It bounds how far a chain
    of agent turns reaches from a person's message (four hops with the default
    of 5), not how many turns follow it, since several agents a person's
    message asks for each answer at depth 1. A turn the limit stops is not
    given and is recorded once as Section 8.3 says; its agent stays queued,
    and its turn answers the next event that asks for it within the limit: a
    person's message, which opens a new chain, or a request from a shallower
    one (rule 8). Each turn has a reentry budget of its own, `10 × max_depth`
    passes (Section 8.3), whoever asked for it, a regeneration included: the
    budget of the work a call is made from does not follow it into the
    discussion's queue. Its depth does: a message, a post or a regeneration
    an ASYNC hook's body makes stands at least one deeper than the event the
    hook runs for (Section 8.3), and the turn that answers it at that depth,
    so `max_depth` ends a hook that asks an agent again after each of its
    answers, in every process that gives the discussion's turns. A turn of
    its own (rule 7)
    past the limit does not wait: an instruction's is dropped and reported as
    dropped (rule 16), there being no stored event to record it against; a
    regenerated answer's is recorded once and dropped. An autonomous
    discussion, with no person to open a new chain, needs a `max_depth` that
    lets its work through.
12. **Listening only.** An implementation that provides Discussion MUST
    provide `listen_only(room_id, channel_ids)` and `talk_again(room_id,
    channel_ids)` for the host, which binds them to what a person does (a
    console's "@sre hold on", "@sre you can carry on"). The discussion keeps
    the state, and it means what the listening state of Section 6.4 means: an
    agent that only listens keeps its place in the queue and takes no turn an
    agent's message asks for; a person's message that names it gives it one
    turn, and it goes on listening (one that names nobody, routed to
    `everyone` or to the agents that asked that person, gives it none);
    `talk_again` ends the state. An agent
    whose speak policy also listens (Section 6.4) is silenced by either.
    Setting the state on the agent whose turn runs cuts that turn, as a
    `Cancel` steering directive does (Section 21.3), or, for an external
    agent, as its channel's cancellation does (Section 6.4): what the turn committed
    stays in the room; a turn given but not running yet, which no `Cancel`
    reaches, is abandoned before it runs. Talking again, its next turn reads
    the whole room (rule 9).
13. **Staying silent.** A turn a message asked for is submitted to the agent's
    speak policy, when it has one, as any event the agent would answer
    (Section 6.4); an instruction's turn is not, as Section 6.4 says. A
    `silent` decision runs no generation and ends the turn. Without a policy,
    or when the policy lets it speak, the model may stay silent itself: a text
    row of the turn whose only text is `silent_token`, ignoring case,
    surrounding whitespace, a final period and the brackets around the token
    if it has some, says nothing; a turn whose text rows all say nothing
    stayed silent. Its row is stored with `status = BLOCKED` and `blocked_by =
    "discussion_silent"`, read for no name and delivered nowhere: the start of
    a streamed answer is held back until its text can no longer be the token,
    since a streamed segment once delivered is not taken back (Section 6.4). A
    turn that ends with no text produces no row and says nothing too. A silent
    turn counts as a turn (rules 7 and 15).
14. **What a turn knows.** Each turn's notes (Section 6.4) carry, as the
    runtime's own block and not a participant's words: the agent's own
    handle, the other agents of the room by their handles, with the `name`,
    `role` and `description` of those
    that carry an identity (Agents, Section 19.1, and external agents given
    one, Section 6.4); the people the agent may address, by the
    names rule 4 gives them; which event the turn answers and who asked for
    it, a person's label and their words quoted (Section 6.4); and how the
    room works. That last part is the host's `rules` when the discussion has
    them, `{handle}` in them standing for another agent's handle with its `@`
    (an example the agent can follow) and `{silent}` for the silence token;
    without them, it is the default, which tells the agent to end its
    message with the handle of the agent that must act next, says that a
    name without `@` reaches nobody and a message that names nobody wakes
    nobody, and gives the silence token for when it has nothing to add.
    The rest of the notes, what the turn knows of the room, is the
    discussion's alone. That one agent speaks at a time is stated with the
    agent's own handle.
15. **The end.** The discussion is over once `done` holds, checked before each
    turn is given, or once `max_turns` turns were given in the room, from the
    moment the last of them is given. It gives no further turn and drops its
    queue; an instruction addressed to an agent afterwards, and a regenerated
    answer asked for afterwards, are refused, their result blocked with the
    reason `discussion_over`; a turn running then ends as it would; the room's later
    events are stored and delivered with no agent asked. `done` is the host's:
    a mission's state, a person's word, a budget. A host that wants the agents
    to answer again uninstalls the discussion (rule 1).
16. **Its state, across processes.** Installing a discussion stores it with the
    room, as `ConversationState` is (Section 19.2): its configuration (the
    agents' channel ids and their handles, `people`, `addressed_only`, `everyone`, `max_turns`,
    `max_depth`, `silent_token`, `rules`, whether it has a dispatch policy, and the
    agents its installs attached to the room) and its
    speak queue; a configuration stored without handles addresses each
    agent by its channel id. Every process that
    serves the room follows the stored discussion, whether or not its host
    installed it there: it asks no agent at broadcast (rule 3), and reads
    names and queues (rules 4, 5, 8, 10) by the stored configuration, read
    again once another process replaced it (rule 1). Every
    change of the queue is read and written under the room lock (Section
    13.5), so the processes that serve one room keep one queue, and the queue
    and the count of turns given outlive a restart. Uninstalling, in any
    process, one that only follows the discussion included, ends it in all of
    them, posts the task results the discussion took and has not committed
    (rule 19), then unbinds the agents its installs attached (a configuration
    stored without them names none). A process that gives no turn, because it only
    follows the discussion or its host installed another configuration, keeps
    no instruction and no task result for a turn: it reports the instruction
    dropped and posts the result at once.

    A process where the host installed the discussion may give its turns
    while the configuration its host installed is the stored one: a process
    whose host installed another (the stored one was replaced elsewhere) gives
    up the lease and only follows, until its host installs the stored one.
    `room_strategy_is_current(room_id, Discussion)` (Section 19.7) is how
    the host learns it. A host that finds it false installs the
    configuration it wants again while its own state still wants the
    discussion, so that a room no longer waits on a process that replaced it
    and stopped; it does not reinstall a discussion its own state no longer
    wants, which would bring back one another process uninstalled. One
    process at a time gives the turns: the one that holds the room's
    **lease**, stored with
    the queue with the time it expires (15 s by default). It gives the turns,
    renews the lease while it holds it, and another process that installed
    the discussion takes it once it has expired: a process that stopped gives
    up its turns that way, and its running turn has ended (rule 6). A process
    that queues a turn without holding the lease makes it known through the
    stored queue, which the holder reads again at least once a second; a
    change that concerns the running turn (its agent set to listen only, rule
    12) reaches the holder the same way. `speaking` is stored with the lease
    and names the holder's running turn. `done` is the host's and is checked
    by the process holding the lease, which asks its dispatch policy too
    (rule 18). A process that only follows the
    discussion never gives a turn: with no process that installed it alive,
    messages are queued and wait.

    A queued turn's instruction is kept in memory only, by the process that
    received it, as an instruction is stored nowhere (Section 10.1.1). Its
    entry names that process. When the turn comes and the holder is another
    process, the holder hands the lease over; an instruction whose process
    does not take the lease within one lease period is dropped. An
    instruction the discussion drops (it is over, uninstalled, or its process
    stopped) is reported through `ON_SPEAK_QUEUE` as dropped.
    A task's result to post (rule 19) is queued as an instruction is, its
    entry naming its holder; unlike an instruction, it is also kept, from when
    the discussion takes it until it is committed, with the room's private
    state (Section 14.1): its id, agent, chain depth and the message it posts,
    apart from the room's metadata, which a reader of the room gets whether or
    not the posted message's visibility (Section 7.3), or a hook that blocks
    it, would show it to them.
17. **Following the queue.** The host reads a room's `SpeakQueue` at any time,
    and each change of it fires `ON_SPEAK_QUEUE` (Section 9) with the room,
    the queue as it now is and what changed: an agent queued, a turn given or
    ended, a turn skipped as its agent is offline (rule 7), a queued
    instruction dropped, an agent listening only or talking
    again, the discussion waiting for a person or no longer waiting, the
    discussion over. The host's calls take the organization a room belongs to
    (Section 17.2): a room of another organization holds no discussion for it. A console
    that shows who speaks, who is next, who only listens and whether the
    discussion waits for a person follows it, and draws the room's agents from
    the room's intelligence bindings and the agents' identity (Section 19.1),
    each shown and named by its handle (rule 4): a command that names an
    agent reads the name as rule 4 does, and the queue's channel ids are
    shown as handles.
    A person's message returns once committed and broadcast, with no agent's
    answer in its result (Section 10.1 step 18): the answers come in the turns
    that follow, as a regenerated answer the discussion queued does.
18. **Who takes an unaddressed message.** A discussion MAY carry a dispatch
    policy, which decides, for a person's message with no address and no
    name (rule 8), which agents take it and in which order, or that none
    does. Without one, rule 8 gives that message to the agents that asked
    that person, else to `everyone`: a room where every agent is asked every
    remark spends turns on agents with nothing to add (each says nothing,
    rule 13, but its turn runs), the agent that should answer may come
    third, and an agent that asked the person a question takes the person's
    next message even when it answers nothing of it (a request for another
    agent, a thanks). The policy is asked for that message only: a message
    with an address, or that names an agent or only people, is routed as
    rule 8 says, and a discussion with `addressed_only`, where a message that
    names nobody asks no agent, takes no dispatch policy. A name stays the
    person's word: no policy overrides it.

    ```
    DispatchPolicy (interface)
    └── decide(turn: DispatchTurn) → DispatchDecision

    DispatchTurn
    ├── room_id: string
    ├── event: RoomEvent                    # The person's message
    ├── recent: list<RoomEvent>             # The conversation before it, oldest first: the room's messages a candidate may read
    ├── speakers: map<string, string>       # Who said `event` and each of `recent`, by event id: a person by their transcript label, an agent as `@handle`
    ├── candidates: list<DispatchCandidate> # The agents it may pick: those that asked the author first, then `everyone`'s order
    └── asked: list<channel_id>             # The candidates that asked the message's author and wait for the answer (rule 10)

    DispatchCandidate
    ├── channel_id: string
    ├── name: string | null                 # An Agent's identity (Section 19.1), as a turn's notes give it (rule 14)
    ├── role: string | null
    ├── description: string | null
    └── handle: string | null               # The name the room addresses it by (rule 4); null: its channel id

    DispatchDecision
    ├── agents: list<channel_id>            # Who takes the message, in the order they answer; empty: no agent
    ├── reason: string = ""                 # Why, in a few words, for logs and hooks
    └── judgments: map<string, float> = {}  # What the policy weighed, by name
    ```

    The candidates are the agents that asked that person, in the order they
    asked, then `everyone`, in its order, less the agents the message does
    not reach (its visibility and their access, rule 4) and those that only
    listen, which an unaddressed message gives no turn (rule 12). With no
    candidate, the policy is not asked and no agent is. The agents a decision
    names are put at the front of the queue in its order, as rule 8 puts
    `everyone`; one that is not a candidate, or named twice, is left out, so a
    policy is no way around visibility or the listening state. An empty
    decision asks no agent: the message is stored and delivered, and the
    discussion goes idle (rule 10). The recent events a policy reads are
    those a candidate may read: a policy may hand them to a classifier
    outside, and an event no candidate may read MUST NOT reach it that way.

    The decision is the room's, taken once per message, off the room lock, by
    the process holding the lease (rule 16): routing the message leaves it
    waiting for a decision in the stored queue, with the candidates it
    reaches, and the holder decides it before it gives another turn, so the
    agents a person's message asks for still come before the agents queued
    after it. Messages waiting are decided in the order they were committed;
    once the discussion is over, they are dropped with its queue (rule 15),
    and a process that stops while it decides leaves the message waiting for
    the next holder. At most 16 messages wait: past them, the oldest asks
    what it asks with no policy (below), undecided, so a room with no holder
    alive keeps a bounded queue. The discussion bounds
    the wait for a decision (`dispatch_timeout`, 5 s by default). A policy
    that fails, does not decide in time or returns no readable decision does
    not silence the room: the message asks what it asks with no policy, the
    candidates that asked its author, else every candidate, and the decision
    reported names them with the reason `fallback`; so does a process
    holding the lease whose host gave it no policy, and any failure in
    deciding.

    Every decision applied fires `ON_DISPATCH_DECISION` with the room, the
    message, the candidates, the decision and how long the policy took (the
    bound, when it did not decide in time), so who took what, why and at
    what cost can be followed and measured without wrapping the policy. A
    decision on a message another process decided first (it took the lease
    over meanwhile) is neither applied nor reported: each message is
    reported once. The decision is
    not stored with the message: its `addressed_to` stays null, and a
    regenerated answer to it with no answer left asks `everyone` (rule 7),
    not a new decision. An agent picked still answers through its speak
    policy, when it has one (rule 13).

    RoomKit provides a policy built on a classifier (Section 6.8). It asks one
    yes/no question per candidate, all in one call: whether that agent should
    take the message, given what each agent's identity says it does, over the
    message, its speaker and the recent conversation named by speaker; an
    agent that waits for the speaker's answer is marked as such, so that it
    is picked when the message answers it and not otherwise. The
    candidates whose probability reaches a threshold (0.5 by default) take it,
    likeliest first, at most a number of them (2 by default); with none
    reaching it, no agent takes it (thanks, small talk). Each candidate's
    probability is reported with the decision, under its channel id. Each
    candidate is presented to the classifier by its handle, the name the
    conversation it reads uses for it; an agent with no identity is judged
    by its handle alone.

19. **Talking and working.** A turn talks; long work runs as a task (Section
    23), off the floor. An agent given the background tool (Section 23.4)
    starts one and says once, in a sentence, that the work is under way, and
    its turn ends there; the host starts one for an agent with `start_task`,
    and a person through what the host gives them. Tasks run in parallel with
    the discussion's turns and with one another, and the floor stays one turn
    at a time: a question asked while a task runs is answered in its turn, not
    after the task. A task's result comes back as its hand-back, an
    instruction addressed to the agent the task is for, which the discussion
    queues at the front for a turn of its own (rule 7), results served in the
    order they come; a task cancelled or failed says so the same way (Section
    23.3). A posted result (`hand_back = "post"`) takes the same place, and
    its turn posts it as the agent's message without running the agent's
    model: it never cuts a turn under way, and the names it carries ask no
    one, its worker having written it outside the room. Each turn's notes list
    the room's tasks (Section 23.4), so an agent asked how a task goes answers
    from them, and `cancel_task` or the host's `cancel_task(task_id)` stops
    one. A worker runs in its own child room, outside the discussion, so an
    agent of the discussion may work through any intelligence channel, an
    external agent among them. A task outlives an uninstalled or ended
    discussion: a relayed hand-back is then an instruction like any other,
    refused once the discussion is over (rule 15), its result kept on
    `ON_TASK_COMPLETED` and the StatusBus; a posted result, which asks no
    turn, is posted once no turn runs, one queued when the discussion ends or
    is uninstalled included.

    Uninstalling, in any process, posts every result the discussion took and
    has not committed, whichever process holds it and whether it is queued,
    waits for the floor or is being committed, before it unbinds the agents
    its installs attached: a posted result is the agent's message, committed
    through its binding (Section 23.3) and through the hooks of the process
    that uninstalls, so every process serving a room registers the same hooks.
    It waits for no commit under way: a host that uninstalls while it holds
    the room lock, which that commit needs, has the result posted by the
    uninstall itself. A result's idempotency key is the id the discussion took
    it under, not the id of the message it commits (Section 13.4): the post
    that comes second, the holder's own once it learns of the uninstall (its
    agent detached by then included) or the commit under way once the lock is
    released, is a replay and stores nothing. A result a closing process did
    not post, or whose post failed, stays kept, and nothing posts it before
    the next uninstall, not the process that gives the next turn nor a
    restarted process that installs the discussion again: it then comes after
    the room's later messages, and a discussion never uninstalled never posts
    it. One committed but still kept, whose message was deleted for good
    meanwhile (Section 10.3), is posted again, its key gone with it.

The rules of Section 19.7 for a strategy in several rooms hold: the speak
queue and who only listens are the room's, and the same agents may hold a
discussion in another room with a speak queue of its own.

requirements.applies: §19.7.5 Discussion; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**Left out of this version.** Voice: a turn would end when its playback
ends, which no event reports yet; a person speaking names no one with `@`;
an agent's written names would be spoken. Realtime channels, whose turns run
outside the room's queue, and agents that think while they listen, which
need every event without a turn. The room's tools for an external agent:
its tools are its own (its workspace, what its agent accepts), and this
version wires none of the room's into it. One turn at a time: work that does not need the
floor runs as tasks (rule 19), but turns themselves never run in parallel,
each reading a room the others' answers would have changed. The text an agent writes between tool rounds still
reaches the room as messages; only the names they carry wait for the turn's
end. An approval a person gives for one production change is a tool's
concern (Section 21), and a mission's shared state is the host's (`done`).
An agent that asked a person may still be named by another agent before the
person answers. A dispatch policy decides for a person's message only: an
agent's message that names nobody still asks no agent. Threads (`parent_event_id`): an agent's answer already stays
in the thread of the event it answers, but this version keeps one queue for
the room and gives every turn the whole room; a later version makes each
thread a conversation of its own (its own queue and chains, a turn reading
its thread with the room before it as background, an agent taking one turn
at a time across the room).

requirements.text: **Conformance.** Level 2, with the rest of Section 19.

requirements.applies: §19.8 StatusBus; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
The `StatusBus` enables inter-agent coordination through status messages:

```
StatusBus (interface)
├── post(agent_id, action, status, detail = "", metadata = null) → StatusEntry
│       # Publishes without waiting for the subscribers
├── post_async(agent_id, action, status, detail = "", metadata = null) → StatusEntry
│       # Waits for the subscribers
├── subscribe(callback) → void              # callback(StatusEntry) on every post
├── unsubscribe(callback) → void
├── recent(n = 10, agent_id = null, status = null) → list<StatusEntry>
│       # Most recent entries, optionally filtered
├── recent_text(n = 10) → string            # Recent entries as text, for an agent's context
├── has_completed(agent_id = null) → bool
│       # Whether a COMPLETED entry is among the last 50 completed ones
└── close() → void

StatusEntry
├── ts: string                              # RFC 3339 time of the post, in UTC (§1.4)
├── agent_id: string
├── action: string                          # What the agent is doing or did
├── status: StatusLevel                     # OK, FAILED, PENDING, INFO, COMPLETED
├── detail: string = ""
└── metadata: map<string, any>              # room_id here names the entry's room
```

`StatusLevel` values are written `ok`, `failed`, `pending`, `info` and
`completed`. One bus serves the framework; an entry names its room, if any, in
`metadata.room_id`. The framework's own posts bound `detail`, a summary for
whoever follows the bus: cut at a word, the cut ending in `…`, never in the
middle of a word or a number. A `completed` entry whose detail was cut keeps the
whole outcome in `metadata.result`, bounded at 4,000 characters and its cut
marked the same way: an agent reads an outcome back from it (Section 23.4),
never from the summary, which once turned a 14.9 °C forecast into "1". Status posts fire `ON_STATUS_POSTED` hooks in that room; an
entry that names no room reaches no room's hooks. The framework follows its bus
from its first room activity on, which waits for the subscription when the
backend's does not end at once: an entry posted once that activity is over
reaches the room's hooks. The hooks fire at least as
deep as the work that posted, read as it posts (§8.3): what a hook sends into
the room is that deep, so a hook that tells the posting agent again ends at
the depth limit. They fire during the framework's close too, until it seals
its store (Section 12.10.4): the end of a task the close cuts reaches them. Its framework event,
`status_posted` (§8.2), is the bus's and names no room, whichever room the
entry names: a reader finds that room in the entry's `metadata.room_id`. Agents MAY use the StatusBus to
signal completion, progress, or request attention without sending room events.
The framework posts each delegated task on the bus (Section 23.3), and an agent
reads its room's tasks through the `task_status` tool (Section 23.4); an agent is
never pointed at a tool it was not given.

requirements.applies: §20 Memory System; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
The Memory System provides pluggable AI context construction. Instead of
always using a fixed sliding window of recent events, implementations MAY
choose different strategies for building conversation history.

requirements.applies: §20.1 MemoryProvider Interface; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
```
MemoryProvider (interface)
├── retrieve(room_id, current_event, context, channel_id) → MemoryResult
│       # Build conversation context for AI generation
│       # Called by AIChannel before each generation
│
├── compact(room_id, history, usage, channel_id) → list<AIMessage> | null
│       # The history to send in place of `history` between two tool rounds
│       # Called by AIChannel after each tool round it ran; null by default
│
└── close() → void
        # Release resources
```

A provider is handed history, it does not fetch it: the `context` it receives
MUST already be the requesting channel's view of the room (§7.5 rule 8). Making
each provider apply the visibility filter itself would put the rule in five
places and leave every third-party provider outside it; making the caller apply
it once puts it in one, and a provider that summarizes what it is given can then
never summarize something the channel was not allowed to read.

The `current_event` is the event the turn answers, and what the turn reads
MUST keep it whatever the provider's window or budget: when events follow it
in the `context` (a discussion's deferred turn, Section 19.7.5), it reads at
its place in the history, before them, and is never folded into a summary. A
provider returns it there, or leaves it out as it does a turn's input and the
channel places it there; either way a window cannot drop it, which would
leave the model answering an event it cannot read.

`compact` is how a memory keeps a long tool turn within its window, which a
read at the turn's start cannot (Section 6.4, "The history compacted between
two rounds"): `history` is what the turn sends before its input, `usage` the
token counters of the round's generation, disjoint, as its provider reported
them (empty when it reported none). A provider that does not define it answers
nothing, and the turn is left as it is. A provider that wraps another and
does not compact itself hands the call to the one it wraps.

requirements.applies: §20.2 MemoryResult; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
```
MemoryResult
├── messages: list<AIMessage>               # Pre-built AI messages (summaries, instructions)
├── events: list<RoomEvent>                 # Raw events for AIChannel to convert
├── notes: list<string>                     # What was retrieved for this turn alone
└── speakers: list<string>                  # The labels the messages name participants by
```

When `messages` is non-empty, the AIChannel uses them directly as conversation
history. When `events` is provided, the AIChannel converts them to AI messages
using its standard conversion logic. Both MAY be combined — `messages` are
prepended before converted `events`. A user text the `messages` end on joins
the user message that follows it, a blank line between, rather than standing
as a second user message in a row, or, before no user message, stands as a
user message of its own, its text alone; a system message stays a message of
its own.

`speakers` names the participants the `messages` speak of by the labels they
use (a summary's lines, `Alice`, `@sms`): each counts as a speaker toward
labelling the turns (Section 6.4), unless a turn's speaker already has it, so a
conversation a summary named several people in reads as labelled turns.

`notes` carries what a provider retrieved for the current turn only, knowledge
passages for one: it changes from one turn to the next, so it rides the turn's
notes (Section 6.4), after the input, and never the history, which a provider
that caches a prefix would otherwise bill again at every turn. A provider that
wraps another and rebuilds its result MUST carry the inner provider's `notes`,
and one that keeps the turn within a token budget MUST count them: nothing
trims the turn's notes, so the history is what makes room for them.

requirements.applies: §20.3 Built-in Implementations; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
| Implementation | Strategy | Use Case |
|---|---|---|
| SlidingWindowMemory | Last N events | Default, simple conversations |
| CompactingMemory | Merges older events into compact summaries | Long conversations, reduce tokens |
| SummarizingMemory | AI-powered summarization of history | Complex multi-topic conversations |
| RetrievalMemory | Knowledge sources queried with the turn's text | Knowledge-backed answers (RAG) |
| BudgetAwareMemory | Token-based truncation with priorities | Strict token budget enforcement |

requirements.applies: §20.3 Built-in Implementations; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**SlidingWindowMemory** is the default when no MemoryProvider is configured.
It returns the most recent `max_context_events` events of the room as the
channel reads it, the turn's event the newest among them, which the channel
places as the input: the turn reads at most one fewer before it. The agent's
tool rows are not counted: its earlier rounds are replayed apart, at their
place (Section 6.4).

requirements.applies: §20.3 Built-in Implementations; the source unit and enclosing sections retain their capability conditions, defaults, exceptions and planned status. Conformance levels are declared in §26.
requirements.text:
**SummarizingMemory** calls an AI provider to summarize older history,
keeping recent events intact: each older turn is read on one line after its
author's label, and the summary's message stands for them, a user text joined
to the turn after it. The summary is cached and refreshed
periodically or when the event count exceeds a threshold. Its thresholds are
shares of what its `max_context_tokens` leaves once the turn's footprint
(below), its reply budget included, and the current event are paid for: past
the first it shortens the older events' long texts, past the second it
summarizes them, and the messages, notes and events it returns are then cut,
from the oldest event, to what is left, its latest event always kept.
Between two tool rounds it compacts once the round's counters, summed, pass its
second threshold taken as a share of `max_context_tokens`: a model summarizes
the history's older messages, each text read on one line after its role, a
call after the tool it names and its arguments, a result after its tool, and
the latest messages are kept whole, those that fit what the history must give
back to come under the threshold once the summary's tokens are paid for, its
`min_events` latest at least, a call's results never kept without their call.
A summary the history still holds as a memory's message, its provenance kept,
is carried into the new one; a summary the channel placed in the turn, joined
to a user message or standing as a user message of its own, its text alone,
is read as one of the messages. Its first threshold does not apply between
rounds, and the memory it wraps is not asked.
